item.title: 93% of Paint Splatters Are Valid Perl Programs (2019)
item.author: zenincognito
item.content:encoded: In this paper, we aim to answer a long-standing open problem in the programming languages community: is it possible to smear paint on the wall without creating valid Perl?We answer this question in the affirmative: it to smear paint on the wall without creating a valid Perl program. We employ an empirical approach, using optical character recognition (OCR) software, which finds that merely 93% of paint splatters parse as valid Perl. We analyze the properties of paint-splatter Perl programs, and present seven examples of paint splatters which are not valid Perl programs.Accepted for publication at SIGBOVIK 2019, held April 1st 2019 in Pittsburgh. Winner of a Unwitting Participation Ribbon, “an unwelcome brand we’ve affixed to each paper determined after careful scrutiny to have included a genuine artifact, thereby furthering the admirable causes of open science and fruitful procrastination.”Here’s all the paint splatters on a single page, along with the valid Perl source code corresponding to each. “Not valid” is written in red for those images which did not parse as valid Perl programs. If different OCR settings recognized multiple valid Perl programs, I chose the one that seemed the most “interesting”, according to my own aesthetic sense.(source code not available yet because i am bad at GitHub)There are a few paint splatter Perl programs that I didn’t recognize as “interesting” until after the SIGBOVIK submission deadline. For example, this splatter is recognized by OCR as the string , which evaluates to the number in Perl:The image below is recognized as the string , which also evaluates to the number in Perl:Another surprising program is shown below; OCR recognizes this image as the string , which evaluates to the string in Perl:Finally, this image is recognized as the string , which evaluates to the string in Perl:

item.title: Lock Your GitHub Actions
item.author: gslin
item.content:encoded:
Because GitHub Actions are fetched from Git, the previous advice was to pin to a full SHA instead of a tag. This is because tags are mutable and susceptible to supply-chain attacks where an attacker points a previously safe tag at malicious code.For example, an old workflow looks like:Here’s how I set up lockfiles.The workflow now uses tags and looks like this:And it generates a lockfile at .github/workflows/actions.lock:Commit modified workflows and the new lockfile.They suggest copying this
into your repo. I decided to put it into my existing lint workflow, but in its own job so it runs independently and in parallel:Note I’m using the lightweight runner here. Also, it’s pinning to v0.4.1; we’ll have to update that at some point or figure out a way to automate it. That’s for another time.Don’t forget that we just modified the actions in a workflow, so need to relock with . Nothing actually changes if adding to because it’s already locking . But if you created a new file like , you’ll need to relock for that. The CI will let you know.zizmor is a security linter for GitHub Actions and . If you don’t use it, please do.Versions before v1.32.0 tell you to hash-pin actions, and v1.32.0 is the first to support lockfiles.I use zizmor in prek, so add/update zizmor in :

item.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
item.author: herpderperator
item.content:encoded: United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as and to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances."As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group. "United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app. United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline.""But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

item.title: Gemini Decisions API
item.author: iamdelirium
item.content:encoded: Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one passBuilt on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer: Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria.choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate. Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities.The field uses the same block format as the Interactions API. Here is how to check a photo of a breakroom counter, together with a text note, against all three question types in one request:

item.title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
item.author: zerop
item.content:encoded: Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query.As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution — a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs — rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs — is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently.In Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions, a paper presented at ICML 2026, researchers from Apple train small neural networks (NNs) — once, offline, for a fixed database of keys — that learn how to route queries toward their best match faster. Their approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time through these small NNs.A fundamental principle in MIPS is to leverage the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search: Typical MIPS systems split the set of keys into clusters — is typically much smaller than the total number of keys — keeping track of a representative centroid for each cluster. When receiving a new query, the system compares it with these centroids. The query is then routed toward the cluster of the representative centroid it is closest to, and subsequently compared exhaustively with all keys stored in that cluster. If the database has keys and evenly distributed clusters, the effective number of keys that will be considered in that second step is on the order of / — a factor-of- speedup when compared to the comparisons done in the naive exhaustive approach. Unfortunately, this routing mechanism can result in errors, since centroid routing is not an exact approach, as illustrated in Figure 1 below.Figure 1: Geometric approaches to search can fail and miss nearest neighbors. This is due to their reliance on partitioning the space based on distances to centroids. In the animation, a nearest neighbor is missed as it is not associated with the nearest centroid.What makes MIPS interesting from a machine learning perspective is that it is built on a mathematical structure that had been largely overlooked before this work: The function that maps a query to the largest inner product with any key in a set is the support function of that set, a well-studied object in convex analysis. This function has two important properties: First, it is convex, so it can be approximated by a class of neural networks specifically designed for convex functions, input convex neural networks (ICNNs). Second, the gradient of that support function at any query returns the best-matching key itself.The broad idea behind this work is to a neural network that can mimic the ground-truth support function (or its gradient directly) for a much lower computational cost. This can be achieved through a classical ML technique known as regression: one simply needs to precompute a large number of training examples formed by sampling input vectors (user queries) and pair them with the relevant output signal produced by MIPS (either the optimal score or the optimal key vector itself). All that is then needed is to train a suitably parameterized neural network to replicate the output given the input.If the regression problem were to be solved perfectly, according to the mathematical approach outlined above, the same neural network that is trained to mimic the support function could also output the optimal key by evaluating its gradient (through automatic differentiation). In practice, we observe that training separate, specialized networks for each of these two tasks works best:The neural network architecture can learn the support function directly, using a (loosely constrained) ICNN. The approach is mathematically principled and aligns with the convex structure of the problem. We find that this approach can shine when used to compute one support function per data cluster to improve routing quality. models learn to output the best-matching key vector when fed a query. A consistency loss derived from Euler’s theorem for homogeneous functions keeps their predictions geometrically grounded in the underlying support function, even though no convexity is explicitly enforced.Both models are trained on examples drawn from the relevant query distribution: for each sampled query, the ground-truth best match is computed once via exhaustive search and stored, creating a supervised dataset that captures the MIPS solution landscape for the distribution of queries that actually matter.As shown in Figure 1, the simplest way to handle larger scales is to split the keys into clusters, compare the query to each cluster’s centroid, and route the query to the most promising clusters based on these scores. This provides a cheap yet coarse rule that can be prone to mistakes because a centroid alone cannot account for the spread of its cluster. Indeed, a cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to the query, and when the query is near such an outlier, centroid routing scores the cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match.If one were given access to the support function of each cluster, then one would instead be able to do exact routing, since each support function quantifies exactly to what extent any key within each cluster can match the query with a large score. This is illustrated in Figure 2, in which the support function of each of the four clusters is plotted for a query that varies in the space of embeddings.Figure 2: Relying on distances to centroids can be misleading as those distances do not account for every key in each cluster. Given access to each cluster’s support function, assignment can be made based on how well a given query matches any key in a cluster.Leaning on this theoretical insight, we propose to learn these support functions jointly with a trained SupportNet that can output scores at once. We can then use the largest of these scores to route any new query instead. The SupportNet model can answer a more useful question than a simple comparison to the centroid can: “How good is the key inside this cluster for this query?” SupportNets are trained in a classic machine learning fashion, also known as regression: we generate sample queries that are drawn from the distribution (typically embeddings for text queries), compute the ground-truth support functions at those queries, and train a neural network to replicate these values.Figure 3: SupportNets approximate the support functions of each cluster and assign queries to clusters based on the best match with any key, not only centroids as typical geometric approaches do.We trained SupportNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L → 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) on Natural Questions partitioned into 128 clusters. Natural Questions is a retrieval benchmark that pairs general-knowledge questions with passages from a large document database, roughly 2.6M unique passages in our setup.Figure 4 below shows the retrieval performance in terms of recall as a function of different notions of cost. Routing recall is the fraction of queries whose true partition, the one holding the exact best key, lands among those the router chooses to probe. For both plots, an exhaustive search is carried out in the top- clusters matched with the query, where grows as powers of two . Naturally, all methods reach a recall of 1 when they survey all 128 clusters.The first tab shows that for a fixed retrieval performance the learned routers reach it at lower latency than centroid routing. The small SupportNet model hits 95% routing recall about 1.9× faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms), and gains are even greater with the large model, which hits 97% in 1.74 ms. This plot explicitly factors in the additional compute incurred by running our small NNs rather than simply comparing to centroids.The plot on the second tab looks exclusively at routing quality, neglecting the overhead incurred by running NNs. At a fixed budget of explored clusters, they find the right partition more often: scanning just 5% of the database, the learned routers recover the true partition ~90–93% of the time — up to 92.6% for the mid-size (M) — versus 87.5% for the centroid baseline.SupportNet Router Size FamilyFigure 4: Routing performance (recall) due to SupportNets of various sizes versus latency or the fraction of the database we allow the router to scan. Routers, all with a depth of 16 layers, are trained on a 128-cluster Natural Questions dataset. SupportNets dominate the centroid router: given a latency target, one can get a higher recall with a SupportNet or conversely, that recall can be achieved at lower latency by a SupportNet than by a centroid router.SupportNet routing replaces the simple centroid-based routing found in existing inverted file index (IVF) systems. With KeyNet, we can also keep the IVF system as is and just feed it a modified version of the query. In that scenario, KeyNet works naturally as a in front of a standard approximate search index: predict where the best match is likely to be in embedding space, then ask your favorite IVF system to look there instead of starting from the original query. Because the IVF index is highly optimized, it can find the result faster when assisted by KeyNet. We also rely on regression to train KeyNets, as summarized in Figure 5: sample queries are matched with their ground-truth, best-matching key, and the KeyNet neural network is trained to reproduce that association.Figure 5: KeyNets are trained to map a query to its best match in a database. Combined with an IVF index, pre-processing queries via such a mapping makes search much easier: the resulting transformed query is now much closer to the target it is intended to retrieve.We evaluated KeyNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L → 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) and in Figure 6 below, we show recall–cost tradeoffs for these different sizes. On the first tab, the search budget is wall-clock latency: reaching 99% recall takes up to ~8× less time with the largest model (0.23 ms vs 1.8 ms for the raw query). As before, the second tab focuses exclusively on the boost in “quality” provided by replacing the original query with its KeyNet transformation. The x-axis is the fraction of the database the index actually scans: scanning just 0.001% of the database, KeyNet-mapped queries retrieve the true key 89–97% of the time — up to 96.7% for the largest model (L) — versus 86% for the raw query, and reaching 99% recall takes up to ~11× fewer keys (0.009% vs 0.10% raw). Better recall for the same cost, or the same recall for a fraction of it.KeyNet Searcher Size FamilyFigure 6: Search performance (recall) using an IVF index to search a database made from the Natural Questions dataset. The plots compare results due to querying the IVF index directly with raw queries against a search executed after mapping queries with KeyNets of various sizes, all with a fixed depth of 16 layers. Latency in the plots corresponds to the total time required to map a query and search, except for the raw-query case, which accounts only for search. Pre-processing queries with KeyNet is worth it no matter the size: the pre-processing overhead is compensated for by faster search downstream. We show examples obtained from the same Natural Questions dataset discussed previously, served through a FAISS IVF index. It is one of several datasets we studied, and the trend is consistent across them. Querying the index with KeyNet’s predicted key consistently beats querying with the raw question, across the full search-budget sweep.Namely, Figure 7 below shows five Natural Questions examples: top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query.The choice between the two ends up being a practical one. Use when inference speed is the bottleneck and you just need to approximate the best key. Use when you also want a calibrated score (for re-ranking, thresholding, or downstream use), or when compute is tight at small model sizes — a regime where SupportNet stays competitive. Both train similarly, integrate with existing approximate-search infrastructure, and are reasonably robust to mild distribution shift in the query patterns. Ultimately, a very large-scale MIPS system for which the set of keys is huge may require both: train a SupportNet router over all clusters, and then one KeyNet per cluster to help its regular indices zero in on the best key faster.Amortized MIPS reflects a shift in how retrieval can be approached when query distributions are known in advance — a common condition in production ML systems. By encoding MIPS solutions directly into network weights, the approach trades a one-time training (so-called ) cost for fast, lightweight inference and opens a practical path toward learned retrieval systems explicitly tailored to the queries they serve.

item.title: A false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
item.author: mbac32768
item.content:encoded: Published on 10 Nov 2026 by mbacarella A war story from Jane Street's systems team: a false smoke alarm, a datacenter with no cooling, and a sprint to pull every power cord before the sprinklers went offAI disclosure: this story was written entirely by human hands, with AI doing proof-reading and light edits. Some tasteful imperfections kept to heighten Wabi-Sabi effect.Everyone’s heard of how awesome Jane Street is. Fewer people have heard about the times something stupid nearly put it out of business and it was saved by grit and dumb luck. I was on the systems team for some of those. Jane Street didn’t do titles, and we on the systems team weren’t above getting our hands dirty. You could think of us as the firm’s blue-collar OCaml programmers: when something broke, we were the ones running through the corridors to fix it. Call this story a Star Trek: Lower Decks view of Jane Street.For the longest time Jane Street insisted on having its machine room close to its trading floor. When it was 10 people it was cute. When it was 150 people it was starting to feel… odd. Part of the reason for this was intellectual property concern: they didn’t want to risk having their servers stolen by spies who would learn their precious trading strategies. Another reason was technology risk: they wanted to make sure out-of-control automated trading systems could always be shut down by running across the hall and pulling power cables.Yes, tools existed to mitigate both of these fears. But Jane Street moved irritatingly slowly on this stuff, and they still wanted the last-resort option of yanking power cords. Their risk culture didn’t exclusively come from reading heady thinkpieces. A lot of it was instilled by a partner who’d served on a nuclear submarine, and it showed, mostly in a good way! On a sub, you don’t trust the automation unless there’s a big red-painted, mechanically connected lever you can pull to turn it off.As the company grew this humble machine room was built out into a respectably sizable datacenter, complete with an online UPS, Computer Room Air Conditioner (CRAC) units, refrigerator-sized network switches, a subterranean diesel backup generator and about 10 rows of server cabinets, 10 cabinets deep. Oh, and it was all crammed into the middle of a skyscraper called 1 New York Plaza, which was otherwise just a normal office building.When I first landed my job at Jane Street I was commuting to the southern tip of Manhattan all of the way from Queens, an hour or more each way. I’d gone to a magnet high school in the city, so I’d been doing commutes like that since I was a teenager, and I was tired of it.Now that I was making big Wall Street money I decided I’d get an apartment. A real estate agent kept trying to show me what they called “panty droppers”, but I was only interested in one thing: proximity to the office. I ended up in a 200 square foot studio that was a 9 minute commute on foot from my apartment door to my desk on the trading floor. I would weirdly boast about it to the rest of the systems team, but it also meant everyone at the office knew I was a stone’s throw away in case there was an emergency.And that day came soon enough. One evening after work, just as I was about to climb into the elevator at my apartment building, my phone rang. It was our Hong Kong office, and when Hong Kong had a New York problem, mine was (now) the number they called. The smoke alarm in our NYC datacenter had gone off.We had contractors working on a prep room next to the datacenter. While cutting into stuff, some dust was kicked up and it set off the smoke alarm. This is bad, but not for the reason you might think. Office buildings have sprinklers in them for fire suppression. You may have seen it go off in movies where someone just holds a lit cigarette up to the sprinkler on the ceiling and it floods the entire room. In reality they’re not quite that dumb, but it’s close.Firstly, the sprinklers over a machine room like ours usually aren’t kept full of water all of the time. This saves you from having to deal with any leaks that might develop overhead over the years. Secondly, the sprinkler heads don’t have smoke sensors. Instead, a different system detects the smoke, and that’s when the pipes fill with pressurized water, but they don’t spray yet. What triggers the spray is heat: each sprinkler head has its own heat-sensitive plug, which opens once the air around it becomes hot enough. The logic is that the smoke alarm must be real, whatever fire triggered it hasn’t been brought under control since it’s gotten very hot, and the sprinklers should douse it with water.Of course, the ceiling of our datacenter was full of sprinklers set up exactly this way. We’re still fine because even though contractors might have set the smoke detector off by kicking up dust, there’s no actual fire producing heat, so the sprinklers wouldn’t spray, right? Well, no. One final piece of this contraption is that if the smoke alarm detects smoke, it would be absolutely terrible to keep circulating air through the room since that would help feed any fires, so the smoke alarm is wired to shut down the CRAC units(!)Can you see the problem now? Rooms full of computer racks have high cooling demands. If you shut down the cooling, the temperature starts climbing. If you have a bunch of sprinklers that have just become pressurized because of a smoke alarm, you now have a serious, potentially business-ending problem on your hands.And so my mission was made clear: as fast as I possibly could, get back to Jane Street, get into the machine room, and pull the power cord on every device in that room before the temperature climbed past 150 F and the sprinklers destroyed everything.I ran down the (ironically named) Water Street in the Financial District faster than probably anyone has ever run down it, mashed the elevator button in the lobby of 1 NYP, waited very impatiently for the elevator to climb the 33 floors, slammed my keycard against the reader, booked through the main office door, took a hard right turn to the machine room door, slammed my keycard against that, stepped into what felt like a sauna and went row by row, cabinet by cabinet, yanking power cables out with both hands.Then I watched the temperature monitor. 141 F. 142. 143. 143.5. 143.6. Finally it stopped. A quiet I’d never heard before set in on the machine room.The machine room had been kept across the hall so that someone could always run in and pull the power cords. I doubt anyone had pictured doing it to save the servers from the goddamn sprinklers.Since the major NYC markets were closed for the day, the downtime from this fiasco was minimal, and we were up and running the next morning.There were a couple of meetings after that. You might picture Gordon Gekko coldly deciding whose career was over, but meetings at Jane Street were never like that. They were matter-of-fact, level-headed and honestly kind of fun, closer to engineering students in a college dorm arguing over what went wrong. The outcome of all that level-headed discussion: the sprinklers would stay, we would tighten up procedures and surveillance, and we would continue hosting servers in our office building right next to our trading floor. That is, until Hurricane Sandy smacked us upside the head, but that’s a story for another day.As for me, when the next morning came around I knew what had to be done. Our Hong Kong team had only caught the problem by luck: someone happened to see on a display that server after server was popping up a climbing temperature condition. No one server was configured to alert just because it was a little hot, since that happens from time to time. But an across the board increase in temperature on many servers means there’s a generalized cooling failure.What we needed was a system monitor built for this exact purpose, one we could trust to be ultimately, unfailingly reliable at the task of asking each Linux server for its temperature and computing a simple mean. Bash wouldn’t cut it for this. Nor would Perl. No, a job of this magnitude called for the most reliable and type-safe programming language imaginable. So I fired up emacs and wrote it in good old OCaml: every minute, ask every server in each location directly for the temperature from its onboard sensors, take the average, and if it’s elevated, blast an alert out to everyone on the systems team to check for datacenter overheat.Yes, we could have also alerted if the CRAC units shut down or if a dedicated temperature sensor in the room was high, but the telemetry for this stuff was nowhere near as reliable, and unknown unknowns can still ruin you, so the most durable thing sometimes really is to ask your fleet of Linux boxes for their temperature and freak out if the average is just a little too high.Our team didn’t interact much with the partner with the nuclear sub experience, but I’d like to think he would have approved.

item.title: Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available)
item.author: ambewas
item.content:encoded: I've been developing applications for a long time and have turned to game development as well lately. One of the things that frustrated me the most was that using AI agents for game development is very annoying in the art department. Your only options right now are to either use an image genAI model and roll the dice every time you want to make an edit, or have your agent draw with something like vectors.I was looking for an application that would allow me to ask an agent to make a first draft of whatever art I needed with actual brushes, and then be able to go in myself and edit every last stroke or layer that it created.Klad is that application. Written in Rust, it can be fully controlled by an agent through the CLI, and every function is available in a nice UI as well: a brush engine, frame-by-frame animation (and bones/IK), vectors, text layers, colours, layer effects, infinite undo (even after re-opening the file!),…Why I think it's useful for a wider audience: Adobe showed agents editing Photoshop files at MAX this week, with a private beta planned for early 2027.Klad is built on the same core idea, with editable paint strokes as core architecture, and it works today.You can basically point Claude to the repo, ask it to build it, and pick up the drawing skills. Then ask it to make any drawing you want! (After that, you or the agent can change absolutely every brush stroke in the app again, which makes edits a breeze.)The quality of the drawings really depends on the agent you use. I have tried it with Claude Fable 5.2 since it came out on Monday, and the drawings are already quite impressive. I'm confident that this will only improve.I use it every day on Mac, so that definitely works well. It builds on Linux too (tablet pen pressure still needs some work there). Windows builds in CI, I haven't used it there myself yet but I have some reports that it works perfectly fine.Coming up next is support for pixel art. I'm in the testing phase with this right now, and I expect it to go live in the repo sometime this weekend.Klad is source-available rather than open source: free to build and use for individuals and small companies, and I plan to sell pre-built binaries later, the way Aseprite does. The file format, CLI reference and agent skill are MIT.What I want to hear from people who try it: Can your agent work out the CLI without help, and where does it get confused? Can you go in and change one of its strokes easily?I'll be here answering any questions about the technical side as well, as it's a pretty interesting challenge to build a performant engine with editable brush strokes that render as paint.

item.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
item.author: brownrout
item.content:encoded: Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings.Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer.As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman.I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy.To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp).I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use.Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

item.title: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
item.author: linsomniac
item.content:encoded: Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machineStart a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex on another machine — with all context intact. Install, then run Over the past year or two, how I use my terminal has changed dramatically. For years I was the sole user of my shell, and everything in my Atuin history was authored by me. Now, more than half the commands running on my machines weren’t written by me.These days, much of my work happens through a coding agent, typed into a little “Topsy-turvying” text box. But while my shell history follows me everywhere, my agent sessions do not. They're scattered across different tools and machines (a laptop, a dev server, ephemeral instances on exe.dev, a surprisingly cheap bare metal box in Germany), difficult to search, and often forgotten once I've moved on.I started working on Atuin because the history of my work was ephemeral: every command I typed was destined to vanish on line 501 of . But once this work became indexed, everlasting, and easy to recall, I could find the exact command I’d used to fix something years ago, in seconds.Over the years, this data compounded. It became the history of all of my work, the record of how I solved problems and built things.Shell history has always been an excellent record of what happened, but it’s only the surface. It never kept the reasoning… or the intentions behind what I was trying to do. I could only find a command if I remembered a part of it, though often I remembered what I was trying to achieve more readily.Agent sessions store the lot of it. Every command, its output, my intent, and everything I tried along the way to the eventual solution. It’s all there, in plain English, in my home directory! But just as with shell history all those years ago, we don’t put it to work.That is why we built Atuin Threads.Starting with Atuin 18.24, you can search your agent sessions across machines, resume them anywhere, or fork the session into a different agent harness. Start something in Claude Code on a dev server, then finish it in Codex on your laptop.Behind the scenes, this was a natural extension of Atuin. We put a lot of time and effort into building a reliable, encrypted sync engine. It’s generic, and can sync anything that can be modelled as an append-only log. As it turns out, most AI sessions are exactly this.Like shell history, Threads is end-to-end encrypted when synced, so we can't read your sessions. You can use our hosted sync server, run your own, or keep everything local. Capturing agent sessions is opt-in, too.Run , and after setting up, you will see the TUI from the top of this post!It doesn’t matter which agent you started with - you can resume it anywhere. With Atuin’s sync, this works across devices, and keeps your history backed up forever.with more agents coming soon.With MCP, agents can search and reference previous sessions themselves. They can find work you’ve done before, understand why a decision was made, and build on previous investigations without having to dig up the context.Our MCP is available as , and can be automatically installed withatuin mcp install claude/codex/pi/opencode There are all sorts of ways to put this history to work. A few examples:I’ve iterated on our onboarding and setup so many times over the past few months, but never quite been happy with it. When I ask an agent to work on onboarding now, it finds all my previous attempts, as well as why they had been abandoned and what can be done better.These sessions contain the code that never made it into , as well as my initial prompts and iteration. Subsequent agents can use this to figure out exactly what I want, without me having to write up a giant spec.With all the security issues going on in the industry recently, we rolled our keys as a precaution. One of the new object store keys did not have the correct permissions for avatar uploads! We didn’t notice straight away 😬My daily Sentry triage agent picked up on it, and traced the failure down to a command run earlier that day. I hadn’t gotten around to reading it yet, but prompting another agent withseeing some tigris avatar issues?led to the agent discovering the previous investigation, highlighting the cause, and developing the fix much faster than if it had done the whole thing from scratch.Forking threads across machinesBefore releasing Threads, I did some testing on a variety of machines and setups.One machine did not perform well. The agent investigating proposed that this was because of poor IO performance, but that it needed something with a faster disk to confirm.I forked the session onto my MacBook, and it continued from exactly where it left off. With the faster SSD, the investigation concluded that slow disk was only part of the story - we could speed up imports elsewhere, too.Once the benchmarks were complete, the thread running on the original machine could pull the results from the Mac and build a fix. I didn’t have to copy-paste anything or co-ordinate across machines, and the data is now part of the record of my work.While this is tremendously useful as a solo engineer, it gets even more interesting with a team.So much of what we do never makes it into Git, issue trackers, or documentation. The context behind that work ends up scattered across individual agent sessions. What if the rest of the team could learn from it too? What if we could hand off an agent thread just like a Git branch?We’re building opt-in session sharing for teams, and would love to hear from folks using agents day to day. If this sounds useful to you, please get in touch!While agents have radically changed my daily workflow, shell history isn’t going anywhere, and is arguably more useful than ever. Threads is an extension of the same idea that started Atuin in the first place - the history of your work should be useful, accessible, and yours to keep.Threads is out in Atuin 18.24+Install or update Atuin with curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://setup.atuin.sh | shRun to get startedUse the MCP with Please don’t hesitate to reach out with any questions or feedback!

item.title: Apple is killing its Support Community forum next week
item.author: saikatsg
item.content:encoded: “The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site. We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.”

item.title: I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
item.author: Brajeshwar
item.content:encoded: Every TV company is spying on you, not just LG. Like other tech companies, they collect lots of information, and while some is necessary for products to work, not all of it is — and could include details you’d prefer to keep private. Many customers are concerned about how TVs and streaming devices might be spying: listening to what you say, taking screenshots of everything you watch, storing sensitive information on your TV, and sharing your data with the cloud.To find out what TV and streaming device companies are doing, I decided to ask every one to explain itself. I put together 17 yes-or-no questions, like “Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?” so that companies couldn’t just link to a confusing and legalese-ridden privacy policy. TV users deserve to know the answers.Company representatives providing responses Eric Sveum, PR manager Emily Ewing, public relations manager Alex García-Kummert, spokesperson Chris De Maria, director of public relations Sarah Novatt, spokesperson Frank Giancamilli, corporate communications senior manager Rob Manfredo, head of communications and eventsOne month ago, I invited 11 companies, including Amazon, Apple, Google, Hisense, LG, Panasonic, Roku, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Walmart’s Vizio to share those answers. We now have answers from the top three TV manufacturers as well as every major streaming device company. Some companies declined to answer. Below, you can see and compare how each company answered (or failed to answer) each question and then decide how you feel. (One company, Hisense, ignored our emails entirely.)As you’ll see them say, some of this data collection is opt-in, and you can often opt out. We know that many TVs use automatic content recognition (ACR) to figure out potentially everything we’re watching, and use that information to tailor ads, gather audience metrics, and serve up content recommendations based on our viewing habits. But though it sometimes seems like it’s required during the cavalcade of agreements thrown at us during setup, you can generally stop ACR even after you’ve agreed to it.Opting out might not be as effective as it should be, however. A recent Northeastern University study found that Walmart’s Vizio kept on sending data after an opt-out (Vizio told me it was “routine operational data used to support the Vizio experience,” not ACR), while traffic with both Samsung and Roku was limited, but not stopped completely.Below are the answers to our 17 questions. You will notice that some companies would not answer yes or no. We’ve also noted where companies declined to answer at all or ignored the questions. If any company becomes willing to directly answer our questions, we’ll add their responses.1. Do your TVs ever use their embedded microphones, or the microphones in their remotes, to listen to sound in a customer’s home?No. Fire TV includes voice functionality to help customers use their devices and get to content they love and fast, not to surveil homes. The microphones on our voice remotes are designed to only work when the mic button on the remote is physically pressed. And TVs with hands-free Alexa are designed to detect the wake word (and only the wake word) before connecting to Alexa. No audio is stored or sent to the cloud unless the device detects the wake word. Customers can also turn off the microphones at any time. Every Fire TV smart television that has microphones also has a physical button or switch that disables the microphone.Apple TV 4K will use its far-field microphones and the Always On Processor strictly to listen for the Siri wake word. The Always On Processor does not process or act on any other sounds in the home. Users have full control over this and can turn off “Siri” or “Hey Siri” as a wake word, or disable Siri entirely. When using the Siri Remote, users must actively press and hold the microphone button for it to start listening.If Google Assistant or Gemini is enabled or available, microphones (built-in hands-free ‘Hey Google’ or remote push-to-talk button) listen for activation triggers. Microphones remain in passive standby until triggered by hotword or button press.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.Voice recognition is off by default and operates only if the user has opted in by accepting the Voice Information Agreement. Even if the user has opted in, they need to take additional steps for the microphone to be used. They must either press the microphone button on the remote control or they can use Hands-free Voice Control on supported models.Hands-free Voice Control is disabled unless a user opts into this feature and then uses a wake-word. Wake-word detection is performed locally on the TV. If no wake word is detected, the audio is processed locally, promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.While Roku TVs don’t have built-in microphones, some Roku remotes do. Standard voice remotes listen only while the mic button is held, and hands-free remotes can be switched off.No, for private monitoring. Samsung TVs do not listen to or record private conversations.The TV’s embedded microphone only listens locally for the specific wake-up word (like “Hi, Bixby”) and ignores all other sounds, while the remote control microphone only activates when the customer physically presses the button.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.Some TCL TVs and remotes have microphones. Users can activate those microphones to use voice assistance features provided through third-party operating systems or applications. Those third parties control whether the voice features are available and how they are used, under their own terms and privacy policies.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.2. Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.[Recorded audio and/or transcripts based on audio are] stored only if ‘Voice & Audio Activity’ (VAA) is explicitly enabled under Google Account Web & App Activity. Voice & Audio Activity is off by default. If VAA is off, voice requests are processed in real-time and not saved to the Google Account.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.If voice recognition is enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control’s microphone button or using the wake word), certain information generated as part of a specific voice recognition interaction may be stored locally on the TV to support voice-related features. Depending on the interaction, this may include Speech-to-text results derived from a user’s voice command.Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, captured audio is promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Voice commands made via voice-enabled remotes may be retained to improve voice features and provide support, consistent with Roku’s privacy policy. Users can opt out in their Roku account privacy settings.No. Samsung Smart TVs do not store voice recordings or transcripts on the device.However, on secure servers, voice commands and transcripts are stored only to process requests and improve voice assistant services.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.TCL does not collect audio data from TCL TV or remote microphones, or from the use of third-party voice features.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.3. Do your TVs transmit any audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?When customers speak to Alexa by pressing the mic button on the remote or using their chosen wake word, a recording of the request is sent to Amazon’s cloud, where a text transcript of the request is created to help Alexa provide a response. No audio is captured without the customer invoking Alexa—either by pressing the mic button or saying the wake word—and customers can easily review exactly what they asked and what Alexa heard, delete their recording, or even choose not to save them at all.Siri AI processes user requests using on-device processing, and when a request needs more powerful AI models, it extends those same on-device privacy protections to the cloud through a groundbreaking infrastructure called Private Cloud Compute (PCC). When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple, or anyone else, and outside experts can verify this privacy promise at any time.For moments when users ask a question that requires up‑to‑date information, Siri AI can go out to the web and find it, then use Private Cloud Compute to generate an answer. Searches and requests are associated with a random identifier — a long string of letters and numbers — not a user’s Apple Account.If Voice & Audio Activity is turned on, when voice features are activated (via hotword or remote button), captured audio or transcripts are transmitted to Google cloud servers for processing and fulfilling commands. If VAA is turned off, these are deleted.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.Yes, but only if voice recognition has been enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control microphone button or using the wake word). When voice recognition is activated, the TV displays an on-screen indication that voice recognition is active and listening for the user’s command. Once the user finishes the voice command, the command is transmitted to our server, where it is converted into text and processed to respond to the command.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Roku TVs don’t have microphones. Voice-enabled remotes let people control their Roku devices by voice, as described in our privacy policy.No, for ambient or background listening. Samsung TVs do not passively monitor, record, or transmit audio from your home. Audio is only captured and transmitted when you actively initiate a voice command (such as pressing the microphone button on your remote or using the wake word). This voice input is processed securely to fulfill your requests, improve services, and support connected features under our voice privacy policies.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.4. Do your TVs collect any screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers are watching?Apple TV 4K does not use automatic content recognition (ACR), nor does it collect screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers are watching. If a user chooses to ask a question about what’s on their screen, that data is processed by Siri AI. This feature is only initiated by a direct user request.Google TV platform software does not utilize Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) to capture on-screen video or screenshots. (Note: Third-party TV hardware OEMs may install separate ACR software, but Google TV OS itself does not).Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.No. ACR in LG TVs does not collect or store screenshots, screen images, screen recordings, or video recordings from the TV. Instead, it uses audio fingerprints generated from content audio using the TV’s internal soundboard (not a speaker) to identify the content being viewed.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.No. Samsung TVs do not capture or store screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers watch.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.5. Do your TVs store or transmit data on what content viewers watch or listen to through the TV?Yes. For example, customers can opt in to allow Fire TV to collect certain viewing information like what shows they’ve watched in third-party apps to improve and personalize their experience, including by displaying shows and movies in a Continue Watching row on the Fire TV home screen. Customers can manage that setting anytime via their device’s Privacy Settings.Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.[Google TV] stores and transmits viewing history, watchlists, and app interactions for rentals/purchases on GTV and FreePlay. We do not have viewing history on third party apps.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.If the user has agreed to the Viewing Information Agreement, viewing information may be collected or processed in certain circumstances, including the following:- ACR: Where ACR is available and enabled, ACR-related information may be collected and processed to identify content being viewed from supported sources. ACR uses audio fingerprinting technology to identify content rather than collecting screenshots, screen recordings, video recordings, voice recordings, or other audio recordings from the TV. To operate ACR services, LG may process content-identification fingerprints together with device information, content source information, network information, and consent settings needed to support the feature. ACR is optional and is turned off by default, and users can disable the feature at any time through the TV settings. ACR does not operate within third-party streaming apps.- LG Channels: When a user streams content through LG Channels, information about the content being viewed is processed and sent to our servers so we can provide the requested streaming service.- Voice Recognition: When users make voice commands, those commands and current viewing information (such as channel number and program name, and whether the source is an antenna or set-top-box) are sent to the server to process the voice commands and provide appropriate responses.- Usage Information: Certain viewing information may also be collected as part of usage information relating to how the user interacts with the TV and its services, such as information about content selected for viewing or channels the user switches to.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.We collect streaming activity as described in our privacy policy. Smart TV Experience, which can identify other content on screen, is off by default in the US and is enabled only if the user opts in.Yes, but only for TV programming and app viewing history. Samsung TVs do not monitor or transmit your personal files or private media.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.TCL collects limited data only for diagnostics and product improvement from some models of TCL Smart TVs. This collection is disclosed to users at setup and in TCL’s privacy notice, uses pseudonymization to prevent user profiling, and can be turned off by the user.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.6. Do your TVs collect any telemetry about where users are clicking, selecting, tapping, or otherwise looking when using the TV?Fire TV collects data about how customers use the device, such as navigating the home screen or opening apps, to provide and improve features. Customers can opt out of certain data collection and use via Privacy Settings.Apple did not provide an answer to this question.[Google TV] collects device navigation telemetry (button presses, navigation clicks, app launch/exit events) under ‘Usage & Diagnostics’ settings to assess system health and reliability. Does not store “hovering” or “highlight” states.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.To provide and improve smart services, the LG smart TV may collect certain basic usage information about how users interact with the TV, such as the features, menu items, apps, or services they select or use. LG does not collect information about a user’s activity within third-party apps. LG does not track where users are looking when using the TV.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.We collect standard usage data, such as button presses and menu selections, to run and improve the product.For menu interactions and viewing selections, interactions (like clicks or selections) are analyzed primarily in aggregate to improve the user experience and service recommendations.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.TCL does not collect data at the device level regarding what viewers watch, except when a user requests remote diagnostic support, in which case the information is used to fix the problem the user reported.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.7. Do your TVs transmit any information that could identify the location of their owner, including their public IP address, Wi-Fi network SSID, GPS coordinates, and/or actual street address?Yes. For example, IP addresses are transmitted as part of normal network communication, for your device to communicate with the internet and deliver content. There is no GPS hardware on Fire TV devices.Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.[Google TV] transmits public IP address, Wi-Fi scan data (SSID/BSSID), and account/device regional configuration to determine approximate or precise device location.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.To provide Smart TV functionality, the TV must be connected to the internet. If the TV is connected to the internet, then like any other internet-connected device, the Smart TV will transmit its IP address. The IP address may be used to determine its approximate geographic location to provide services appropriate for the user’s region.Separately, when ACR is enabled, the TV’s IP address and information about nearby Wi-Fi networks, such as MAC addresses and signal strength, may be used to estimate the TV’s approximate location as part of the ACR service. This ACR-related location processing is limited to ACR and is not used generally across other TV services.The TV does not contain a GPS module and does not use GPS to determine its location.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Roku TVs don’t collect GPS data. Like any connected device, they transmit a public IP address, which may be used for approximate location, among other purposes, per our privacy policy.No, for physical locations. Samsung TVs do not collect or transmit GPS coordinates, Wi-Fi SSIDs, or your physical street address. However, for network connection, the TV must transmit its public IP address to connect to the internet and run basic features (like the Smart Hub and software updates). This IP address is only used for network communication and general region detection (like country or state), not to pinpoint your actual address.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.To provide location-based services, TCL collects IP address and Wi-Fi network name (SSID) information, as described in the terms and privacy policy to which users agree when they initially set up their TV. TCL uses this information only to identify a country or city in order to deliver services, not the user’s specific location. TCL TVs have no GPS modules, and TCL does not collect street addresses through the TV. If a user creates a TCL account on a TCL Google TV, TCL collects an email address and age to confirm that the user is an adult. Apart from that, TCL’s practice is not to collect personally identifiable information from its televisions.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.8. Do your TVs store or transmit any other potentially personally identifying information about their owners, including their name, age, gender, orientation, and demographic?Fire TV devices are associated with customers’ Amazon account, which includes their name and account information.Apple did not provide an answer to this question.Because Google TV requires a Google Account for smart functionality, linked profile information (name, email, age, gender) is accessed, stored, and transmitted for personalization and age-restriction policies.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.When creating an LG account, the user provides their name, email address and date of birth (to confirm applicable age requirements). If a user creates an LG account from their Smart TV, the TV will temporarily store and then transmit this information to LG’s servers.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Users provide account information, such as name and email, when they create a Roku account, as described in our privacy policy.Samsung SmartTVs do not collect/store or transmit name, age, gender, orientation or demographic information.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.If a user creates a TCL account on a TCL Google TV, TCL collects an email address and age to confirm that the user is an adult. Apart from that, TCL’s practice is not to collect personally identifiable information from its televisions.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.9. Does your company store any of the kinds of information in Question 7 or 8 in the cloud or other remote servers? If so, which?Yes. Information transmitted to Amazon’s cloud is encrypted in transit and stored securely.Apple did not provide an answer to this question.Both location data (IP address/Wi-Fi) and Google Account profile data (name, email address, age/gender demographics) are stored on Google’s cloud servers linked to your account profile.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.Yes. Information such as IP addresses, device-level identifiers, and, if a user has an LG Account, account information such as name, email address, and date of birth, is stored on LG’s cloud or other remote servers. When ACR is enabled, the ACR-related information described above, including nearby Wi-Fi network information such as MAC addresses and signal strength, may also be stored on remote servers.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Data may be stored on Roku’s servers or with major cloud providers to operate the service, as described in our privacy policy.Yes. The information described above is stored in encrypted or hashed form within secure cloud infrastructure managed by Samsung.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.The limited information described above is stored with cloud service providers, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, subject to TCL’s terms and privacy policy.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.10. Do your TVs transmit any information about the other devices on an owner’s home Wi-Fi network?Apple did not provide an answer to this question.[Google TV] discovers nearby Cast-enabled devices and smart home hardware via local network protocols (mDNS, SSDP, Matter/Thread) and transmits device discovery/connectivity logs.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.To support connectivity capabilities, LG smart TVs identify other devices on the user’s Wi-Fi network. Where necessary to support device-discovery functionality, information about nearby devices detected on the local network may be transmitted to a third-party service provider acting on LG’s behalf to identify compatible devices.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Roku TVs may detect other devices on the home network to support features like AirPlay, as described in our privacy policy.No. Samsung TVs do not scan your home Wi-Fi network to collect or transmit an inventory of other connected devices. The TV only communicates with compatible devices that customers actively choose to connect (such as for casting or via the SmartThings app under their Samsung Account) to provide smart home control, not to monitor other devices on your network.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.Users may connect their TCL Smart TV to other devices so they can control those devices. For some on-device functions, such as screen casting or connecting devices to each other, the TV may detect other devices on the same Wi-Fi network. That data is normally exchanged only between the devices. If a connection problem occurs, diagnostics may report the name of the device involved. When a consumer chooses to control the TV through a voice service such as Amazon Alexa, data is exchanged between the TV, TCL’s cloud, and Amazon so the service can function.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.11. Can users entirely opt out of transmitting all forms of data?No. Basic functionality like downloading apps and streaming content requires transmitting data. However, Fire TV does provide customers the ability to control the collection or transmission of certain data, including data about the frequency and duration of use of third-party apps and about what customers have watched in third-party apps.Apple did not provide an answer to this question.Users cannot opt out of 100% of data transmission while connected to the internet. Essential system telemetry (device model, OS version, activation status, security updates) is mandatory for basic operation.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.Users can stop the transmission of personal data associated with smart TV services by withdrawing their acceptance of the Privacy Policy or Terms of Use. If they do so, smart TV services will no longer be available, and the data transmission required to provide those services will cease. The TV can still be used for basic functions that do not require smart TV services, such as Live TV or HDMI inputs.Users can also separately choose whether to use optional features such as voice recognition, ACR, and interest-based advertising. These features require separate agreements and can be reviewed, managed, or withdrawn through the TV settings at any time. Declining or withdrawing these optional agreements does not prevent users from using core smart TV functionality.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.No, but Roku offers privacy settings for voice data, Smart TV Experience, and ad personalization.No, not all forms. At minimum, data is needed to run a digital platform (e.g. to provide the service and security).Sony did not provide an answer to this question.Some data is transmitted to TCL because the Smart TV services and functions the user chooses depend on such data. Users can opt out of sending TCL the limited interaction data collected for diagnostics and product improvement.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.12. Are users automatically opted out by default when setting up the TV?Customers are not opted out of all data transmission by default. Again, basic device functionality requires data to be transmitted. However, there are some Fire TV features like Automatic Content Recognition that are default off and that customers must affirmatively turn on in order to allow those features to work and transmit data.Apple did not provide an answer to this question.During initial setup, options such as Usage & Diagnostics sharing, personalized recommendations/ads, and Google Account Web & App Activity tracking are enabled by default unless opted out.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.Yes. Users can choose to opt-in by accepting each applicable agreement before the relevant services or features are enabled. Optional features such as voice recognition, ACR, and interest-based advertising are not enabled by default . Users can also manage or withdraw their consent through the TV settings at any time.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Smart TV Experience is off by default in the US.Yes. For Viewing Information Services (VIS), which includes Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), consumers are opted out by default and must affirmatively enable it.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.Users can opt out of sending TCL the limited interaction data collected for diagnostics and product improvement.The ACR technology on those TCL Smart TVs which support that feature comes from the operating system provider or third-party software providers. Users choose whether to turn on ACR when they first set up the TV, and they can turn it off at any time in the ACR provider’s privacy settings. Before ACR is turned on, the user must agree to the ACR provider’s terms and conditions. Those terms and privacy policies explain what viewing data the provider may store or transmit with the user’s consent.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.13. If users opt out, does the TV store any of these forms of data internally for potential use at a later date?No. If a customer has opted out of Fire TV collecting data, that data will not be collected unless the customer re-enables collection.Apple did not provide an answer to this question.If cloud tracking is disabled, local temporary caches and system operational buffers remain on-device for immediate system execution and local performance before deletion.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.No. If a user withdraws consent under an applicable agreement, data previously collected under that agreement is handled in accordance with LG’s applicable data retention and deletion policies, including deletion or anonymization where appropriate, and is not retained for potential future use.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Roku’s ad personalization setting affects which ads users see. Data is still collected and used for other purposes, as described in our privacy policy.No. If users opt out, the TV stops collecting new viewing data immediately and does not store it internally for later use. Once you disable the Viewing Information Services (VIS), any previously collected ACR data is deleted from our servers and can no longer be associated with your device.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.14. Does disconnecting a TV from the internet prevent all these forms of data transmission?Apple did not provide an answer to this question.Severing internet access (disconnecting Wi-Fi or removing Ethernet) halts all outbound external data transmission to Google cloud servers. Of course this also stops any streaming service from operating.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.Yes. A TV must be connected to the internet to transmit data. For voice recognition specifically, voice data is not stored for later upload when the TV is offline and is not transmitted when the connection is restored.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Data can’t reach Roku’s servers without an internet connection.Yes. A TV without internet access cannot transmit data to Samsung. Bluetooth is used only for local connections the customer sets up, such as remotes, headphones, or soundbars, and is not used to transmit viewing or advertising data. Samsung TVs do not connect to open Wi-Fi networks on their own.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.Disconnecting a TCL TV from the internet stops data from being sent to remote servers.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.15. If users disconnect a TV from the internet, does the TV store any of these forms of data internally for potential use at a later date?Yes, smart TVs will store some data locally to transmit once connectivity has been re-established. For example, if an application were to crash while your smart TV was offline, the device might store that data locally to be able to transmit it once connectivity has been reestablished—for the purpose of ensuring your devices and services are working as they should.Apple did not provide an answer to this question.Android-level system event logs and diagnostic buffers are stored locally on-device and may sync or transmit crash/error reports once an internet connection is restored.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.No. If the TV is disconnected from the internet, it does not store this information internally for later transmission or use when the internet connection is restored. For example, voice recognition data is not stored for later upload while the TV is offline and is not subsequently transmitted when the internet connection is restored.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Some usage data may be briefly held on the device until the connection returns or the device is turned off.Yes, but is dependent upon what features are enabled on the TV and the model year of the device.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.Unless a consumer has opted out, the TV stores certain diagnostic and performance data while offline, which is processed once the TV reconnects.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.16. Is collected data encrypted on device? Is it encrypted in transit? Is it encrypted end-to-end?Data is encrypted in transit.Apple did not provide an answer to this question.On-device: YES (Android file-based encryption). In transit: YES (TLS/HTTPS). End-to-end: NO for standard queries/telemetry, as Google servers must decrypt requests to process voice commands and content recommendations.Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.Personal information, such as LG Account information, is encrypted. Other information, such as STT results, may be stored without encryption. All data transmitted from the device to the server is sent through an encrypted channel.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Roku uses industry-standard security measures to protect data, specifically end-to-end encryption.Yes. Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) information collected by Samsung TVs is hashed for privacy, and is encrypted in transit and at storage.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.Data collected by TCL is encrypted in transit.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.17. Can users erase data that has already been collected by your company and its partners?Yes. Customers have a variety of ways to easily manage data Amazon collects, including deletion options.At Apple, we respect users’ ability to know, access, correct, transfer, restrict the processing of, and delete their personal data. Users worldwide can delete data associated with their account at the Apple Data and Privacy page at privacy.apple.com.Users can review, manage, and permanently delete their activity history, voice recordings, and personalized search data via the Google My Activity portal (myactivity.google.com).Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.Users can request deletion of their personal information by contacting LG via the email address provided in the Privacy Policy. They also can request deletion of certain data—including voice information and viewing information—directly through the TV’s settings.When a user withdraws consent or requests deletion, LG deletes the relevant data in accordance with its data retention and deletion policies.Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.Users can submit a deletion request at privacy.roku.com, and we process it in accordance with applicable law.Yes, customers may request to have their data deleted. Customers may also reset their device advertising ID, which means previous Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) data can no longer be associated with their device.Sony did not provide an answer to this question.Users can ask TCL to delete data it has collected through TCL’s official privacy request channels.Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.
