item.title: Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?
item.author: emschwartz
item.content:encoded: Last week, MIT CSAIL published Sparks of Weight-Space Programming. Given the raw weights of a small network, GPT-6 Astra could tell which game it had been trained to play. Given only a game’s rules, it could write the weights of a small network from scratch and beat networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. No gradients, no training loop, just reasoning about what the weights compute. They coined this .In another experiment, they asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math by editing its weights. Astra changed only 0.016% of the weights, and MATH-500 accuracy jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%.Looking at Astra’s edit, I realized most of its search was solving a linear program by trial and error. It spent about 8 hours and 28 forward passes choosing which weights to change and by how much. A couple of LP solves, about a minute each, do the same job with 8× fewer changed weights. In this post I’ll walk through the edit, why it’s an LP, and what that says about the fix itself.Small reasoning models have a common failure: they get stuck in , repeating the same few lines over and over instead of finishing their reasoning. Qwen3.5-0.8B is especially prone to it, and its model card says so. On MATH-500, 93% of the base model’s answers ran into the 32,768-token limit without ever reaching an answer.The edit fixes the loops, so it helps anywhere the model loops. That includes instruction following: IFEval went from 21% to 62%.On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, Astra couldn’t meaningfully improve its math ability. As the authors put it, editing the weights could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but couldn’t add one the model lacked.How Astra fixed the loops#Transformers use residual connections: each layer’s output is added to its input rather than replacing it. Follow one token through the network and you get a single vector that every layer adds to, called the (1,024-dimensional in this model). When the model is looping, the residual stream shifts in a consistent direction. Astra’s fix was to edit two layers so that what they add points the opposite way.Finding the loop direction#Astra wrote four pairs of short texts, each a piece of productive reasoning and a looping version of the same reasoning. It ran all eight through the model and recorded each token’s residual stream vector at one layer. Averaging over the looping texts gives one vector, and averaging over the productive texts gives another. Their difference, normalized, is the $u$: the way the residual stream moves when the model loops.Each MLP ends with a matrix $W$ (called ). At every token, it turns the MLP’s 3,584-dimensional hidden activation $h$ into a 1,024-dimensional output $Wh$, which gets added to the residual stream $x$:$$x \leftarrow x + Wh, \qquad Wh = \sum_j h_j \, w_j$$So the MLP’s output is always a weighted sum of the same 3,584 vectors, the columns $w_j$ of $W$. $W$ fixes what those vectors are; the activations $h_j$ decide how much of each one gets added at each token.Each column points partly along $u$. That amount, $u^\top w_j$, is how much column $j$ pushes the model toward looping whenever $h_j$ is active. Astra’s edit subtracts a multiple $\alpha$ of it:$$w_j \to w_j - \alpha \, (u^\top w_j) \, u$$At $\alpha = 1$ the component along $u$ is gone, so the column no longer pushes toward looping. Doing this to every column in layers 15 and 19 took accuracy from 9% to 33% on GSM8K and MATH training problems. At $\alpha = 6$ the component is flipped: a column that wrote $+a$ along $u$ now writes $-5a$, and pushes the model from looping whenever it’s used.Every edited column changes by a multiple of the same vector $u$. So the whole edit is one direction $u$ plus one number per column, $v_j = -\alpha\,(u^\top w_j)$, which is zero for columns left alone. That’s a change:$$\Delta W = u\,v^\top$$At each token, it adds $(v \cdot h_t)\,u$ to the residual stream: some amount of $u$, set by how active the edited columns are. No other direction changes.That leaves $v$ to choose: which columns to edit, and how large $\alpha$ should be. Astra worked it out by trial and error, testing each edit on a fresh batch of those training problems:Random direction (control)Pushing harder than $\alpha = 1$ helped more, and a random direction did nothing. The final edit used $\alpha = 6$ on only the 64 columns per layer that wrote the most $u$ on looping text.The paper released Astra’s full logs: every tool call, every forward pass, every note it wrote to itself. Astra had a Python kernel with the weights loaded and a budget of 50 forward passes, each a batched run of the model on training problems or texts of its choosing.The edit was frozen after about 10 hours, and the last 17 passes re-tested it without changing anything. Of those 10 hours, finding $u$ took 15 minutes. Finding $v$ took about 8 hours.Choosing v is a linear program#Astra was searching for a $v$ that strongly pushes looping tokens away from $u$ while barely touching productive ones. Since the push at token $t$ is $v \cdot h_t$, linear in $v$, both requirements are linear inequalities.I labeled tokens from the base model’s own traces: tokens ($R$), deep inside a loop, and tokens ($P$), well before any loop starts, and recorded their activations $h_t$ at layers 15 and 19. Each one becomes a constraint, and the LP picks the $v$ with the smallest L1 norm $\sum_j |v_j|$:$$ \begin{aligned} \min_v \quad & \sum_j |v_j| \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & v \cdot h_t \le -\delta && t \in R \quad \text{(at least } \delta \text{ away from } u\text{)} \\ & |v \cdot h_t| \le \varepsilon && t \in P \quad \text{(at most } \varepsilon\text{)} \end{aligned} $$In practice no $v$ satisfies every constraint, so each one gets a penalized slack variable.Minimizing L1 tends to make $v$ sparse. The L1 ball is a diamond, and when you grow it until it touches the feasible region, it usually touches at a corner, where most coordinates are exactly zero. So the LP picks the columns as well as the amounts.To get exactly 8 columns per layer, I kept the 8 with the largest effect and solved again with the rest fixed at zero.That replaces Astra’s 8-hour search, including its choice of columns and $\alpha$, with a couple of LP solves. An off-the-shelf solver (HiGHS) took over 20 minutes each on these constraints, so I wrote a GPU solver (PDHG, the algorithm behind PDLP) that gets within 0.2% of its optimum in about a minute.I tested two LP edits. Both use Astra’s layers. One uses Astra’s direction $u$. The other uses a : label tokens in the model’s own traces as looping or productive with a simple repetition detector, then take the difference of their average residual streams. It’s the same recipe Astra used, minus the hand-written texts, so no LLM is involved. I tuned the LP’s settings on a separate 128-problem dev set; everything in the chart and table is on data never used for fitting or tuning.With Astra’s direction, the LP matches Astra’s edit on every benchmark, within noise, while changing 8× fewer weights. With the heuristic direction, it gets about 93% of the way there.A few other things showed up:The search mattered, and the LP replaces it. On the dev set, reusing Astra’s recipe (top 64 columns, $\alpha = 6$) on the heuristic direction without searching again scores 44.5. The LP scores 54.7.Different columns, same fix. The LP’s 8 columns share only 3 (layer 15) and 1 (layer 19) with Astra’s 64. Many sparse solutions work; what matters is the total push along $u.$A random direction does nothing. On the dev set, a random $u$ of the same size scores 10.2, against 10.9 for the base model.A steering vector does the same job#An edit can only tell a looping token apart from a productive one through its activations, and a loop isn’t recognizable from them until it’s well under way. So on the dev set, asking the LP to push only on loop-like tokens did no better than pushing on every token.The LP’s 8 columns in layer 15 are active on 89% of tokens, and the push they add barely varies from token to token, so the edit is close to a constant push along $u$. A constant push doesn’t need a weight edit. It can be added directly as a , a fixed vector added to the residual stream at every token.The table below adds the LP edit’s average push along $u$ to the unedited model at layers 15 and 19, at three strengths:Steering strength (× the LP edit’s average push)For comparison, on the same runs: the LP edit scores 62.5 on the dev set and 53.2 on MATH-500, Astra’s edit 59.4 and 50.0, the base model 10.9 and 7.0. MATH-500 here is one sample per problem.At 1×, the steering vector recovers essentially the whole fix. The window is narrow: at 0.5× the loops come back, and at 2× they stop but the reasoning falls apart.The only difference is delivery. The LP edit is an ordinary checkpoint; the steering vector needs extra code at inference time.Limitations and what’s next#This is one model. The LP still relies on Astra for the layers, and the best results use Astra’s direction too. The heuristic direction gets most of the way without an LLM, but not all of it.Loops also turned out to be fixable with a constant push, so the LP’s per-token constraints didn’t end up mattering much. A behavior that should change some tokens and leave others alone would be a better test of them. Choosing the layers without an agent is the other open piece.Lastly, this was only tested on removing loops. Many other behaviors, like refusal or sycophancy, can be steered by adding or removing a single direction in the residual stream. If a behavior can be steered with one direction, choosing how to build it into the weights should be the same LP, but that still needs testing.Code, edits, and the full write-up are on GitHub.Please cite this work as:Barry, Nathan. "Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?" nathan.rs (Nov 2026). https://nathan.rs/posts/weight-space-lp.Or use the BibTex citation:@article{barry2026wslp, title = "Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?", author = "Barry, Nathan", journal = "nathan.rs", year = "2026", month = "Nov", url = "https://nathan.rs/posts/weight-space-lp" }

item.title: We need more goat sacrifices
item.author: iamnothere
item.content:encoded: Just a quick thing before this week’s post. If you’ve preordered THE STRANGEST IDEA IN THE WORLDSubmit your preorder receipt and your mailing address hereBefore anybody enacts a major social policy or launches any philanthropic programs, they should sacrifice a goat. There ought to be an entire liturgy of grotesqueries, in fact—pricked fingers, names written in blood, robes, candles, chanting, obsidian blades, still-beating hearts, the whole shebang.Most of those are left-coded failures, so here are some right-coded failures:nothing ever dies; it merely becomes embarrassingIt’s inevitable that some of our interventions are going to fail. (If they don’t, we should either be suspicious of the results, or we should be more ambitious with our programs.) What we really want to know is: when we try to improve the world through some policy or program, how often do we succeed?We don’t have a good answer to this question, but we do have a good joke about it.The Iron Law of Evaluation and Other Metallic RulesThe Iron Law of Evaluation: The net expected impact of a large social program is zero.The Stainless Steel Law: Better-designed evaluations are more likely to find null effects.The Brass Law: The more a program is intended to change people, the more likely the impact of that program will be zero.The Zinc Law: The programs most likely to be evaluated are those most likely to fail.tried to walk back his laws shortly before he died in 2006You can always find a one-off study showing that an intervention works, but if we’ve learned anything from the past 20 years of social science, it’s that one-off studies ain’t worth much. It’s so easy to juice your stats and journals are so hungry for positive results that entire literatures can be suspect, and decades of research can culminate in a shrug. “Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t, it depends on all sorts of factors that we can’t really specify, so uh, good luck!”Even if we take Rossi at his word and there are as-yet-unnamed programs out there that are reliable and effective, the question still remains: why aren’t there more of them? Why do so many of our best-laid plans end up like this:The answer lies, I think, in a 50-year-old study that is almost certainly false.The Illusion of Controlover 30 million copiesHere’s the real evidence of our illusion of control: we’re so certain our interventions will work that we forget to check whether they do at all.an analysissaida report from the Government Accountability Officeputs ithasn’t changedbig pile of debta much bigger pile of money$564,000$200kapplications are up 47%When people see our big heap of failed interventions, they tend to go through three stages of grief.Okay, fine, these high-minded, utopian interventions don’t work, so what we really need is Common Sense and Obviously Good Ideas. For example, if you want to make poor people better off, you should give them money. That’s just Common Sense! That’s an Obviously Good Idea!keep finding null effects of unconditional cash transfersone studyit maybe made them more depressedresults are more promising in low- and middle- income countriesno true Scotsmanmake them more likely to vote for a Republican two weeks laterAcceptance sounds good, but it isn’t. Once we realize how hard it is to improve people’s lives, it’s tempting to believe that doing so is simply impossible, and so we are excused from even trying.do not understand the fundamental workings of the human mindscientific maturityWe misunderstand what it feels like to be in the middle of things. Almost no one who read Galen or Aristotle ever thought to themselves, “oh, obviously this is only version 0.1 of our knowledge, all of this is tentative and incomplete, and one day it will be overturned and replaced with something better, something that actually works.” No, they thought to themselves, “Thank u Mr. Aristotle for your many true and useful facts.”we can’t even get people to go to the gymI revere the discoveries of wisdom and their discoverers [...] For me those things were acquired, for me they were labored for. [...] Let us make larger what we have received. Let this heritage pass from me to posterity increased.enacted by forceunknowable and will remain so forever

item.title: My AI agents found an unmapped Maya site?
item.author: eyvindn
item.content:encoded: 5 min read (Last edit: 11 Nov)Update (11 November): it turns out the site had already been mapped in Estrada-Belli et al. 2025. The agents missed it while going through the literature, so they rediscovered it rather than discovered it (it just wasn't in the register of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History, INAH, yet). Still work to do then! The rest of the story still holds.By analyzing NASA lidar data, my AI agents found a Maya site in Mexico that wasn't in the official register. (It turned out archaeologists had mapped it already, more on that at the end.) It took to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive.Disclaimer: I'm not an archaeologist.I'm going to tell this story as a diary, because the timeline is probably the best part.I was traveling in Peru, Gemini-ing about the history of the place, when I learned about Hiram Bingham, the American explorer who "discovered" Machu Picchu in 1911. "What luck!" I thought. He was actually looking for a different city, Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Incas, when a local farmer in the valley below guided him to the ruins. "Imagine if Bingham had our tools," I thought. "What would he do?"I brainstormed a bit with a few agents (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok), and they all said lidar. From above, a ruin in the jungle is just a bunch of trees (like Machu Picchu before it was cleared), so satellite photos don't help much. Lidar, instead, fires laser pulses through the gaps in the canopy and maps the ground underneath.So the agents went looking for lidar data. Peru isn't well covered, and hiring a company to do a survey meant permits, costs and bureaucracy, so I gave up on that. Then I thought: why not the Maya? Their region is much better covered by public lidar.That night, I asked the agents to analyze it and went to bed.I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses. They turned the lidar strips (about 1,200 km² of jungle) into images, and 48 agents went through them one by one like very patient archaeologists, looking for pyramids, platforms, and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes, and roads. There was no special model or classifier involved: the agents literally looked at the pictures, following a precise guide. That's awesome! Please check which of these villages haven't been discovered yet. Search both the literature and the archives. One major village doesn't seem to have been registered.This is the hilltop from the top of this post. It sits on the edge of a cliff, under the jungle, and it has straight edges and sharp corners. Nature doesn't really do straight lines.Zooming in, there's a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8–12 m tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that might have been a water reservoir.And this is what it looks like in 3D.The site in 3D, from the lidar. Heights exaggerated ~1.5×. You should contact INAH (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History), write a report on your discovery, and check whether the site is in their register. Sometimes they have unpublished results. OK, how do I contact INAH? How does the reporting process work?…instructions for the report… + email addresses OK, please do the report.I iterated on the report a bit, since a few things were off, and translated it into Spanish to improve the chances of getting a reply (at least, that's what Claude suggested). I don't speak Spanish, so I had to trust the agents on that one.The agents also checked the raw point cloud, to make sure the shapes were really on the ground and not created by the trees. Green dots are leaves, brown dots are the ground.Then I sent the report to INAH.INAH replied: they checked their records and found no registered archaeological site at that location.At that point I thought nobody had put it on a map before. I was wrong (see below).This part is speculation, from a long chat with the agents. It looks like a small Maya civic centre from the Classic period (roughly AD 250–900), basically the "downtown" of a local elite. The plaza is where people gathered, for ceremonies and maybe even a market. The pyramid was probably a temple, and the raised courtyard next to it might have been where the local ruler lived. The hollow could have been an , a rainwater reservoir: Maya towns needed them to get through the dry season. Or it's just a hole. The three platforms around were probably houses.I asked Gemini to imagine how it looked back then:For similar studies, have a look at how NASA's G-LiHT instrument works (Cook et al. 2013) and how lidar collected for environmental research can be reused for archaeology (Golden et al. 2016). In 2024, archaeologists found a whole Maya city in Mexico this way (Auld-Thomas et al. 2024), others mapped settlements across the Maya lowlands, including this very site (Estrada-Belli et al. 2025), and another study found what may have been ancient Maya marketplaces (Šprajc 2026).The site is now in the hands of the people who should have it: Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) and the archaeologists who mapped it first. If anything comes out of it, I'll post an update.You can just do things. I'm not an archaeologist, so I didn't know this was supposed to be hard. I just picked an old problem, tried the most obvious thing and threw some compute at it. Being a naive outsider might be a superpower now.And it turned out professional archaeologists had already mapped the same site. I guess that's a good sign: an outsider with agents ended up in a similar place to the experts.And I don't think this is really about archaeology. So far, most agentic AI stories have been about coding, math and physics, but it's much more general than that, and I hope this small example makes it a bit more obvious. We are on the brink of a revolution in all the sciences, and the only bottlenecks left will be curiosity and imagination (and compute).At this point, we should probably lidar the whole planet and let the agents discover the rest.

item.title: Using voltage glitching to unleash the A100 in my mining card
item.author: lae
item.content:encoded: I’ve discovered a voltage fault injection vulnerability on the GA100 die, allowing an operator to blow arbitrary fuses. Utilizing this vulnerability, I’ve converted my CMP 170HX 8GB card into what is effectively an A100-80G! Further, my unlocked cards actually perform ~1.2x faster than a retail A100 by having all functional SMs enabled (~120-126, die-lottery dependent), rather than the yield-safe 108 SMs NVIDIA chose for all production A100 cards. Finally, CMP-disabled features like NVLink, PCIe Gen4, NVJPG, NVDEC, MIG are all unlockable with this approach, though I haven’t specifically tested NVJPG/NVDEC/MIG.Here’s how my “A100-80G” appears and functions.GPU inventory and topologyCPU affinity 0–127 · NUMA 0hardware-unlocked CMP 170HXNVIDIA uses fuses for product segmentation, security features, and other fun access control features - and crucially, there are several functions where blowing a fuse on an NVIDIA die can grant you access, not less. In a properly secured design, a blown fuse should always induce a more restrictive state, because a blown fuse cannot be unblown in an economically feasible way. NVIDIA’s design allows one to restrictions by blowing more fuses!In this post, I will go over the GA100 die, its fuse controller, the use of VFI, and future research directions. I’ve decided to publish some of the work that enabled my research here.My work builds on prior research by Jon Pry and numerous others who have dedicated much of their time towards better understanding the GA100 die. I am disclosing my findings subsequent to another security researcher independently discovering the same vulnerability; I believe it to be in the best interest of the public to make this information publicly available. These findings were disclosed to NVIDIA’s product security team ahead of the publication of this article.The GA100 is an NVIDIA die that has been used to power almost 20 different SKUs - the A100 being the most well-known variant. I won’t delve into every SKU, but I will present the GA100 manifestations that matter to my work, covering the different versions of the CMP 170HX and the A100.As fabbed, the GA100 die has 128 SMs, 12 FBPs, 5 NVDEC units, a PCIe Gen4 x16 controller, and depending on the framebuffer size, comes with 4-6 stacks of HBM co-packaged with the die. NVIDIA uses eFuses for yield-control and product segmentation–undifferentiated GA100s turn into more restrictive variants based on defect testing and manufacturer demand.In one of the most extreme manifestations of product segmentation, the CMP 170HX, an Ethereum mining card with nominally 8 or 10 GB of application-exposed framebuffer capacity, actually comes with, respectively, ~80 and ~40 GB of HBM onboard! This work chiefly centers around how to fully unlock and use that capacity. Previous work has made great strides in unlocking the GA100 via software methods; VFI takes us across the last mile.So, how does NVIDIA utilize fuses to produce both a datacenter A100 and a mining CMP card from one die? To understand this, we need to take a closer look at the fuse controller located on the GA100.The fuse controller is a block that contains 16,384 eFuses (512 rows of 32) and a bunch of logic surrounding that raw fuse macro. Its job is to perform fuse readout and programming, protect the underlying fuses, and provide usable “option words” to the rest of the die. These option words subsequently decide how the die functions and what features are enabled.Each eFuse can be in one of two states (blown=1, unblown=0), and the 512 rows are divided into 4 regions:Regular fuses (rows 0-221). These are straightforward; often single (pairs of) fuses will map to an option word, such as OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM (an option word that determines whether further fuse programming is allowed or not). Regular fuses have built-in redundancy: for example, OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM consists of a PRI and RED (primary and redundant) fuse, in this case the primary instance is fuse 0 of row 0, and the redundant is fuse 0 of row 1. Some option words are scalars, such as OPT_X_COORDINATE, which is 9 bits wide and ostensibly holds the x-coordinate of the die on the fabbed wafer. Importantly, if a regular fuse is blown, there is basically no remedy to persistently unblow it (save for RIR later).Fuseless fuses (rows 222-487). This is a weird one. Apparently NVIDIA got frustrated with accidentally blowing regular fuses and ruining their engineering samples, and came up with a system to encode effective option words in a JTAG chain-like format (see this patent). Think about FF as essentially a that describes what option words should have what values. FF fuses (excuse the RAS syndrome) concern most of the functionality we can unlock using VFI. This is because FF option words can be trivially cleared by simply writing new FF rows! We’ll about this more in depth, later. For now, you should know that NVIDIA also knows this, because under normal conditions, you are strictly prevented from performing any FF fuse blows.IFF fuses (rows 487-512). These contain instructions in a different format than the FF one. They’re out of scope for this post, and they’re mainly useful for on-the-fly reprogramming of fuse controller option words. They are usually not accessible in a production card.RIR fuses (8 rows of 32 fuses, which are technically not part of the 512 rows). These are provided by the designer of the fuse macro (TSMC datasheet here) and are essentially the first party designer’s intended “fuse repair” mechanism. The RIR section on a GA100 has space for 16 repair instructions, each overriding the value of an identified single fuse in the main 512 rows. Unfortunately for us, specifically in the 8 GB 170HX SKU, 15 of the 16 RIR words are all ones, and the 16th word encodes a useless repair instruction that can only be rarely leveraged for any interesting unlock. The story is different for the 10 GB SKU, but that’s a matter for another day…There are two really interesting groups of fuses for the VFI-based unlock:“Control fuses”. The term comes from NVIDIA’s Tegra hardware headers, they use it to refer specifically to rows 0 and 1, which specify the values of highly security-sensitive option words.Fuseless fuses, which encode all of the interesting option words that decide whether a GA100 is born to be a measly mining card or an AI datacenter workhorse.Before we name some of the FF-encoded option words, we’ll have to first understand the FF record format in a bit more detail, then talk about the die blocks that govern the features we are interested in.Each FF row is a 32-bit record. Bits 0–4 select a chain, bit 5 distinguishes FF from IFF (0 for FF), bits 6–15 select a 16-bit block, and bits 16–31 supply that block’s new value. The JTAG-chain picture from the patent is quite literal here: the controller builds the option data by replaying these records into chains. Fixed locations in each chain correspond to individual option words.If two records address the same chain and block, the later record wins. For example, means chain 1, block 23, data . Appending that record can clear an bit set by an earlier FF record. No physical fuse is unblown; a new row replaces the old 16-bit block. This works for FF-backed options, not the regular control fuses in rows 0 and 1.Now that we know how FF words are encoded, here’s a list of the interesting words and their locations. These were discovered by a particularly helpful researcher who cross-compared FF values and effective option words from different GA100 SKUs in order to differentially understand the FF chain/block to option word mappings, as there is no known official mapping.Chain 1 bits 83–106; blocks 5–6Chain 1 bits 107–130; blocks 6–8Memory subpartition floorsweepChain 1 bits 131–138; block 8NV_FUSE_OPT_TPC_GPC0_DISABLE through NV_FUSE_OPT_TPC_GPC7_DISABLEChain 1 bits through for GPC ; blocks 11–15Chain 1 bits 251–274; blocks 15–17Chain 1 bits 307–318; block 19Framebuffer partition floorsweepNV_FUSE_OPT_ROP_L2_DISABLEChain 1 bits 319–342; blocks 19–21NV_FUSE_OPT_NVLINK_DISABLEChain 1 bits 368–370; block 23NV_FUSE_OPT_DISABLE_GEN3_SPEEDChain 2 block 39; which of bits 1 and 9 is unresolvedPCIe Gen3 speed restrictionNV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_MAGIC_BITS_D[25]NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_BOOT_GEN23_DISABLENV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_BOOT_GEN3_DISABLEChain 2, bits 593–608; blocks 37–38Chain 2, bits 609–624; blocks 38–39NV_FUSE_OPT_SYS_PIPE_DISABLEChain 1, bits 372–379; block 23Multi-instance GPU enabled pipesThe acronyms FBIO/FBPA/FBP/TPC/GPC/PES/ROP all refer to microarchitectural elements, please see this diagram from the GA100 whitepaper to further understand how these are related to each other:FBP is the internal NVIDIA term for a “framebuffer partition”, with 2 FBPs to one HBM stack. FBPAs are subpartitions, 2 FBPAs to one FBP. PES/ROP are blocks (seemingly graphics-related) that are required for an SM to function.With this knowledge in hand, we could write new FF rows that set the _DISABLE words to be all zeroes, or at least, as permissive as possible given die defects? If we look at how the _DISABLE options are used in conjunction with other elements, we’ll quickly see that these _DISABLE words are the primary lever we have in preventing parts of the die from being “floorswept”. After illuminating the “what-if”, I’ll talk about the “how”: the exact application of voltage fault injection and the fuse controller safeguards we can defeat with VFI.NVIDIA puts these options in charge of setting floorsweep signals, which will render a die element unreachable (and likely powered down). From experiments, I believe the floorsweep lines are specified in RTL, emanating from the fuse controller and terminating in individual functional blocks and controlling some master power/clock domain switch within the block. I have observed the floorsweeping behavior to correspond with very little latency with the value of the fuse controller’s effective status words for each functional block.Let’s take FBP floorsweeping, for example. On one of my 8 GB cards, was : FBPs 1, 4, 6, and 11 were masked. The separate mask was , covering 6 and 11. After I reduced the FF-backed disable mask to with a replacement FF row, the extra masks on 1 and 4 were gone, but the defective 6 and 11 stayed disabled. That leaves 10 of the die’s 12 FBPs in the effective mask. Functionally, FBPs 1 and 4, which refused register reads and writes when was , became responsive after this fuse write.Although the functional blocks can be “unfloorswept” with FF writes, this does not fully suffice to render the block fully available to an end application - the default framebuffer geometry configuration uses only a portion of each available HBM stack, for example.To bypass that, we can utilize what is essentially a small modification to cmpunlocker’s method. The usual driver patch for the 8 -> 64 GB unlocks writes to a particular set of feature configuration words (FBPA_CFG, SM_SPEED_SELECT, etc.). The default values are chosen to succeed for the commonly found variant of the 170HX, which has the _DISABLE FF-derived option words preventing certain functional blocks from being used (any attempt to use them will return floorswept errors). With the unlocking FF burns in place, we can write even more permissive words into the configuration registers, resulting in what is functionally an A100-80G.With the information we have, it seems straightforward that if one could blow arbitrary FF fuses, any GA100 could be fully unlocked to its maximum capability, as determined by die yield and the populated memory stacks. But how do we blow FF fuses? Let’s take a look at the fuse programming functionality of the fuse controller to understand more.To request a fuse blow, one must write to the FUSEADDR, FUSEWDATA, and FUSECTRL registers belonging to the fuse controller. Although not nominally accessible to the host or to unprivileged requesters, with the Canary in the Crypto Mine ROP, opening up the responsible privilege level masks is trivial. And so, many researchers have attempted to coerce the fuse controller to blow fuses in the FF region. Some of our shared observations follow:The fuse controller has an internal FSM, and it indicates its current state via the FUSECTRL_STATE bits.The fuse controller enters a WRITE_PROGRAM state per each “hot” bit in the requested FUSEWDATA value. This tracks with the expected fuse programming behavior.However, unless a specific option word is cleared, writes to fuse addresses outside of the FPF range (rows 96-221) do not actually take place. Fuses in this region (believed to be “field programmable fuses” indicating a watermark of which ucode versions have run, alongside other field-relevant information) take effect, and the fuse controller state machine behaves identically between FPF and non-FPF regions.The specific option word I am referring to is OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLE (“SBFE”), and it is set to be 1 in all production cards. When this option word is clear, fuse programming is allowed in any address. When it is set, only FPF fuses may be blown. To date, no one has found any way to burn FF fuses with SBFE=1, even when operating the fuse controller from HS contexts. It is not clear what “secured burn” truly means, I speculate that there must be a software-only way to perform non-FPF burns even with SBFE=1, and we just don’t know what the “secured” adjective really means here., , , …; I am delving into using a bunch of NVIDIA-specific terminology in this section as the explanation gets deeper. For a really in-depth explanation of what these mean, I refer you to other sources such as Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon.Importantly, as people have figured out on more permissive cards, it is possible to perform FF burns with SBFE=0! And as it turns out, achieving this state is how we achieve the GA100 unlock. After much trial-and-error, I have resorted to inducing this state via voltage fault injection, and I was able to achieve it. Let’s talk some more about voltage glitching.Much has been said about VFI, and I’ll leave the in-depth explanation to other sources. In short, applying brief pulses of low supply voltage will often cause unexpected behavior in integrated circuits. I asked GPT-6 Astra to design an STM32G4 based board that taps into the PWMVID signal on the CMP PCB. PWMVID is an NVIDIA standard for voltage regulators, and my glitcher intercepts the PWM signal emitted by the GA100 die, and replaces it with its own waveform fed into the MP2888B VRM driver IC. With my setup, I can induce the card’s own VRM to produce timed glitches for me, which is simpler than MOSFET-based setups and enables faster glitching than attempting to directly drive the PMBus.The glitcher requires two connections to the PCB, ideally done with magnet/enameled wire. One wire taps NVVDD for voltage sensing, and another wire taps the PWMVID signal. The only other required step for the glitcher to function is the removal of a 0402 0ohm resistor, which will break the connection between the GA100 output PWM pin and the VRM IC. Finding where to place the taps is trivial by tracing the pinout of the MP2888B, specifically its PWMVID and VOSEN pins (the MP2888B shares a footprint with its sibling public chip MP2888A). Test points directly adjacent to the MP2888B enable relatively easy installation of the PWMVID tap.With this tap in place, a single glitch attempt involves this sequence:Start a timer (“glitch timer”) as soon as NVVDD crosses a thresholdExecute a proposed voltage waveform by issuing a PWMVID signal, aligned to the glitch timerObserve card behavior, repeat from step 1 as neededMy setup achieves steps 1/2 with a simple ACPI S0 -> S3 -> S0 transition, which can be done in a few seconds on a modern desktop platform. More intrusive modifications or expensive rigs can probably achieve a better experiment rate, but in my experience this setup suffices to unlock cards in somewhere between 1 hour and 48 hours of glitching time using the approach described later.For the NVVDD threshold, the Astra-authored firmware uses an STM32 comparator to detect when NVVDD crosses 225mV, after which a tight DMA loop drives the desired duties on the PWMVID pin. After S0, the host inspects the card state and decides what to do next; if it involves another glitch, the glitcher board will be commanded over USB with a glitch pattern. Then the host induces S3 with an RTC timer to wake back up in ~3s (empirically derived period for decent stability).Sometimes the host will fail to return to S0, I’ve remedied this with relegating bookkeeping and glitch campaign preparation to an SBC (Radxa Cubie A5E) which also can drive the motherboard power/reset button pins via GPIO if the glitch target host is unresponsive.More specifics are shared in the GA100VFI repository if you’re interested. For now, let’s take a look at the different interesting states we can trigger via VFI, as well as the specific glitch state that we need to burn FF rows. To help illuminate the differences between each glitch state, I have built an empirical model of how the fuse controller starts up when voltage is applied. Note that without the RTL that implements the fuse controller, all we have are guesses. Here are the hypothesized boot stages:Sense RIR, as required by the fuse macroSense (from fuse macro into readout register) control rowsLatch control rows into control row-derived option wordsLatch regular fuse values into their option wordsLatch FF chain values into their option wordsThese hypothetical stages are based on what I can actually read from the die: controller states, raw rows when works, the published option words, and whether the PRI ring can still reach the rest of the GPU. By looking at a few key values, we can tell glitch outcomes apart. Importantly, glitch patterns and outcomes are very much die-specific, so consider these example waveforms and responses to be just that, examples. Let’s take a look at 3 interesting glitch states.1. All fuses sensed as zeroSome glitches make almost every published option word read as zero. In one captured state, 669 of 672 named option reads were zero; the other three were error responses. The controller’s CRC status was (not parsed yet), the PCIe ID read as (the base GA100 PCIe product ID, does not correspond to a real retail product), and the GPU’s PRI ring was held in reset.This state is consistent with a catastrophic failure on behalf of the fuse controller. The card comes up basically unusable, because almost all boot functions are disrupted by the all-zero state. However, interesting enough, the card trains at PCIe Gen4 natively! Some slightly altered variants may showcase sections of fuses being successfully latched, or containing garbled values instead of all-zeroes. I was not able to push any of these states towards an FF burn; in almost all of them the fuse controller is unreachable or dysfunctional.Reading the RIR data on the CMP 170HX 8GB reveals its exact effect: 15 noop repair instructions, and one write that changes the value of a fuse in row 18, whose option word we can monitor. Further, because the RIR sense is consumed internally by the fuse macro instead of directly by the fuse controller, we can observe a disrupted RIR latch by attempting to read the raw row - the observed bitflip remains consistent across the flipped option word as well as the raw fuse row. This sets an interesting chronological checkpoint in investigating die boot (RIR sense must happen prior to other fuse sensing), but is not a useful glitch in itself.The successful three-pulse state on my first card seemed to disrupt precisely the row0/1 based option words, while leaving other fuses and option words intact. In this state, all of the row0/1 derived option words are zero. The initial readbacks look like this:; BAR0 and the PRI ring respond (both halves parsed without errors)OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLEFUSECTRL/FUSEOPT privilege masksBoth still , unchanged from before the glitchAt this stage, we are still not yet capable of issuing FF writes, because ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0. I am honestly not sure why ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM would be zero, given it’s 1 in retail boards, so this almost reads to me like a way to implement a glitch-detection canary (or at least it would be elegant to do so).Fuse sensing happens one row at a time, with all 32 fuses powered for sensing with one line, meaning it is much more challenging for an attacker to make a single fuse appear as cleared or set. It would make sense, then, to include a “canary” fuse that disables security-critical features (like fuse burning) when it is cleared, because usually the attacker can only manipulate fuse sensing at the row granularity at most. So, when the row0/1 option words come up as all cleared, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0 stops us from burning any fuses.However, take a look at what we have in this state: DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE=0. This word is normally 1, and it stops us from setting the EN_SW_OVERRIDE register to 1, which then lets us “shadow” most of the option words exposed by the fuse controller. Doing so involves writing to a register CTRL_OPT_*, corresponding to option word OPT_*, which then determines the effective value STATUS_OPT_*. This is what lets us shadow SBFE to be 0. But, even though we have DSOV=0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM turns out to be one of the option words that are impossible to shadow, even with DSOV=0. So it seems we’re stuck.At least that’s what I thought, and I banged my head against the wall in this state for a while. Then I noticed that there is one fuse controller command I haven’t tried issuing yet: SENSE_CTRL. I had refrained from issuing this, because on the face of it it seems like all of the row0/1 (control fuse) derived option words would match their fused values, which would reset SBFE, turn off software option word shadowing, and leave us unable to fuse. To my surprise, when I issued this command, all of the control-fuse-derived options went to their fused value, DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE, which remained 0!With DSOV=0, we can trivially set SBFE to 0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM is 1 because it matches its fused value, and we are off to the races! One wrinkle remains in that FUSEWDATA may have a locked down PLM, but with DSOV=0, we can just write 0 to OPT_SECURE_FUSE_WDATA_WR_SECURE to set the PLM to be all-ones, opening host access for fusing.At this point, all that’s left to do is to calculate _DISABLE words that match the _DEFECTIVE values for the features we are interested in, and issue FF burns. Note that the occupied FF space and defective bits differ per die, so each burn must be die-tailored.On 8 GB cards with 80 GB intact (seems to be around ~90% of 8 GB cards from my limited sample size), the unlock yields the full 80 GB as a usable framebuffer. Multiple synthetic tests (writing pseudorandom words throughout the full framebuffer and reading them back after L2 invalidation) as well as real workloads (such as vLLM and SGLand) are fully functional. As mentioned, one of my cards has only 64 GB intact. In this case, the hardware unlock yields no framebuffer advantage.The 170HX is limited to 70 SMs out of the box. In practice, there are almost always >120 SMs non-defective on the die, and the unlock allows using them all. This results in a significant performance uplift, ~1.7x compared to the software-only 170HX unlock, and even an impressive ~1.2x over a retail A100!software-unlocked CMP 170HXhardware-unlocked CMP 170HXThe only thing that stops cmpunlocker from advancing beyond PCIe Gen2 are the FF option words. With relevant bits cleared, Gen3/4 train and are confirmed to be fully functional. When combined with the PCIe decoupling capacitor mod, up to PCIe Gen4 x16 is attainable, matching a retail A100 PCIe variant.Zeroing out the OPT_NVLINK_DISABLE word is only one of the required mods for NVLink to actually work. Because the CMP 170HX PCB is missing the U11 IC (which connects PCIe 3.3v to an NVLink bridge pin), a stock board fails to bring up the reference clock generator on attached NVLink bridges. Simply bridging two of the pins on the footprint of U11 resolves this issue, although it removes whatever regulation or protection was provided by U11. Be careful if you’re bridging GPUs powered by different power supplies, as this will connect the +3.3V rails together unless you leave U11 unpopulated on some of your GPUs! The NVLink bridge works fine if you just patch U11 on one of the boards in the pair.On the firmware side of NVLink enablement, there is a ROM check that needs to be bypassed with additional host-side commands. I’m sure your clanker can figure it out ;)While investigating the NVLink unlock, I also found a few interesting quirks with NVIDIA’s NVLink implementation on the GA100. I will be posting a further blog post on this, so stay tuned!With arbitrary fuse burning, we mostly gain feature unlocks. Some security-sensitive options are shipped unblown by default, and burning them may lead to interesting footholds. But what’s more interesting to me are the deeper glitch states where many default-blown security-sensitive fuses sense unblown, enabling routes like debug HS execution, which grant unprecedented access to die internals.

item.title: Tim Peters has died
item.author: ayhanfuat
item.content:encoded: I wrote this some time ago about Tim:I worked with Tim and the rest of Python Labs for a couple of years in the early 2000s. Tim was a hugely positive influence on me throughout my Python career.Before I had ever spoken to Tim, he was already legendary. He had worked for Cray Research writing compilers for supercomputers, and for Dragon Systems, writing speech-to-text software at a time when such a task was considered largely impossible. He took up Python on a lark in its very early days, becoming something like Python’s second real user after Guido.Guido came to rely on Tim heavily. Tim will demur about this, but as far as I can tell, Tim and Guido were largely partners in the design evolution of very early Python, and before most important features made it in to Python, you could be sure that they had been examined from every angle, shaken, stirred, and thunk about very hard by both of them.Tim often played the role of gatekeeper and polisher. You have Tim to thank at least partially if you were a refugee from Java or Microsoft languages, which made excuses for their sprawling verbosity, complexity, and poor readability. Python, at the time, made none of those and had none of that (it now does). Tim was crucial in ensuring it stayed that way during his most active years. He will claim differently, but, by my observation, it is no accident that Python ballooned in complexity after his exit as day-to-day core developer. Perhaps this was more due to the resignation of Guido as BDFL and the new Steering Council model, which was also coincident, but not having Tim around didn’t help either.It was pure joy to read Tim’s Usenet and mail list posts, which were full of humor and good nature and measured positivity and not a little winking darkness. They somehow resonated with me on my journey from becoming a new programmer to a not-so-new programmer and they lit a path to becoming one on which you could be dramatically competent without becoming cryptic and insufferable. He was intensely knowledgeable, and unfailingly precise when arguing for or against some design change. But he was always gentle and patient and matter-of-fact, preferring to use humor and warmth rather than bile and authority as the currency in which he dealt.Tim penned “the Zen of Python” (“beautiful is better than ugly…”) which can be seen via “import this” to this day. You can see a bit of his wonderful humor and style in the prelude to his introduction of the poem . His enthusiasm was infectious, and in the days when he was most involved, most everyone could be witnessed spouting Tim-isms (winks and “'lys” and whatnot).When I did get the chance to work with Tim, he was just as influential. He had absolutely no pretensions. If I hadn’t already known him to be a computer savant, I would have assumed he was a biker or mechanic due to his long grey locks, full mustache and and working-class fashion sense. I would later find out that he had indeed worked at Harley-Davidson. I think he’s originally from Wisconsin, but an East- or West-Coaster not fluent in Midwest tongues could be excused for believing his disarming accent is Chicagoan. He seemed just like a regular-looking neighborhood punch-the-clock guy, not unlike all the mechanics and deliverymen and cooks and dishwashers and event staff I’d worked around as a kid and in my 20s. Except he was pretty much the smartest guy in every room he entered.Tim’s demeanor and lack of pretense inspired me to think that despite my own lack of education and pedigree, with enough effort and grace, that I might become a half-competent programmer. And eventualy I did. But before meeting Tim, it was not a given. I was alienated by the pretensions of my community peers, and I was often reminded that they were not necessary only by Tim.He was somewhat private. He could often be found with a pen and paper outside the building just standing alone, staring blankly off into space, presumably thinking about some mind-boggling algorithmic topic with which he had just been charged by our CTO, or perhaps mentally designing some aspect of a pet project, scribbling something every few minutes. He applied himself to our code, which included a custom database written in C and Python. He diagnosed and fixed a data-destroying bug in that byzantine codebase for our largest customer. This saved the account, and likely gave us enough runway for another year or so.Everyone who worked there was in awe of his programming and debugging skills, and while we tried our best to let the poor man be, we often asked him questions, many of which were pedestrian and dull. I remember one of our teammates trying to engage him into a debugging session, claiming that some fault seemed to happen every six runs. He smiled winkingly and asked “have you grepped the source for six?” It was a minor jab but given the sincerity of the question, and the person from which it had come, it occurred to me at the time that it might not be the worst theory of debugging from which to start.Tim was a Director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014, bringing Python across an uncanny valley from a time where it was “interesting but ignorable” to “the planet’s default language” along with a cast of other incredible people. If you use Python, it’s not in small part due to Tim.When I started my own open source projects, it was Tim whom I channeled during design discussions and sprints. I quite consciously used tricks I had learned from him to make the process fun and welcoming. Rather than become prickly about some technical conflict, I would try to use low-brow humor to defuse things and I would try very hard to learn everything I could about the topic before responding such that I could gain and rely on the respect of other contributors. I often failed, of course, because I’m not Tim, but I was at least a twentieth a Tim, and at the time, I think my co-contributors would have agreed that the projects I led were fun and worthwhile to work on.It is in this way that Tim’s influence is likely most obvious to people today, because I’m not the only one who channeled him; any Python project started between 1995 and 2010 has a bit of Tim culture in it.

item.title: Show HN: Black Ops II statically recompiled to native ARM64 macOS
item.author: adrbn
item.content:encoded: I grew up with Black Ops 2 and wanted to see if I could make it work on my 2020 MacBook Pro. So I used Claude Opus 5.5 to create a tool that converts your copy of the game (from Steam) to a native ARM64 Mac app, with almost 60fps in all areas. The whole game is statically recompilated ahead-of-time (AOT) and does not use any emulator whatsoever, be it Wine, Crossover or Rosetta. The best thing is the performance, although some heat issues are still to fix. You get to play the whole Campaign, local Multiplayer (with bots) and local Zombies (all DLCs maps; you need to have them in your Steam library obviously) at about 60fps. Split-screen was not in the PC version, but I've been working on it lately; it's coming soon! LAN mode is on the roadmap for later too :)

item.title: Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave
item.author: js2
item.content:encoded: Update, November 11, 2026: I’ve since switched to Secretive, which keeps keys in the Secure Enclave with a much better prompt. Part 2 is coming. I’ve also corrected one error, marked below.I’ve been paranoid about my SSH keys for a while now. They just sit there in , protected by nothing but file permissions. Any malicious script that gets access to my filesystem could just copy them and get into all my servers. Also, there have been many stories out there online about fake interview assignments that asked to clone a repo and run it on your local machine. This is one of the reasons I switched completely to using devcontainers, but even that was not really enough for me (and it shouldn’t be enough for you or anybody else really).So I finally decided to do something about it.I have decided to go with the native macOS Secure Enclave approach (using only out-of-the-box tools) because it ended up plain ugly and I can’t live with that. However, it is a fully functional, working solution that I would definitely use otherwise.After some research, I found several ways to protect SSH keys:Native macOS Secure Enclave — no third-party apps, built into the OS — third-party app that stores keys in Secure Enclave — hardware security key with FIDO2 support — store keys in an encrypted vault, use their SSH agentI already use 1Password, but I might switch to something else in the future. Bitwarden recently added SSH key support (even on the free tier!), but it’s still a software solution — the keys are encrypted at rest but decrypted in memory when used.What I really wanted was hardware-backed security. The private key should literally be impossible to extract, even if my Mac is fully compromised.That left me with YubiKey or Secure Enclave. I have a YubiKey 5C, but I wanted to try the native approach first — no extra hardware to carry around, no third-party apps to maintain.What is Secure Enclave SSH?Since macOS Sequoia (and Tahoe), macOS supports SSH keys backed by the Secure Enclave, a security subsystem on the Mac’s chip that is isolated from the main processor. The private key is created inside it and never leaves.When you SSH somewhere, your Mac asks the Secure Enclave to sign the authentication challenge. If you enable Touch ID, you have to approve each signing operation. The actual private key never exists in memory or on disk.The workflow is surprisingly similar to regular SSH keys: (a file)Just a reference (useless without this Mac)Copy public key to Touch ID prompt, then worksStep 1: Create the Secure Enclave KeymacOS provides the command (Smart Card Authentication) to manage CryptoTokenKit identities. Despite the name, it works with Secure Enclave too. — a label for your reference (only visible locally) — NIST P-256 curve, on-xportable (the key can never leave Secure Enclave) — require metric (Touch ID) for every useYou’ll be prompted for Touch ID to create the key.Problem 1: Touch ID ErrorWhen I first ran this command, I got a scary error:Error: Error Domain=NSOSStatusErrorDomain Code=-25293 "Failed to generate keypair" (errKCAuthFailed / errSecAuthFailed: / Authorization/Authentication failed.) UserInfo={..., NSUnderlyingError=... "Failed to get bio catacomb UUID for user 502." ...} Turns out my Touch ID enrollment got reset somehow. After re-enrolling my fingerprint in System Settings → Touch ID & Password, the command worked fine.You can verify the key was created:Key Type Public Key Hash Prot Label Common Name Valid To Valid p-256-ne A71277F0BC5825A7B3576D014F31282A866EF3BC bio ssh-MacBook ssh-MacBook 2027-01-26, 10:18 YES Step 2: Export the Key HandleNow we need to create a “key handle” file that SSH can use. This is NOT the private key — it’s just a reference that tells SSH “go ask the Secure Enclave to sign this.”When prompted for PIN, just press Enter (it’s not used for biometric keys). Touch ID will pop up. This creates and in your current directory.Move them to your SSH directory:Step 3: Configure SSH to Use the Secure Enclave ProviderAdd this to your (or ):If you search for “macOS Secure Enclave SSH” online, you’ll find a lot of guides telling you to run . Don’t. It’s deprecated:WARNING: The -K and -A flags are deprecated and have been replaced by the --apple-use-keychain and --apple-load-keychain flags, respectively. And even the new flags don’t work for Secure Enclave keys — they’re for the traditional macOS Keychain, not CryptoTokenKit. The environment variable is the correct approach.Step 4: Get Your Public Keysk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... ssh: That at the end is the comment. The key’s FIDO2 application ID is stored inside the key itself (the last field of the base64 part). copies it into the comment, so the line shows it twice. You can replace the comment with anything when copying to ; the key stays the same:sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... macbook-secure-enclave Correction, November 11, 2026: An earlier version said the trailing was the FIDO2 application ID. It’s the comment; the application ID is stored inside the key. Thanks to computerfriend on Hacker News for pointing it out.Step 5: Copy to Your ServerOr manually paste the public key (with your comment) into on the server.Step 6: Configure ~/.ssh/configProblem 3: SSH Doesn’t Find the KeyAfter setting everything up, I tried to SSH… and it asked for my password.The verbose output () showed SSH was only trying my old RSA key:debug1: Offering public key: /Users/sergii/.ssh/id_rsa RSA SHA256:... The problem: SSH doesn’t automatically look for files named . It only auto-discovers standard names like , , .The fix is to explicitly add it to your :SSH tries identity files in order, so put the Secure Enclave key first if you want it to be the default.⚠️ If you’re using 1Password’s SSH agent (), it might conflict with this setup. I had to comment it out while testing.You should get a Touch ID prompt, then connect.One thing I’m not thrilled about: the Touch ID dialog says “ctccardtoken needs to authenticate to continue” instead of something friendly like “SSH wants to use your key.”This is because the prompt comes from CryptoTokenKit — a low-level framework that Apple hasn’t polished for end-user SSH. If this bothers you, provides a much nicer UI while still using Secure Enclave under the hood.Why Touch ID for Everything?I initially thought about creating two keys — one with Touch ID for “important” servers, one without for convenience (like Git operations).But then I realized: without , malware could use my key silently. With , I always know when something is using my SSH key. A few extra taps per day is a small price for that visibility.So my recommendation if you’re planning to store your SSH keys this way: just use for everything. If it ever gets annoying, you can always create a second key later.Secure Enclave keys are tied to your specific Mac. If your Mac dies, the keys die with it.That’s by design: the key can’t be exported, so it can’t be backed up either. Keep more than one key instead. Add your Secure Enclave key AND a backup key (from a YubiKey, or another Mac) to your servers’ . If one device is lost, you still have access via the other.It seems to be a proper way to store your SSH keys securely, and it is way better than storing them on your hard drive.With the implementation above you get:✅ Private key literally cannot be stolen (it’s in hardware)✅ Every SSH operation requires Touch ID (I know when my key is used)✅ No third-party apps needed✅ Works with existing workflowHowever, I’ve been somewhat surprised by the ugliness of the UI. Not sure why Apple released such an unpolished thing. In each and every presentation they have a section on security (where their Apple logo becomes an Apple lock), so I was expecting an actual aesthetically appealing look for their security features. It is definitely not the case. My sense of beauty is not compatible with this ugliness, so I will be looking into other solutions to store my SSH keys in Secure Enclave such as Secretive.I also still need a backup option in case anything happens to my Mac.
