item.title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
item.author: speckx
item.content:encoded:
The following subscription-only content has been made available to you by an LWN subscriber. Thousands of subscribers depend on LWN for the best news from the Linux and free software communities. If you enjoy this article, please consider subscribing to LWN. Thank you for visiting LWN.net!
By November 10, 2026Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.Synaptics and DisplaylinkThe dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu.The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities.A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices.Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software.He posted the first patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. "If you have knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see, help would be very welcome." He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings, but no advice specific to the problem he was trying to solve.Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few issues. There was no reply to his issue.He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is available in this PDF compiled by Lothian. He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics:The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK.From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions.Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the "intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink", so he wanted to make him aware now rather than "have the situation become more formal later". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which explains why the email made reference to the UK.On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice. The letter stated that Lothian had not "" to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued with "public statements and further development activities". It included an appendix with a list of 125 patents that "cover fundamental aspects of DisplayLink's architecture and operation", but did not specify which patents might be infringed by the work.Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance with, including ceasing development of "any software or other implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent", withdrawing submissions of materials "made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or organization", and to identify in writing every location "in which the relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or distributed". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands.Lothian, instead, posted version three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on August 26. He said that the previous two versions had "", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko.On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. "A claim chart mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for me to understand and properly respond to your concerns."He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which was created to help open-source developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to "reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source software".He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims "interact with our respective OIN commitments", and expressed a desire to sort things out with Synaptics constructively. "I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities".
Lothian did not think he could "reasonably provide the signed undertaking" Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work.Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned: As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now we are escalating as we deem appropriate. The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be "single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN, and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other organization.Bateman sent a follow-up letter, dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010 and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply would result in the company seeking "monetary compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to create the attached documentation of your infringing acts". That amount would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were complied with.Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts "ideally with someone qualified to help me read them". Bateman replied that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that "DisplayLink is not a member of OIN" and none of its technology was licensable through OIN.Synaptics a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory. In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion.OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System Definition, but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs ("a component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still image or audio data stream or signal") are not covered unless specifically mentioned in this list of components.I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation.Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's demands. For now, he may continue working on some of the components that are not affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted to the kernel. "Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics."Perhaps amusingly, Lothian told me that someone from Synaptics finally replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not intend to follow up on the comments: "You can't threaten to sue me and then say 'can you update your pull request?'"For the time being, Synaptics has succeeded in shutting down an effort to improve the way DisplayLink docks work with Linux. It is an unpleasant reminder that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for free-software developers and users.

item.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
item.author: paulirish
item.content:encoded:
+JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge.200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1]I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU.We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.)People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided. DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal" DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src
If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler!

item.title: Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data
item.author: Yorothegoat
item.content:encoded: Today we’re launching Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta, and Claude Dashboards becomes generally available as Claude Data. Whiteboards is a shared board where your team brainstorms with Claude, Sheets is a spreadsheet Claude builds and edits with you, and Claude Data adds data stories, certified queries, and live sharing. These are available on all paid plans.Working with Claude on a project often meant moving the output over to another tool or program, where Claude didn’t have live access to follow progress and changes. Now, your documents, boards, sheets, and dashboards can stay in Claude, with access for your team to continue editing together. When ready, you can bring the outputs directly into tools from our partners and continue working there.Many people use Claude as a thought partner, but brainstorming with it has typically meant copy-pasting the results elsewhere so you can then start brainstorming or collaborating with your coworkers. Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add their notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft the action items for each person. You can focus on any part of the board by dragging a box around it and asking Claude questions. When you’re done brainstorming, Claude can turn the board into a doc or deck, or bring it into tools like Lucid, Miro, or Vani by Zoho, where you can continue working on it with your team.Claude can now generate spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-downs, often from just a prompt like asking for a campaign tracker or a hiring budget. It can edit in the cells, outlining each new edit so you can track changes. You can share sheets with your team, so you and Claude can work on them together.For now, sheets have simple spreadsheet functionality, but we are working on adding more. When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel. You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet.Claude Dashboards launched in beta in October, enabling teams to ask quick questions of their company’s data in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery, and ClickHouse. Starting today, it’s generally available as Claude Data. We changed the name because the way companies use their data is broader than dashboards, and the product now covers how they work more broadly. Certified queries and live sharing are in beta. Here are some ways teams can use Claude Data:Create certified definitions of metrics. Your data team can certify the queries everyone should use, so you don’t end up building or working on dashboards with conflicting data. Charts built on these metrics carry a "certified" badge showing they’re certified. You can work with Claude in Claude Data to draft data stories or narrated videos from your metrics, for you to review before sharing.Share current numbers with With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access.Match your look-and-feel. Design systems are now supported in Claude Data.Get faster loading with caching. Previously, every dashboard would reload on every load. Now, dashboards support caching, and refresh cadences can be set on a per-dashboard basis.Claude Data now has tracked changes, so you can see who has made edits and roll back to a specific version if needed.Our partners for Claude Data include Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog, and Sigma.Starting today, interactive connectors can open as full apps beside your conversation or in full screen, so you can work in tools like Adobe, Atlassian, Box, and Notion yourself, or ask Claude to make changes with you.Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Data work on web, desktop, and mobile. Claude Data needs a data connector, such as a warehouse or CRM. On Team plans, all three are on by default. On Enterprise plans, Claude Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, and Claude Data turns on by default on November 19, 2026. You can change these anytime in Organization settings > Artifacts.

item.title: Val Town is winding down
item.author: tosh
item.content:encoded: We’ve made the difficult decision to wind down Val Town.You took a big leap of faith to build on us. We thank you for your trust, and we’re sorry we can’t continue to serve you.We are pausing billing today, and will continue servicing existing subscriptions for free. If you pre-paid for our annual plan, we will issue you a partial refund.Here’s the timeline on our wind-down:New signups and plan upgradesRead-only mode (not including sqlite and blob storage)Thank you, the members of the Val Town team, for giving it your all over the past four years. Thank you Tom, Jackson, Charlie, Pete, Potluck, Charmaine, Max, Andre, Sophie, Wolf, Justin, Rodrigo and JP. It was an honor.Thank you, Dan Levine, for being the best investor I could’ve asked for. Thank you, my other investors, for your trust, support, and capital.Thank you, our customers and users, for building on us with passion and creativity.

item.title: AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast
item.author: pixelpoet
item.content:encoded: Hello you fine Internet folks,Today we’re looking at AMD’s next-generation Zen 6 CPU core family. We’ll explore the changes from Zen 5 and what the differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c tell us about AMD’s approach to microarchitecture.At a high level the changes AMD made to the integer schedules stand out, returning to a layout reminiscent of Zen 3 and Zen 4.Zen 5 had the best direction predictor of any core we have measured and Zen 6 seemingly builds upon that same direction predictor.Zen 6 has also improved the ability of the core to do 2 branches per cycle with Zen 6 able to do 2 branches per cycle within the L1 instruction cache.When the footprint exceeds the L1i, then it falls to just a single branch per cycle for the rest of the BTB except for the 64B test which goes up to 4 cycles per branch for the L2 BTB.When comparing the BTB of Zen 6 to Zen 5, Zen 6 appears to have focused on improving the speed of the BTB compared to beefing up the capacity.The accuracy of Zen 6’s Branch Predictor Unit is very similar to Zen 5’s while also being faster which is a good thing considering that Zen 5 already had a very accurate Branch Predictor.Zen 6 carries forward the same dual decode cluster schema that Zen 5 introduced but, unlike Zen 5 where a single thread could only effectively use a single decode cluster, now with Zen 6 a single thread can use both decode clusters.Outside of the L1i, Zen 6 looks very similar to Zen 5’s behavior on the instruction side of things.The execution engine of Zen 6 is overall very similar to Zen 5, but there are some important differences to be mindful of.On the integer side, Zen 6 brings back Zen 4’s NOP pairing behavior, retiring up to 16 NOPs per cycle. Zen 6 also comes closer to theoretical peak throughput for simple integer instructions than Zen 5, sustaining 5.96 64-bit adds per cycle against Zen 5’s 5.25 with the same six ALUs.AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two. According to AMD, Zen 5’s third integer multiply unit did not justify its area cost.On the vector side, the floating-point units are unchanged, with Zen 6 still handling two 512-bit FADDs, FMULs, or FMAs per cycle. The change is in VNNI, where Zen 6 doubles the number of units from two to four and our 512-bit VNNI test goes from 1.99 to 3.88 instructions per cycle, with Zen 6c matching it. VNNI instructions are useful for operations like calculating the inner loop of quantized inference as well as for video codecs using them for video filters as well.Moving over to the other notable change, Zen 5 could already perform four per cycle, but our test shows only two of them could be vector loads, regardless of if they were 256 or 512 bit loads. Zen 6 raises 256-bit loads to four per cycle on both cores while leaving 512-bit loads at two, so both widths now reach the same 128 bytes per cycle which matters because most shipped vector code still targets AVX1/2.In the past the difference between the Classic cores and the Dense cores in terms of the architecture were, for all intents and purposes, functionally identical with the biggest changes being in the number of cores on a CCD and the amount of L3 cache per core. With the Zen 6 family, that has changed.Starting inside of the core, the changes occur after micro-op dispatch and seemingly end after the load queue.The main differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c lie in the capacities of their out-of-order structures. Several of these structures are larger on Zen 6c, allowing it to keep more work in flight and absorb more latency than Zen 6. The reorder buffer grows from 576 to 640 entries, the integer register file from 288 to 352, the vector scheduler from 138 to 180, and the load queue from 280 to 330.The differences suggest that AMD is specializing the two designs. Zen 6 appears tuned for high frequency, while Zen 6c has more capacity to tolerate comparatively high memory latency.Zen 6 and Zen 6c use 12-core and 32-core CCDs, respectively, but both provide 4 MB of L3 cache per core. That gives the 12-core CCD 48 MB of L3 cache and the 32-core CCD 128 MB.L3 latency has increased from about 47 cycles on Zen 5 to 55 cycles on Zen 6 and 66 cycles on Zen 6c. The larger caches and greater number of mesh stops likely contribute to the increase. In nanoseconds, Zen 6’s higher clock hides most of the increase, at 10.7 ns against 10.3 ns on the Zen 5-based EPYC 9355P, while Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger CCX put it at 16.4 ns.Moving over to bandwidth, we see that Zen 6 fixes Zen 5’s odd L2 bandwidth behavior, where a core pulled only about 42 bytes per cycle across most of the L2’s capacity, in Zen 6 the read path now reliably delivers 64 bytes per cycle. The rest of the cache hierarchy is largely unchanged in bandwidth per cycle.Store-to-load forwarding is seemingly unchanged from Zen 5 and is where the behavior of Zen 6 and Zen 6c re-unify.A 32-bit load from the same address as a 64-bit store completes with effectively zero latency which lets Zen 6 handle two dependent store-load pairs per cycle. Loads fully contained within the store complete in 7 cycles regardless of alignment with partial overlaps costing 14 cycles, matching Zen 5.The EPYC 9686F is near the top of our estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 results. It roughly matches the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, AMD’s highest-end client CPU from the previous generation, in integer rate and beats it in floating-point rate. At a matched 4.1 GHz, the 9686F leads the 9950X3D2 by about 4% in integer and 11% in floating point, despite the X3D part’s much larger L3.The EPYC 9996 is no slouch either. It roughly matches the previous-generation EPYC 9575F in single-threaded performance, despite running at lower clocks and having four times as many cores. It also edges out NVIDIA’s Vera in integer and leads it by about 20% in floating point.The EPYC 9686F leads on almost every subtest and finishes about 18% ahead of the EPYC 9996 in both suites. It scores 6.20 versus 5.25 in integer and 10.6 versus 8.99 in floating point, with some of its largest leads in 714.cpython, 766.femflow, and 772.marian.Against the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F, the 9996 scores 5.25 versus 5.13 in integer and 8.99 versus 9.01 in floating point while running about 900 MHz slower. The 9996 also edges out the 9686F in 721.gcc and 765.roms, two subtests where the 9686F’s higher clock provides no advantage.Top-down breakdowns of pipeline slots on the two Zen 6 chips show where the 9686F’s lead comes from. The integer-rate profiles look almost identical in core-bound subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, 710.omnetpp, 735.gem5, and 753.ns3, retiring slots account for nearly the same share on both chips, with differences of less than one percentage point.Memory-heavy subtests show larger gaps. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 37.9% to 50.0% of pipeline slots in 729.abc, from 19.0% to 34.1% in 723.llvm, and from 24.8% to 33.2% in 708.sqlite. The share of retiring slots falls accordingly. Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger shared L3 cache may help explain its lower memory-stall share.The floating-point profiles look similar for most subtests. The retiring share in 731.astcenc, 772.marian, and 767.nest differs by about one percentage point or less, and 709.cactus spends over half its slots stalled on front-end bandwidth on both chips.The larger gaps again appear in memory-heavy subtests. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 42.5% to 55.3% of slots in 765.roms, from 60.9% to 67.6% in 749.fotonik3d, and from 17.8% to 33.8% in 782.lbm. These are also tests where the 9686F’s higher clock helps least: it trails the 9996 in 765.roms, roughly ties in 749.fotonik3d, and leads by about 11% in 782.lbm, despite clocking up to roughly 29% higher.Running the 9686F at 4.1 GHz to match the 9996 removes the clock advantage, and the overall picture flips: the 9686F scores 4.92 and 8.64 at that clock, putting Zen 6c about 6.7% ahead per clock in integer and 4% in floating point. At the same clock speed, Zen 6 and Zen 6c look almost identical in core-bound integer subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, retiring slots account for 67.3% of the total on the EPYC 9686F versus 67.6% on the EPYC 9996.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5.However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior.The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs.AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs.

item.title: .name Grandfathered
item.author: p4bl0
item.content:encoded: After a long and expensive battle, news just dropped that Verisign is retracting its plan to terminate 22,000 domain names and email redirects. Although they will be closing new registrations for 3rd-level .name domains, all existing domains (including this website) and email redirects will remain indefinitely.This was a team effort. It was inspiring how many talented people joined this fight. From Doytchin who kicked everything off, to Jim who flew to Bali to make the case to ICANN in person, to Patrik, Troy, Huyen, Keith, Judy, Erik, and Ryan who wrote formal reconsideration requests, to my lawyers Jan, Flip and Diégo who threw the book at ICANN, to Beverly, Stefan, Vaughan, Irv, Pablo, Larry, Lionel, Daniel, Ori, Markus, Kirk, Ed, Jeremy, Stephan, Matija, Jan, Simon, Mark, and Evan who filed letters of support. I'd also like to sincerely thank selected individuals within ICANN who had the courage to stand up against the bureaucracy. Without exception, everyone I spoke with was a remarkable person.

item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
item.author: meetpateltech
item.content:encoded: Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning.Two weeks ago, we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program. Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops.Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity’s WANDR, and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model.To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.

item.title: Palantir hires a former Democratic senator as it faces scrutiny in new Congress
item.author: DeepLogin
item.content:encoded: Tech companies are expecting a wave of scrutiny from Democrats for the industry's ties with the Trump administration when they take over Congress in January. In anticipation, many are hiring former Democratic lawmakers and aides to make their case to the incoming House and Senate majorities. Related Story: NPRAmong the latest to make that move is Palantir, which has hired former Sen. Jon Tester, a colorful Montana Democrat who's also an organic farmer."My agreement with Palantir is advisory in nature, it is not lobbying," Tester, who lost reelection to the Senate in 2024, told NPR in an interview.The secretive American software and artificial intelligence company has drawn the ire of Democrats in Congress during President Trump's second term. Palantir — named by billionaire founder Peter Theil after the mythical "seeing stone" from J.R.R. Tolkien's — has been accused of abetting mass surveillance on Americans and immigrants."Perception is reality in Washington, D.C. and in politics in general," said Tester. "But the fact is, I think Palantir has got a good story to tell, and they need to tell it. And hopefully folks will be receptive to it."Palantir has long denied claims it aids mass surveillance on the American public — saying it doesn't gather or manipulate data at all, but instead creates tools for government agencies and private companies to organize and optimize their own information. The company has said it is committed to "protecting privacy and upholding liberal democratic values."Earlier this year, while in the minority, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., along with 30 other Democratic lawmakers demanded answers about Palantir's contracts with the Department of Homeland Security and whether its tools are part of efforts by the federal government to surveil Americans. Palantir denied the accusation and said it is "neither conducting nor enabling mass surveillance of American citizens," but Wyden wasn't fully satisfied with its response, according to his Senate office."Senator Wyden has a number of questions about Palantir's work to facilitate the Trump-Vance abuse of government data that he intends to ask again as chairman of the Finance Committee," Wyden's staff wrote in a statement to NPR. "If Palantir is not responsive next year, compulsory processes will be on the table."It's not a coincidence that tech companies are turning to Democrats to help burnish their reputation, said Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former State Department official."I think at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money and they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability," Ibrahim said. Related Story: NPRDuring Trump's second term, Palantir's CEO and co-founder Alex Karp — a self-described liberal — has been highly critical of Democrats on issues like immigration and AI."I would say to my Democratic friends, also of which I still have, I hope many," Karp said in an interview with Axios in 2025 specifically referencing his support for much more restrictive immigration policies. "You have to grow a spine because a lot of these people actually agree with me in private."During his 18 years in the Senate, Tester was an outspoken critic of the PATRIOT Act that passed shortly after the 9/11 attacks that expanded the Justice Department's surveillance powers. When asked whether his concerns over government surveillance remain and whether he has the same concerns with his new employer, Tester said Palantir is different and that the company doesn't build "big databases" or trade in private data."I wanted to do away with the Patriot Act because it was about privacy," Tester said. "It was about making sure that I am not being watched by anybody, including Big Brother. And by the way, I've talked to many people within Palantir. They believe the same way I do. This is an organization that believes in privacy." Related Story: NPRLast year, over a dozen former Palantir employees criticized the company over its $30 million contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to create a tool that provides "near real-time visibility" into the movement of migrants. The former employees argued the company violated its own code of conduct by working with the Trump administration on such products. Related Story: NPRValued at over $350 billion, Palantir currently holds $2 billion worth of federal contracts, according to government records. The lion's share are with the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and State — but the software firm also works with the Departments of Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and Health and Human Services.Tester said he'll be focused on the government services side of Palantir's work.The former Montana senator called the midterm election results a blue "tidal wave" after two years of a Congress that gave him "great disappointment.""It is going to make a difference as far as the policies that are being advocated for," Tester said of the upcoming Congress. "I don't think you're going to see the kind of aggressive tactics that were taken forth by ICE moving forward." The tech industry is bracing for a new Democrat-controlled Congress. A company that is likely to face scrutiny has just hired a prominent Democrat. NPR's Luke Garrett reports.LUKE GARRETT, BYLINE: Palantir is a secretive software firm with $2 billion worth of contracts across the federal government. The majority are with the departments of Defense and Homeland Security. Last year, former employees told NPR the company's products gave DHS near-real-time visibility into the movements of migrants in the U.S. Now some Democrats have vowed to investigate Palantir's work with the Trump administration and whether it's helping the government conduct mass surveillance. Jon Tester, who was a Democratic senator for 18 years, has been hired to advise the company.JON TESTER: You know, a perception is reality in Washington, D.C. and in politics in general. But the fact is that I think Palantir's got a good story to tell, and they need to tell it. And hopefully folks will be receptive to it.GARRETT: The company was founded by billionaire investor Peter Thiel, who named Palantir after the mythical seeing stone from "The Lord Of The Rings." Its CEO, Alex Karp, is a self-described liberal who has worked closely with the Trump administration, and he's been highly critical of Democrats on issues like immigration. Here's Karp on "The Axios Show" last year.(SOUNDBITE OF TV SHOW, "THE AXIOS SHOW")ALEX KARP: I would say to my Democratic friends, also of which I still have, I hope, many, there - you have to grow a spine because a lot of these people actually agree with me in private.GARRETT: Tester tells NPR he'll be focused on Palantir's work streamlining government services for farmers and veterans.TESTER: And I think that's what it's about. I mean, it's about saving money. It's about making sure government works for people.GARRETT: As a senator, Tester aggressively opposed the Bush-era PATRIOT Act, which expanded government surveillance. When asked if he had the same surveillance concerns about Palantir, Tester said he didn't.TESTER: I've talked to many people within Palantir. They believe the same way I do. This is an organization that believes in privacy.GARRETT: Tester's employment at Palantir comes as other tech companies have also gone on a hiring spree of former Democratic lawmakers and aides in anticipation of changing power in Washington. Senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and former State Department official Aya Ibrahim says that's not a coincidence.AYA IBRAHIM: I think, at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money. And they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability.GARRETT: Ibrahim says the midterm results are an opportunity to check the growing power of the tech industry.Luke Garrett, NPR News, Washington.

item.title: Smart home devices should work without the internet
item.author: skittleson
item.content:encoded: I wrote the first draft, AI helped me edit and rewrite it, and I made the final pass. The rules, setups, and talks are my own.TLDR; Nothing core in my house depends on a vendor’s server. If the internet goes down, the house keeps running. That’s been rule one for about ten years, and my other rules came out of it. This post has the rules, then both talks I’ve given on home automation, slide by slide.My Nest integration worked until Google broke the API. That’s the failure I plan around now. The talks have a few more: a Samsung fridge showing a TLS certificate error on its own screen, and a Camp Chef grill controller that needs Wi-Fi to show you the temperature.Everything that matters runs on hardware I own. That’s Tasmota on ESP boards, an MQTT broker, and Node-RED on a Raspberry Pi. I do use some cloud services, mostly Alexa and a few AWS ones. Alexa is just another way to flip a switch. If it’s down, the wall switches and the wall dashboard still work.From the first talk, restated in the second:No internet, no problem. Core stuff has to work with the internet unplugged. Alexa can be a way in, but never the only way.Don’t remove the old way while adding the new one. If someone tapes a wall switch on so a smart bulb keeps power, I skipped this rule.Be agile. Rooms get used differently and people move in and out, so it all has to be cheap to change.Check your automations. I once had four scheduled triggers hitting the same garden pump.Exceptions must be exceptional. I can break a rule, but only for a reason I’d still agree with six months later.Added after year five, once more people lived in the house:A cloud device needs an API with logs or it doesn’t get installed. I don’t want a black box in the house.Config lives in one place instead of five vendor apps.More than one way in: an app, Alexa, a QR code, or an NFC tag.If I keep doing the same steps, they become a routine.Devices talk pub/sub over MQTT instead of point to point.No batteries unless they last a year or more between changes. Nobody wants to swap a door sensor battery at 2am.Talk One: Home AutomationNobody needs any of this. I like building things that just work in the background, and each automation is a small puzzle.Everything talks to a cloud now: phones, laptops, thermostats, locks. Those clouds may or may not be up when you need them, so know what you’re signing up for before you plug something in.Most people start here: a thermostat, a plug, a lock. Each has its own app and account.Every device lands somewhere on this triangle. A cloud camera is cheap and easy, and it costs you privacy. A switch I flash myself takes longer to set up, but I can hook it into anything. I figure out where a device lands before I buy it.Someone (often me) automates a light, then has to tape the wall switch on so the smart bulb keeps power. If a switch in a room ever did nothing, this is why.The better fix is an in-wall Wi-Fi switch. The switch still works like a normal switch and I can still automate it. It’s more work to install than a smart plug, but nobody has to change their habits.Rule one: if the internet goes down, my lights still turn on.It’s never done. Rooms get used differently, people move in and out, new devices show up. Whatever you build has to be cheap to change.The garage cooling flow starts from a manual trigger and checks if the door is closed. Then it opens the door, waits, and turns on the fan. If cooling is already running, it just sends a notification. Small flow, but it has kept the garage from baking more than once.The door sensor and reed switch both report into a transform step that sets a global flag and logs to Grafana. Below that is the chart from a few real days: 21 opens, with spikes showing when each one happened. It’s easy to skip reporting/alerting. This can alert me if the garage was left open, which is useful when I accidentally leave it open.Four scheduled triggers all hit the same pump. It’s easy to end up with automations fighting over one device, so every so often I check whether they still make sense together.I’ve broken all of these plenty of times, so they’re more like guidelines.Three ways to do “event in, action out.” Node-RED is my main tool. Alexa routines and IFTTT-style applets cover the stuff I don’t want to build myself.MQTT keeps things decoupled. The temperature sensor publishes and doesn’t care who’s listening, so a phone and a backend can both subscribe without the sensor doing anything extra. The sprinkler controller in the Tasmota post works the same way.A Sonoff Mini fits inside the fireplace wiring, and the dashboard or Alexa can flip it. A fake fire you can turn on by voice is a good party trick.The whole sprinkler build: the relay and ESP module in the enclosure, the 3D board render, the Tasmota UI with BME280 sensor readings, the Node-RED schedule feeding the pump, and the finished PCB layout. The sprinkler post has the full writeup, including why I picked Tasmota over custom firmware. It’s a bit hacky but I love it :DThe whole talk in five lines. The one I break most is the first, don’t introduce a new way while removing the old one, and I regret it every time. The last one stops me from breaking the others for no good reason. “I was in a hurry” doesn’t count.That was talk one. Most of the “memorable automations” later broke in some new way or got replaced, so there’s a sequel.Talk Two: Home Automation, The SequelEnough time passed between the talks that I had a new list of problems.More devices means more decisions made without me. It’s a little unsettling but mostly harmless.Same slide as before, with more icons.Everyone else is dealing with this too: a fridge showing a TLS certificate error, a grill controller that needs Wi-Fi to show the temperature, and a note taped to a pole about an internet-connected printer someone forgot to log out of.The same rules from talk one, worded a bit tighter, since part of the audience hadn’t seen the first talk.The rules stayed the same, but what they had to survive got harder.My setup assumed one person lived in the house. When that changed, I had to patch a single-user system into a multi-user one. The next few slides are how that went.More people meant more foot traffic and more keys, and longer trips away meant things could fail with nobody around to notice. A water flooding scare finally got me to take leak and presence detection seriously.Same joke, new rules. The first set came after year one, these after year five.These are rules 6 to 11 at the top of the post, written after the house went from one person to several.Now the builds, my favorite part.A motor and PVC pipe rig for outdoor lighting, a UV grow light clipped to a houseplant, and a UV strip under the cabinets for sanitizing.Same sprinkler slide as talk one. It’s one of the few builds that never needed a rewrite.A sensor that sits on a credenza, a robot vacuum that runs on its own, and an AirGradient kit I put together from a CO2 sensor, a particulate sensor and a microcontroller, with its own dashboard. The air quality kit gives me the most peace of mind of anything here.This dashboard replaced more apps than anything else: garage door, side door unlock, front lock, all lights on or off, brightness, a coffee bar color picker, and warm-to-cool for the living room. It’s one cheap tablet next to the thermostat, so nobody digs through five apps.The lights behind the TV run through the same system instead of their own remote.The smart locks came out of the more-people-more-keys problem. The newer one takes a password, the app, a keycard or a regular key, so everyone uses what they’re comfortable with.The parts bin, for anyone who wants to build this.The ESP32 D1 mini handles anything custom. The smart plug is the off-the-shelf shortcut when I don’t need custom. The Pi 4 runs Node-RED and Grafana.LED strips for ambient lighting, power transistors for higher-current loads, and small relay modules so a microcontroller can switch mains voltage safely.The rest of the bin: a resistor assortment, color-coded wire so I can trace a circuit later, and a capacitor kit for smoothing and timing.Node-RED for the logic, Grafana to see what’s happening, Tasmota on anything I flash, Telegram for notifications, and Python or JavaScript for glue code that doesn’t fit in a flow.The garage flow today. The door sensor and reed switch feed Grafana and a global closed state. Toggle nodes publish straight to Tasmota command topics. Notifications go to Telegram and an audio chime, and a light-on counter resets at midnight. The tabs across the top (Lights, Sensors, Garage, Sprinkler, NFC Tags, Door Lock Security) show how much it has grown since the single garage cooling flow in talk one.This is the “is everything okay” dashboard: humidity, temperature, dew point, pressure and gas on one side, and energy use, door opens and on-status history on the other. I built it because I got tired of guessing.Dashboards and Grafana panels work for me. Everyone else in the house just wants the light on.The “more than one way in” rule in hardware: the wall tablet for whoever is standing there, NFC tags and a QR code to tap, and an Echo Dot for anyone who would rather talk to the house.The tools I build and debug all of this with.A soldering iron for permanent connections, a 3D printer for enclosures and brackets you can’t buy, a multimeter for when something isn’t working, and a precision screwdriver kit for devices the manufacturer didn’t want opened.That’s both talks, five years apart. The rules barely changed between them, but the list of problems kept growing.A third talk is coming, built around agentic use cases. The same rules should hold when an AI agent is the one flipping the switches, and I expect to add a few.I shared the “no internet, no problem” rule on LinkedIn and asked for the most pointless internet dependency people had found in a device. Dozens of people answered. A Hacker News thread added more. Here’s what came back.Most examples were basic functions locked behind an app, an account, or a server:A fridge whose temperature can’t be changed because of a bug in the manufacturer’s phone app.A TV that can’t even switch inputs when the internet is down, and another that has to be signed in before it works as a plain HDMI monitor. One reader’s older smart TV has dead apps but still works as a regular TV, which is how a device should fail.A heating system whose app doesn’t work from the local network.A kitchen vent and a dishwasher that need the internet even when you control them from Home Assistant.A smart plug that can’t be set up on an isolated network.Noise-cancelling headphones that search for a Bluetooth device forever, so you can’t just turn on the noise cancelling.Synthesizers and MIDI keyboards that need a cloud login for first use or firmware updates.A meat thermometer that only worked through its app and stopped working when the company went out of business.The meat thermometer bothers me most. The hardware outlived the company, and it stopped working anyway.Offline first, with the internet for extras. A device should do its main job on its own.Treat every third-party dependency as a risk. APIs change, so plan a local fallback or a clear degraded mode. One mobile developer works the same way: the core action works offline or from cache, and only the extras wait for a connection.Decide what must work offline. My answer is turning things on and off, temperature and safety controls, and anything a guest has to use without learning an app. As one reader said, if a visitor can’t turn something on or adjust the temperature without an app account, the design has failed.A stricter version of my first two rules: everything core works with the Wi-Fi or the automation server shut down, and smart features never take away the dumb ones. The wall switch should control the light directly and let automation flip it. A switch that only sends a request to the automation fails. That reader says my sprinkler controller fails this bar too. The only sprinkler controller they’d found with a local API and full control on the device itself was RainMachine, which is gone.Clean up when you throw things away. Remove a connected printer from your account first. An abandoned connected device can be an easy way in for an attacker.Use local protocols. One reader recommends Zigbee and Z-Wave over Wi-Fi, because a switch that doesn’t need the cloud tends to behave the same year after year. Another uses Zigbee for the smart plugs that can’t be set up without internet.Let an LLM find the firmware. One reader buys the cheapest hardware that does the job, ignores reviews that complain about the app, and asks an LLM for local-first custom firmware once it arrives. That has worked for their switches, a thermostat, an air quality monitor, a thermometer, and a window fan. They’d have paid about 2.5x for hardware that was local out of the box.Old Nest thermostats have a way out. No Longer Evil is open source firmware for Nest Gen 1 and Gen 2 thermostats.Smart TVs can be tamed. Reset the TV and never connect it to the network, and the input problem goes away.Remote access is the cost of staying local. I use Tailscale on the router and keep the individual devices off the tailnet. One reader ran OpenVPN on OpenWrt, which worked but felt clunky, and is now trying Tailscale.There’s a gap to fill. One reader would happily pay for a pre-built, open “works with everything” Raspberry Pi image with MQTT. DietPi and OpenWrt come close and have a small footprint, but you need some understanding to get going. Another wanted a hub that ships with the house, like a water heater or a router. Home Assistant sells hub hardware that’s close to that.Right to repair is the bigger fight. Readers pointed to the right-to-repair movement and groups like the FULU Foundation, which work to keep companies from locking you out of what you bought.Connectivity has real uses. A connected meat thermometer lets you watch the game while the steak cooks. The same reader also had an oven decide to update its software in the middle of cooking. One reader pointed out the business model behind all of this: companies would rather sell you a service than a product. Another expects the shift away from internet-connected devices to come from resilience worries rather than consumer complaints, since enough connected homes make a target. And one skips connected appliances entirely, keeping only computers and phones online.(This section has Amazon affiliate links. If you buy through them, I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.)These are the parts from my home automation builds, grouped by project.Lights, switches and plugs

item.title: Show HN: Valencia, Spain in Sim City/Isometric View
item.author: leugim
item.content:encoded: An isometric pixel-art map of València, in the spirit of SimCity and of Isometric NYC. Every building is a real one, drawn from above at the same angle, block by block.The whole municipal term is painted, from the huerta to the Albufera, except a few small huerta exclaves where there's no 3D imagery to paint from. Real 3D city data is rendered from a fixed isometric camera. An image model trained on a hand-picked pixel-art style then repaints it, tile by tile, each tile continuing its painted neighbours so the city stays seamless. The sea, the port basins and the Albufera are drawn in the same style. to move, or to zoom, to zoom in somewhere random · whole map · full screen · search · play · metro · planesThe address bar always holds the current view, so any link you copy opens right here.Tiny València is free and has no ads. Painting it takes rented GPUs, and keeping it online a server. If you enjoy it, you can support it on Patreon.Buildings © Dirección General del Catastro · Aerial photo & terrain © IGN (PNOA, MDT05), CC BY 4.0 · Roads, boundary, coast, metro lines & search © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL · Metro timetable: FGV (Metrovalencia) · 3D reference: Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles via Cesium ion.

item.title: The Hardest Tarball?
item.author: thatslast
item.content:encoded: Here is a curiosity: an archive that can be constructed using a single GNU tar invocation, that is extracted in 8 distinct ways depending on what tool you use.$ printf hello > file $ touch empty $ tar --format=pax --pax-option='delete=?time,size:=512' \ --transform='s,^\./file$,café,' \ -cf hardest.tar file ./file emptyIt creates an archive from three files in sequence, where is repeated so that GNU tar stores the second one as a hard link, and is empty. Exploiting the unique path of the second entry, the hard link is renamed to . This triggers tar to create a pax header to store the file name as UTF-8. We add a record to the pax header, which overrides the default from the hard link. The value 512 is not a coincidence: it is exactly the size of a tar header.Visually, this archive has the following structure, with two basic interpretations based on whether a hard link can have a size or not.Now, POSIX says that data blocks for a hard link in pax archives, but the implications of this are not entirely clear. So the 512 bytes after the hard link are its data, and not the header of as we archived it? How can a hard link have different contents from its previous counterpart ?This archive gives by far the richest and most surprising results I've encountered so far when extracting it with well-known tar utilities and libraries. The results below were produced using the latest releases of all packages at the time of writing.GNU tar, BusyBox, Python, Go and PerlThis group is reasonable in principle: they ignore the size on the hard link, and extract , its hard link , and .This is the system utility of macOS, which is closer to POSIX in spirit regarding the concept of size on hard links, and writes the 512 bytes into the hard link. The end result is that now contains the tar header of .7-Zip, node-tar, tar-fs, and Rust's tar & astral-tokio-tarThis group agrees with bsdtar that the 512 bytes are data of the hard link, but doesn't write them into the hard link. Instead, they skip forward over the data, and you are left with just and , without .This is where you begin to need more imagination. Because contains data, a file is created that contains the header of as data, while keeps its original contents.Makes a separate, empty file, and also extracts . Why not?Does not extract at all, but to make up for it, it creates an empty directory next to and .R has an entirely different approach: it extracts with 512 null bytes. It mistakenly applies the size to instead of the hard link, and those 512 bytes are from an end-of-archive marker.Haskell's tar would be exactly like GNU tar, if only it did not have string decoding issues, which turn the file into on disk (in the year 2026, this is not a rendering quirk of your browser)..NET, Julia and uv's tar-codecThese implementations reject the tarball. I believe this is the best thing you can do, even if it's technically not POSIX-compliant.This tarball is one of 134 tricky tarballs that I'm collecting and categorizing in my test suite haampie/tar-minefield, developed since the last post. Its website https://stoppels.ch/tar features a big table that shows how implementations deal with all these cases, as well as detailed info per test case. A variant from the tarball of this post is included as a test case.If you'd like to discuss this, send me an email at .

item.title: Ableton Live 13
item.author: phaser
item.content:encoded: Ableton Live 13 adds new audio and MIDI workflows, sound design tools and mixing effects. Highlights include:A built-in Step Sequencer, ARA 2 support for compatible audio-editing plug-ins, Capture Automation, and Contextual Browsing for adding devices and swapping presets directly from the device chain.Drum Synth, new Multiband and Mid-Side Racks, expanded Rack controls, and Envelope Clips for automating and modulating effects on return tracks.Device Slots in the mixer, and new Core Library Drum Racks, instrument presets, Audio Effect Racks, samples, and MIDI clips.Arrangement Sync for Ableton Link, support for exporting tempo automation and time signature changes, and more precise event timing in exported MIDI files.Mixer improvements including Send sliders, a persistent Mixer Configuration menu for choosing which sections are visible, smoother mixer resizing, and an Unsolo button on the Main track, plus an updated Phaser-Flanger interface.Live 13 Suite also includes Melodyne essential, Looplet, Clipper, Transient Shaper and the Classic Dynamics & EQ Pack by Softube.Push 3 gains Custom Layouts, a new Step Sequencer layout, a new Performance Mixer, and Device Mode upgrades. Custom Layouts combine Session View, note areas, XYZ and mixer controls on a single page. The Step Sequencer brings the step editing experience from Live to the hardware. Device Mode adds jog wheel navigation and up to 32 Rack Macros.Push 2 supports the new Step Sequencer and most Device Mode improvements (except jog wheel navigation), but not Custom Layouts, Performance Mixer or Expressive Step Editing.Live 13 is the next major version of Ableton Live, following Live 12. It adds audio and MIDI workflows including ARA 2 support, Step Sequencer and Capture Automation, plus instruments and effects, expanded Rack controls, updated Core Library content, and more. Everything you can do in Live 12 you can still do in Live 13.Ableton Live 13 comes in three editions: Intro, Standard and Suite.They share the same core workflow but differ in their features and included instruments, effects and sounds. Live Intro is limited to 16 tracks and Scenes. Standard allows unlimited tracks and Scenes, and adds many more built-in instruments, effects and sounds. Suite includes everything in Standard plus Max for Live, the complete instrument and effect collection, and Live’s full Core Library.Suite also comes with Melodyne essential for ARA 2 editing, plus the Classic Dynamics & EQ Pack by Softube and Looplet as free downloads at release. .If you already own Live 12 – pre-order Live 13 at 20% off.If you don’t own Live 12 yet – buy or upgrade to Live 12 at 20% off during the announcement offer and get the corresponding Live 13 edition free when it’s released.Log in to your User Account and visit the Ableton shop to see the upgrade options for your license. From now until the release of Live 13, you can buy or upgrade to Live 12 and get the corresponding Live 13 edition for free on release day. You can extend your existing plan to cover the cost of upgrading to Live 13 Suite and start using it as soon as it’s released. to see your upgrade options.Limited places for the Live 13 public beta are available to Live Standard and Suite owners. Learn more about the .Most ARA 2 plug-ins work with Live 13, including Melodyne. Live 13 Suite comes with Melodyne essential. A small number have known compatibility issues. See the full for more information.One ARA plug-in can be used at a time, across multiple clips and tracks.

item.title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
item.author: plun9
item.content:encoded: I can only speculate as to the reasons why I was laid off from Meta in May, but I suspect that one of the reasons is that I was a little bit more resistant to adopting AI/LLMs as coding tools than some of my peers. Don't get me wrong, I generated at least 90% of my code using AI in my last few months there, which was the minimum for a decent rating. But AI didn't 10X the amount of code I was writing. It didn't even 2X it.I was focused on code quality. I saw the code being pushed by some of my peers who were heavily reliant on AI, and I saw that it was brittle code. There were many subtle issues that would lead to tech debt in the long term, and even some glaring issues were ignored by very good programmers. For instance, I saw one of the best programmers on my team try to merge code that used javascript events for mouseover CSS effects rather than using the :hover selector, which is a totally unscalable way of writing mouseovers.Now I'm employed at another large tech company and I've fully made the switch to generating 100% of my code using AI because that's the expectation today. Still, I can see lots of people becoming aware that this isn't a sustainable way to continue development of a large scale SaaS product. AI tends to solve the problems that can fit within its context window very well, but it's totally oblivious to the long term issues that can't be understood in that relatively small frame.In this post I'm going to list four ways that AI usage results in a fragile codebase that isn't resilient to the demands of highly available and highly scalable SaaS applications.By the way, every word of this article was written by a human. Even though the following image was generated by AI, this article isn't AI slop.Four ways AI makes codebases fragileHere are the four most common ways that I have seen AI generating a fragile codebase.1. AI writes shallow testsOne of the most obvious failures of modern LLMs is that they tend to write simplistic automated test cases that don't cover the things that matter to humans. Frequently I see AI agents writing lots of tests of get/set methods which are trivial and don't typically require much testing. When AI writes e2e tests, they tend to only cover the cases which are already covered in the codebase. In other words, the AI writes tests only covering one type of user, or only covering surface level interactions. This creates massive gaps in the test coverage that are invisible to developers because they aren't captured by the line level coverage metric.2. AI writes overly complex ccodeAI also tends to write overly complex code. It frequently uses two or three helper methods when a single one would suffice. It tries to follow coding guidelines, such as DRY, to a fault, without realizing that the added complexity of that rigidity makes the code more difficult for human developers to debug or understand.3. Reliance on AI decreases human understandingAnd that's the third issue with AI codebases: Humans don't understand them. The longer a company relies on AI agents to generate the code, the fewer developers are going to understand the codebase. This means that developers can't do the things that are necessary to build a resilient codebase. They don't understand the data structures and algorithms well enough to see when a pull request contains a new abstraction that doesn't work with the pre-existing structures.4. AI moves too quickly to maintain a high quality barAI moves too quickly for human developers to maintain a high quality bar. Each pull request comes faster than the prior one and has to be reviewed in even less time. This leads to developers skimming the code and missing crucial details that result in long term tech debt. Small quality issues like testing gaps and poorly named variables accrue in the codebase until it becomes a morass of spaghetti code.Four signs that you have a fragile codebaseIf you're unsure whether coding agents are harming your codebase or not, then you might look for the following symptoms of a fragile, AI-generated codebase.1. AI generated codebases have more incidentsWhen you switched the department over to agentic coding did the number of incidents slowly start rising? At first when we were all using agents to generate massive amounts of code, it didn't seem that different from traditional coding. The PRs came and were merged and everything seemed alright. But oh, there was that one p0 that came in at the end of the month, then there were two SEVs the following month. Then even more the next month. Now, after a year or two of agentic coding, it seems like there's an incident every weekend. AI coding agents are the reason why there are more incidents impacting customers.2. Recovery from incidents takes longer in AI codebasesNot only are there more incidents, but the incidents take longer to be mitigated. The fact is that the human developers on your team now have a more shallow understanding of the codebase. If your coding agent can't find the issue that your customers are facing, then humans are going to have to dig through a codebase that is highly complex and poorly tested. They will essentially be entering unfamiliar territory, so it takes longer for them to figure out what is going wrong. Hence, companies lose more and more money to incidents that take longer to resolve.3. AI generated codebases create errors that are only visible to usersWhen humans don't spend time in the code, they fail to see all of the use cases. They fail to understand how actual humans are using the code because they aren't ensuring that the AI is instrumenting analytics and catching all the errors properly. Hence, invisible errors start appearing in the codebase. Errors are uncaught and only visible to real world users, as opposed to the types of users that are being tested in automated tests or in developer manual testing.4. AI results in a poor user experienceAnd that leads to the ultimate problem with AI codebases: they weren't made for humans. AI codebases are software made by AI for AI. They aren't being tailored to the way that human users use the product, and they aren't being tailored for the way human developers need to maintain the product. The experience degrades on both the user and the developer side, leading to a vicious cycle of enshittification.Products made for humans require a human touchThe fact of the matter is that for a product to satisfy human customers, it has to be informed by a human perspective. Nobody likes ordering from machines at a restaurant. Shopping for clothes from a website always results in worse fits than shopping in person. The same is true of SaaS products. Any time you leave your SaaS product in the hands of a machine, you are losing the human touch that is valuable to your users and your developers. This may work for the cheapest products that only compete on price, but high quality software products will continue to have a human touch. The best, most expensive products will be tailored for human users by human developers. They will be charming and enjoyable to use. They won't be fragile because they won't be primarily developed by AI.
