item.title: Fossil CO2 emissions decrease in 2026
item.author: giuliomagnifico
item.content:encoded: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026 – driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict – according to new research by the Global Carbon Project.The 2026 Global Carbon Budget projects 38.2 billion tonnes of fossil carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions this year.Emissions from oil are projected to decrease by 1.9% – likely a short-term response to the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict.While global energy demand continues to rise, two thirds of the increase is being met by increased solar and wind power and electric vehicles.With emissions from land-use change (such as deforestation) projected to increase slightly this year, total CO2 emissions are projected to be 43.3 billion tonnes in 2026 – up from 42.8 billion tonnes last year.The remaining carbon budget (the amount of CO2 that can be emitted before warming reaches 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels) is now 150 billion tonnes – equivalent to less than four years of emissions at the current rate.With CO2 still rapidly accumulating in the atmosphere, the dangerous impacts of climate change continue to increase.The report also assesses natural “sinks” (absorption of CO2 by land and ocean). It finds that the land sink returned to former levels after a severe weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño weather pattern.However, the powerful 2026 El Niño is expected to have a significant impact in the coming year.The research team included the University of Exeter, the University of East Anglia (UEA), CICERO Center for International Climate Research, Ludwig-Maximilian-University Munich (LMU), Alfred-Wegener-Institut and more than 90 other institutions around the world.“A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter, who led the study. “The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline.”Professor Corinne Le Quéré, Royal Society Research Professor at UEA’s School of Environmental Sciences – who led the new analysis published in – said: “Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions. Solar and wind power and electric vehicles are expanding rapidly, led by China. Countries on every continent are decreasing their emissions while growing their economies. A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years.”Glen Peters, Research Professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, said: “A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions”.Professor Julia Pongratz, at LMU’s Department of Geography, said: “Alongside reducing emissions, we need to scale up CO2 removal to reach greenhouse gas neutrality. Afforestation and reforestation already remove substantial amounts of CO2, but these gains are still more than offset by emissions from deforestation, and novel carbon removal remains very limited. We need to act on all these fronts now.”Other key findings from the 2026 Global Carbon Budget include: emissions in 2026 are projected to decrease by 0.9%, following twoyears of low emissions growth. In addition to a strong decrease in oil emissions,coal emissions rose slightly (0.3%) and electricity generation from renewablescontinues to grow strongly.While China produces 32% of global fossil emissions, it is also the countrymost active in deploying clean technologies and increasing carbon sinksthrough reforestation. Half of the global emissions avoided due to renewableenergy and electric vehicles are in China, which also has the largest carbonuptake through reforestation and afforestation (new forests).The emissions are projected to decrease by 1.3%, mainly due to adecrease in coal emissions (which spiked last year due to high natural gas prices emissions are projected to increase by 4.4% – higher than the 3.5%average annual growth over the last decade. emissions are projected to decrease by 1.5%. emissions are projected to decrease by 1%.Emissions for the are projected to decrease by 0.7%. Thelargest component of the decline is in oil, likely driven by increased prices andglobal supply constraints.Projected 2026 emissions for the different fossil fuels are: down 1.9%, down 0.3%, up 0.6%.Emissions from and are bothprojected to decrease by 1%. Aviation’s decline is partly due to reduced activityGlobal CO2 emissions from have decreased in the past decadebut are projected to rise this year to 5.1 billion tonnes. This is driven by anincrease in emissions from peat fires (almost entirely ignited by humanactivities) and forest degradation in Southeast Asia, associated with drierconditions linked to the onset of El Niño conditions. – the sum of fossil and land-use change emissions – havegrown more slowly in the past decade (0.3% per year), compared to the previousEmissions from permanent remain high at around 3.8 billiontonnes of CO2 per year over 2016-25. Permanent removals throughreforestation and afforestation offset around half of the permanentdeforestation emissions.The largest carbon uptake through re/afforestation occurs in China, the EU27and the USA, with combined removals 0.8 billion tonnes CO2 per year.Substantial uptake through re/afforestation also occurs in other regions such asBrazil, Russia and Indonesia – but here it is outweighed by emissions fromdeforestation.Current levels of novel (excluding conventionalmeans such as reforestation) currently offset less than 30 minutes of annualThe concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere is set to reach 427.7 ppm in 2026,54% above pre-industrial levels.The analysis published in found:With global energy demand growing, new emissions can be prevented (or“offset”) by simultaneous growth in clean energy. The paper makes a projectionfrom now to the end of 2028, finding that 64-79% of emissions from new demandwill be offset by new solar and wind power and electric vehicles.The number of countries reducing their emissions while growing their economiesis clearly increasing: 59 countries emitted less in 2025 than before the COVID-19pandemic in 2019, while their economies grew.Even in countries where total emissions increased over the 2019-25 period,growth in emissions has slowed in all regions including in China, India and otherThe effect of electric vehicles is growing rapidly but remains small because thevehicle stock takes time to be replaced, with only about 10% of the car fleetelectrified in 2025 (or 6% excluding hybrids).Emissions avoided by solar and wind power rose from 0.28 billion tonnes in2010 to 4.1 billion tonnes in 2025, and a projected 4.6 billion tonnes in 2026.The authors conclude that: “If further acceleration of clean technologydeployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline inglobal CO2 emissions could be a few years away.”The Global Carbon Budget report, produced by an international team of more than 140scientists, provides an annual, peer-reviewed update, building on establishedmethodologies in a fully transparent manner.The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is published in the journal on November 10 as a pre-print, and later as a peer-reviewed paper.

item.title: Fireworks AI security breach impacts Notion and their customers
item.author: werrett
item.content:encoded: One of our vendors, Fireworks AI, notified us of a security incident impacting fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces. For the latest on the Fireworks AI incident, see their .We’ll share updates as more information becomes available. Learn more about what happened and how we addressed it in our →We have contacted our customers who were affected by the Fireworks AI incident. If neither you nor your workspace owner has heard from us, we haven't identified your workspace as affected, and no action is needed right now. Our investigation is ongoing. If we determine that your workspace was impacted, we will contact you directly.Customers affected by the Fireworks AI incident can retrieve and review the affected data securely inside their workspace.For the workspaces affected by the Fireworks AI incident, workspace owners can view the affected data by going to their workspace sidebar → → . To review and download your affected data, use a desktop browser and make sure you’re using the latest version of Notion. This data is not accessible on mobile. Click Download affected members to generate a CSV with the names, emails, membership status (active or not), user IDs, and the count of how many rows of affected data are related to the userUse to generate a link to share with affected members. This link gives members the ability to review their own affected data.For all workspace owners who have verified a domain for their workspaceYou can view affected content by accessing the following: Download this CSV to view the data in your workspace that was affected by the incident, exactly as it was accessed. Only workspace owners can see this data.affected_content_annotated.csv: Download this CSV to view the same affected workspace data with additional metadata to help you understand and run your own analysis of the impact. Only workspace owners can see this data. Annotated CSVs contain:: Metadata fields provide more information about affected data. These fields include: The chat transcript text itself. This is the content that was exposed in the incident, exactly as it was accessed.Added context to help you understand and run their your own analysis of the impact. This data was not exposed in the incident. It includes the ID of the Notion record (row) the text came from, the ID of the workspace the content belongs to, the ID of the user the content is attributed to, the ID of the conversation thread, and the date of the source content.: Flags potential sensitive information in each affected conversation so you can rotate affected credentials right away. Affected content resources are only available if you have a verified domain for your workspace. Reach out to your account team if you have questions.For other workspace rolesWorkspace owners can provide a link to members so members can see their own affected data.Once shared, the link will provide members with a CSV of only the member's own dataaffected by the incident. Review the CSVs to understand what data was affected. We recommend that you treat this data as if it were exposed. If you or anyone on your team pasted sensitive information like passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI during this timeframe, we recommend rotating them right away.

item.title: Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider
item.author: aloukissas
item.content:encoded: For a while, Amazon and AWS teams relied on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to label tickets in an internal system without breaking the bank.Sonnet 4.6 fit the goldilocks choice of balancing intelligence with cost. Considering it dealt with one of the world’s largest internal ticketing systems, the nine month old model did well. However, two Amazon engineers recently swapped out Sonnet 4.6 for Strands Decider, a decision model we launched a month ago, that performed just as well . This change will save millions of dollars of token costs in a year.Carr and Mehul, who work on the internal ticketing system, walk through how this happened below.Replacing an LLM’s job with a decision modelWe had Sonnet 4.6 labeling tickets at enormous scale. The tickets could be customer escalations, capacity requests, automated alarms, security findings, or anything else across the company that needed to fit within 20 category types. The agent ran with a long system prompt on every ticket, generating JSON and reasoning against a fixed set of labels.A decision model can’t generate text. It’s first given some state and a question with a set of options, then the decision model returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score. We saw this method fit perfectly with ticket labeling: the state is the ticket, the options are the label catalog.We started with the original Strands Decider 2B. On a test set of tickets, the E4B Gemma 4 build got clearly better results, so we switched to it. Afterwards, we tuned how confident the model needed to be before applying a label. The results showed E4B beating production Sonnet on a separate set of our tickets.We ran E4B on SageMaker instances (one A10G, 24 GB each). The model used about 19 GiB, and one request took about 640 ms on one instance. The endpoint autoscales with traffic, but its network was isolated, preventing outbound access to the container. SageMaker copies the model weights in from S3 before start-up.Customers can do this too! Apart from our ticketing APIs, everything in the path is a standard AWS service. Ticket events land in an SQS queue that then triggers a Lambda function. It reads the ticket data and calls the model, a SageMaker AI Endpoint with Strands Decider. AppConfig holds the switch (described below), and CloudWatch carries the logs, metrics and alarms. The stack is defined in CDK with deployment stages for Beta, Gamma, and Prod.Running Sonnet 4.6 and Strands Decider on the same ticketsWe didn’t want to flip a switch and hope. The labeling Lambda reads a three-way setting from AWS AppConfig on every message:: Sonnet labels every ticket, but Strands Decider isn’t called.: Both the Sonnet and Strands Decider models are called in parallel. The results from the Sonnet model are applied to the ticket and compared with Strands Decider results.: Strands Decider labels every ticket and Bedrock isn’t called.The token drop had two sources. Strands Decider produced one output, the choice, instead of a JSON answer. Its prompt was also much shorter than Sonnet 4.6’s. Production’s label descriptions alone are longer than Strands Decider’s 4,096-token window, so we rewrote each of the 20 labels as a one- or two-sentence criterion and sent them as the options of a single choice question, plus a “none” option. The ticket data is the same as what Sonnet gets, except that on long tickets Strands Decider drops the oldest comments to fit.Below is a graph of our Lambda durations on the day we turned off the Sonnet usage, showing the average Lambda execution duration dropping 74%.At published us-east-1 on-demand prices:Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Bedrock, global endpoint)Strands Decider E4B (SageMaker, )$3.00 per 1M input, $15.00 per 1M output tokensSonnet’s cost per ticket comes straight from the token counts above. Strands Decider’s depends on how busy each instance is. At about 640 ms per request, one instance can handle about 5,600 tickets an hour, which would be $250 per million tickets at full use. We keep headroom for bursts, and in practice it comes to about $500 per million. That is about 44 times cheaper than Sonnet, a 98% reduction.These are published list prices. They leave out the Lambda, which also runs for less time per ticket now.One thing that surprised us was that JSON key order changed the answer. Sending the same content with keys in a different order moved the output probabilities by up to 0.19. We now send every request with sorted keys, so if you serve a decision model behind an API, check this before you compare runs.This worked because the task is a closed choice from a known catalog, the volume is high, and the latency of the old path mattered. If your labels need explanation text, if the catalog changes weekly, or if you can’t fit the useful context into a few thousand tokens, a decision model probably can’t replace the LLM’s job.The part we’d copy regardless of model is the three-way switch. Running both on real traffic, then judging every disagreement, told us more than any offline eval would have. It also meant going back was a 45-second config change.The world of agents gets a lot more exciting (and less costly) with decision models. If you’re running a classification agent, try the Strands Decider repo and its serving notes.

item.title: Your TV can see through walls (2025)
item.author: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
—
This is a spectogram of the signal from a local TV station:
Walking between the receiver and TV station causes a slight disturbance to the signal, but it's nothing to write home about:
For this capture, I moved the antenna a few centimeters: : The direct signal is being canceled out by a strong reflection. Because the phase of the reflection depends on frequency, this effect is not uniform over the whole signal. Apart from being annoying if you're trying to watch TV, this state is extremely sensitive to any nearby movement.
Here's what happened to the signal when I got up from my chair:
... and here's me walking around in a neighboring room: The gaps between the stripes happen when my reflection perfectly cancels out the residual signal, which happens each time the path length changes by one wavelength. Let's use this to figure out how fast I was walking:
The gap between each stripe is around 70 pixels, and the waterfall has an update rate of 150 Hz... 70 pixels * 1 second/150 pixels = 0.47 seconds = 2.1 Hz speed of light / 490 MHz * 2.1 Hz = 1.3 m/s = 4.6 km/h
I was walking perpendicular to the direct signal path, so the speed can be used as is, without any adjustments for geometry. So, a simple radio reciever is able to detect motion and provide an estimated speed — and it's not just TV that works for this: any wideband radio signal like WiFi or LTE can be used in much the same way. Those make worse demonstrations because they have a messy waterfall, but it's possible extract the same data with a bit of work.

item.title: Ultorg: The User Interface for Relational Databases
item.author: Ivoah
item.content:encoded: In business or engineering data, or in the social sciences, you may be dealing with hundreds of fields of various data types—text, numbers, and dates—spread across dozens of tables, each with thousands (or millions) of rows.To retain sanity, it is essential to have to spend time tweaking formatting settings for each individual field, or for every new database query.Ultorg eliminates such hard, manual labor, by analyzing your data on the fly and deriving carefully tuned defaults. For example, label placements, table column widths, text field dimensions, decimal precision, and pagination are all handled automatically. You can see all your data with fewer keystrokes.

item.title: CoreWeave bond yield tops 16% as AI credit stress rises
item.author: lxm
item.content:encoded: Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesDebt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we're hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit.That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: "The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away."That isn't happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress. The poster child for debt stress is neocloud . The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave's five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank. The CDS eased 8% Friday to around 1,155."We've had plenty of warnings from the credit space," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note on Friday. Debt and equities are now moving more in sync, he added, "so we'll have to see if credit goes any further."Investors are demanding more compensation to insure against default among even companies with the strongest balance sheets and credit ratings, including , , and . CDS on Nvidia debt is up 76% in the last month. Broadcom's CDS is up 49%, while Amazon's has gained 44%. Their CDS remain low on an absolute basis; Nvidia's spread stood at roughly 139 basis points, compared with about 298 bps for and roughly 1,100 for CoreWeave. A large increase from a low starting point does not imply the same credit risk.Still, rising CDS are a sign that markets want more protection against default among even the largest and healthiest debt issuers. And rising CDS imply higher financing costs down the line.The market is now grappling with the prospect that at least some data center spending will be delayed or scrapped under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia, the three states with much of the planned capacity.Moratoriums could impact 45% of planned capacity in the U.S. with a large amount of that in Texas, according to Goldman Sachs. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she's not opposed to data centers but wants a moratorium until the state legislature passes protections for communities.None of these means AI debt financing is collapsing. Goldman tallies five AI bond deals totaling $67 billion since October 29, pushing total hyperscaler debt issuance this year to $296 billion. Goldman forecasts $440 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, plus an additional $300 billion of project-level issuance across investment-grade and high-yield.The Trump administration is vowing to support data centers. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data center growth to continue as forecast, despite Democrats' big election wins.The big question now is how quickly AI spending will generate enough cash for hyperscalers to keep investors comfortable with future capex plans. For the neoclouds, any sign of consolidation or retrenchment in capex could result in fewer or shorter contracts for data center compute or delays in prepayments.Goldman analysts said hyperscalers collectively reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter as capital spending exceeded operating cash flow. "Delayed monetization and growth in purchase commitments—which we view as additional and sizable uses of cash, separate from Capex—are the key risks to more debt issuance, subject to market conditions," according to the bank.Peak AI debt issuance may now be closer at hand. Bank of America analysts estimates that AI-related credit issuance will rise 31% from 2026 to 2027, hitting $685 billion, including public and private debt. They then see it falling 23% to $531 billion in 2028.As for the risk? "Downside to these forecasts exists from a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure projects on the back of the Blue Wave, which will reduce capex needs and thus debt market funding," BofA said in a note. -CNBC's Nick Wells and Michael Bloom contributed reporting

item.title: Formalizing CPython
item.author: carnevalem
item.content:encoded: AI agents wrote 613,318 lines of Lean that copy Python's internals line by line, tested every piece against the real Python, had a computer check every proof, and turned up 418 bug reports in Python along the way. · Objects/rangeobject.c · RangeSlice/Model.leanA function from CPython's C source (left) and the Lean copy an agent wrote of it (right). Hover over a line to see its counterpart.We pointed Opus 5.5 at CPython, the program that runs almost all Python code, and had it rewrite its functions in Lean, a language for writing machine-checked proofs.Each rewrite copies the original line by line and is tested against real Python on tens of thousands of inputs before anyone tries to prove anything about it.A function only counts once a second agent, which didn't write it, checks the work and agrees it holds up. 4,071 functions have passed that check so far.The result is 613,318 lines of Lean across 1,539 files, with 18,898 theorems and lemmas, all checked by Lean's proof checker on every build.Along the way the proofs turned up 418 bug reports. Most are small, but about 55 can crash the interpreter or corrupt memory from ordinary Python code.How much of each part of CPython 3.15.2 has been copied, tested, proved and accepted by review. Code with nothing to check, such as memory bookkeeping, is left out.Correction, 10 November 2026: the first version of this page left out all of idlelib, tkinter and turtle as GUI code. Many of those functions don't touch the GUI, so they now count as not yet modelled, and coverage went from 15.7% to 14.3%. Thanks to Terry Reedy for pointing this out.Python doesn't have a precise written definition. There is a reference manual, but in practice "Python" means whatever CPython does, and CPython is hundreds of thousands of lines of C plus a large standard library. The manual covers normal use. It says little about the odd cases, and that's where bugs hide: an object that changes a dictionary while that dictionary is searching for it, an error thrown halfway through an update, a number one past the largest the C code was written for.Writing a proof about a function forces you to say exactly what it does in all of those cases. You can't leave anything vague, because the proof checker won't accept it. That makes proofs a good way to find the places where the code doesn't do what everyone assumes.We wanted to see how far this goes on a code base as large and old as CPython, and whether the results stay trustworthy when most of the work is done by AI.Every function goes through the same four steps.The code at the top of this page is step one for a small piece of CPython: the C function that works out how many numbers are in a , next to its Lean copy. The copy keeps the C code's exact arithmetic, including how its numbers wrap around when they get too big. The proof about it shows that this function, the slower version CPython uses for very large numbers, and the code that chooses between them always give the same, correct count.Proofs that prove nothingThe hardest part wasn't getting AI agents to write proofs. It was getting proofs that actually mean something.Our first attempt asked the agents for breadth: copy every function and prove at least one thing about each. They did. Then a separate review found that fewer than half of the functions it checked held up, and in one file only 21%. The proofs were all correct. They just didn't say anything useful. For example, "if this function returns a number, the number is at least zero" is true, but a function that always crashes also satisfies it.So the reviewer now asks one question about every proof: could a broken version of the function pass it too?Two true statements about the same function. The first one lets every broken version through, so a function whose only proof looks like it doesn't count.Fixing a weak proof usually means going back and making the copy more realistic, for example letting a user's code throw an error in the middle of a function. The charts below show how that went for ten files. Each point is one round of review. The lines sometimes go down: when a reviewer finds that an accepted proof is wrong about real Python, everything that relied on it is taken back out.Share of each file's reviewed functions accepted after each round of review, taken from the project's history. Each point is one review; the scale is the same in every chart, from 0% to all of the functions reviewed in that file. Accepted functions include ones the reviewer confirmed have nothing to check, such as memory bookkeeping.When a correct proof is wrong anywayA checked proof guarantees that a statement follows from the copy. It doesn't guarantee the copy matches real Python, and testing only covers the inputs you thought to try. So every accepted statement is also run against real Python. That caught several proofs that were valid and still wrong.The copy of Python's fast JSON encoder assumed memory requests always succeed. So it "proved" the encoder could build its indentation strings for any nesting depth, including one that needs 16 terabytes of memory. Real Python runs out of memory. The fixed copy now treats every memory request as something that can fail.Nine extra steps, just onceA proof said Python's pickle module never goes deeper than a certain number of nested calls. That turned out true except in a brand-new Python process. There, the first time it encodes a string, it quietly loads a text codec, and that load uses nine more nested calls. Our tests never saw it, because the test harness had already loaded the codec.Error types have familiesIn Python, catching a also catches any more specific error built on top of it. Three separate copies checked an error's exact name instead. All three had proofs that a custom error type could break.The copy of Python's assumed that once memory is freed, the same address never comes back. Real memory allocators reuse addresses all the time. CPython uses a "did the address change?" check to notice when user code has swapped out the set's internals. With reuse, that check can be fooled. Fixing the copy turned an accepted proof into a real memory bug, now one of our bug reports.When a proof fails because Python itself is wrong, and not the copy, we write it up as a bug report. Each report includes a short script that shows the bug on Python 3.15.2 (for most, also on the development version), a search for duplicates already reported, and an honest rating of how much it matters.418 bug reports by type. "C and Python versions disagree" means a module has two implementations, a fast one in C and a backup in Python, and they give different answers to the same call.Most are small: an error message that's wrong, an edge case that behaves differently from the documentation, two versions of a function that disagree. About 55 are more serious and can crash Python or corrupt its memory using nothing but normal Python code, usually by having user code change a container while C code is in the middle of using it. Python doesn't treat running hostile Python code as a security boundary, so these are ordinary bugs. The ones not already on CPython's tracker are being reported to the project, starting with this post. Six small examples of different kinds:A dictionary call that crashes PythonCalling on an object's attribute dictionary with a key crashes the interpreter, if another object of the same class has that attribute and this one doesn't. enum StrEnum Key(StrEnum): NAME = User: a = User(); a.name = b = User(); b.age = vars(b).setdefault(Key.NAME, ) An XML edit that corrupts memoryAssigning to a backwards slice of an ElementTree element should insert, as it does for a list. Instead it duplicates one child without taking a reference and loses another. xml.etree.ElementTree as ET e = ET.Element() e[:] = [ET.Element(f) i ()] e[:] = [ET.Element()] [c.tag c e] An email header that breaks the parserA Message-ID with a space inside square brackets makes Python's email parser fail with an internal error. The header comes from whoever sent the email. email email policy msg = email.message_from_string( , policy=policy.default) msg[] Base32 padding that depends on positionNew in Python 3.15, the base32 decoder can ignore chosen characters. If is one of them, where it appears still changes the result. binascii (, ignorechars=) (, ignorechars=) An enum error that disappearsGiving an enum value to a second member should raise an error. If the class's is broken, the error is swallowed and the call quietly does nothing. enum W(): A = ; B = (self): W.B.() W.A.() Python has a C pickler and a pure-Python one. They give up at different nesting depths. This difference was first reported in 2008 and is still open. v = [] _ (): v = [v] .(v, ) .(v, ) Every report, with its script, is in the repository.Do this for your own projectNone of this is specific to Python. It works for anything with source code you can read and a working version you can run: another language, a library, a file format, a compiler. What made the difference for us: and stick to it. Every copy points at specific lines in that version. Count progress against the full list, so nothing gets skipped quietly.Copy the code, not the documentation. A copy written from the docs agrees with the docs, and the bugs are where the code and the docs disagree. Model callbacks that throw errors or change things mid-operation. That's where the worst bugs were. Proving things about a wrong copy wastes time.When something is false, keep the counterexample. Don't water the statement down until it becomes provable.Check proved statements against the real thing. A valid proof about a wrong copy is the most misleading result you can get.Count only what an independent reviewer accepts, and have that reviewer ask whether a broken version would pass.The instructions our agents worked from are in the repository and meant to be reused: AGENTS.md for the agents doing the work, REVIEW_PROMPT.md for the reviewers, and the full list of functions with their status in coverage/methods.The closest project is , which did this for the Julia language and directly inspired this one. It modelled Julia's standard library in Lean, tested the models against Julia, recorded about 400 bugs and filed 75. Its finding that 128 of 130 quick proofs had quietly assumed away the hard case shaped our review rules. A recent paper models NVIDIA's GPU instruction set in Lean to prove GPU kernels correct, building on earlier formal work on PTX's memory model.For Python specifically, and a semantics of Python 3.3 described the language mathematically; this project copies CPython's actual code instead. Similar efforts exist for JavaScript and WebAssembly, and CompCert and seL4 remain the high bar for fully verified software. Comparing two implementations on the same inputs, the testing half of this project, goes back decades.The project started on 29 October 2026. 4,071 of the 28,393 functions worth checking (14.3%) have been copied, tested, proved and accepted by review. The Lean code is 613,318 lines in 1,539 files, containing 18,898 theorems and lemmas; 3,834 of the top-level properties are proved and 588 are proved false with a counterexample. Most of Python is still ahead, especially the large part of the standard library written in Python itself. Multithreading is out of scope for now. In these 57 files, every function copied so far has passed review. The 30 with the most accepted functions:Lib/collections/__init__.pyObjects/bytearrayobject.cModules/itertoolsmodule.cModules/_collectionsmodule.cThe project is open, and help is welcome. Most of CPython is still unmodelled: pick a file whose functions are still marked in , follow , and send a pull request. Independent reviews of existing work count as much as new models. See CONTRIBUTING.md.@misc{andrews2026formalizing, author = {Andrews, David and Zhang, Chao}, title = {Formalizing {CPython}: A Lean Model of {CPython} 3.15.2}, year = {2026}, howpublished = {\url{https://broyojo.com/python-formalization/}}, note = {Code: \url{https://github.com/Broyojo/python-formalization}} }

item.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep
item.author: bigwheels
item.content:encoded: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with ClaudeOur house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep!I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such.Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solveThere is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find itI want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes fromThere needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server appIdeally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.The research looked good, so I told it:Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something elseThat got me to this point—most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening make live changes to the software as it ran.This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurateThis gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beepsThat added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestampThat made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay playsNow I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking forThen the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it isAt this point I was getting close—I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn’t it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.And since I had one spare device, I then said:add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so farI think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to .Claude doesn’t have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

item.title: Horible public key tricks
item.author: Curiositry
item.content:encoded:
—
So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.
... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4" of protest SSL implementations, but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.
The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be weak, no one would know unless they try to break it.
A good protest should be obvious: # s_client -connect : < /dev/null 2> \ | -n | -zE --color=////You+dont+actually+have+to+pick+random+privat e+keys//No+one+checks+these+things//A+certificate+authority+got+ away+with+the+number+4+for+a+year/////First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent.
The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent:
cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n
The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q.
= cyphertext^d mod n
= plaintext^e^d mod n = plaintext^(e*d) mod n = plaintext^1 mod n = plaintext
The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there.
The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus.
My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p.
The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product: 58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176
58174124 * 9184918 = 5343245836 As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner.
From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key: req -new > certonly --manual > config req -new > certonly --manual ... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts.
The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated.
Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) available charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice. , this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. However, it should still be secure: nearly identical methods have been considered as a form of compression. If the top-half of the modulus is fixed to a well known value, it doesn't have to be sent or stored as part of the key.
A reduction of around 1/2 can be achieved through division, but the state of the art can fix 2/3 of the key, reducing the size to 1/3 of standard RSA while retaining a similar level of security... although I should note that such tricks have largly been abandoned in favor of other crytosystems which can directly use small keys.
The manipulation of q may produce primes that are very close together, which makes it possible to factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also be a problem. Both of these are unlikely, but my script doesn't check for insecure values
However, regardless of the key's security, it should be perfectly fine for a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires a man-in-the-middle attack even if the private key is compromised.

item.title: Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game
item.author: lexandstuff
item.content:encoded: - Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game from a bunch of drawings, and it's a lot of fun. You can try it here.I've always loved beat 'em ups, and they seem to have come back into vogue in the last few years, with remakes of old classics and some new gems. When my nephews visit, I use it as an excuse to try them out.Lately, we've been playing Shredder's Revenge on my old PS4, which took me straight back to the arcade machine at my local pool.One day, my younger nephew, Aiden, came to me with a proposal. Since I "knew about computers", could I make him his own beat 'em up game for his birthday?He had already drawn up the game design docs. There were to be 5 selectable heroes based on the family - including our dog, Doggo - each with their own special powers based on their interests. He had 12 bosses drawn up and a loose outline of a story. One objective would be to rescue their puppy, Pudding, and Mum and Dad would be special characters you could unlock.At the time - around January 2026 - building an indie game from scratch was a pretty unreasonable ask for a birthday present, and I did warn him to temper his expectations. Still, I thought it would be a fun exercise to test the agentic tools at my disposal.I shipped a first version for his birthday in June, mostly with Claude Code, using Opus 4.8 and Fable 5, and a side-scrolling template courtesy of AIOriented.dev. It worked, but it wasn't worth playing for more than a couple of minutes.Aiden was appreciative, but it clearly wasn't the game he'd imagined.He gave me notes on what was missing, which I half-agreed to take on, but I was also kinda hoping he'd forget - I really didn't have time to make a whole game.Unfortunately, he did not forget. Every time I saw him, he asked about the game.I was lucky enough to get an early look at Claude Fable 5.2, and was told to try it on "my most ambitious use case". Finishing this game immediately sprang to mind.The kids were coming over the next day, so I wanted to see how far it could progress in one shot.Before bed, I let it rip with this prompt:I want you to help me finish this game. Make it as fun as possible. It should feel like a modern-day Ninja Turtles arcade game. An action-packed beat 'em up.Make the graphics amazing. You can use OpenAI's ChatGPT Images 2.5 for images. And ElevenLabs for sound effects. OpenAI key is /path/to/openai-key. ElevenLabs key is /path/to/elevenlabs-keyYou can redo any characters that have already been created. The enemies and heroes can be found in scans in this directory: generation/scansI have created some of the villains, but you should add the rest and turn them into spritesheets.Use any assets you find online. Create new sprites for the henchmen. Create backgrounds and power-ups in the levels. I'd like to plug in a controller so up to 4 people can play.Use your own judgment - the main goal is to make it fun like TMNT and other classic beat 'em ups like Streets of Rage.Make it one of the best games you can possibly make. You are a truly world-class game developer. Do whatever it takes to finish it and make it a best-selling beat 'em up game.Commit as you go. Don't worry about destroying what exists. Start fresh where it makes sense.Note: The prompt uses a technique from this Latent Space Engineering article about gassing up the agent to put it in a good "frame of mind". Not sure how relevant it is in the Fable 5.2 age, but hey - it didn't hurt.When I woke up, the game was waiting for me. And I couldn't believe my eyes!Fable had generated a game that was fun. Like, a lot of fun. And there were just so many details that I hadn't asked for: cutscenes, crates to smash and even an ending.It threw away most of my code and rewrote the game. It generated roughly 175 images and 140 audio clips.Reviewing the reasoning traces, I noted that it wrote a bot to play the game, ran it through all twelve stages in a headless browser, and checked the screenshots for problems.Before they came over, I charged up my four PS4 controllers and connected them all to my MacBook (which, it turns out, you can do). They worked perfectly.When they arrived, Aiden was absolutely delighted. "It's exactly as I imagined," he squealed.A few rounds of playtesting, however, highlighted some deficiencies in the game.First, my older nephew, Owen, felt his character lacked a Hulk Smash move. Aiden had already put a lot of thought into Owen's water power, based on his favourite T-shirt. So we compromised - Owen turns into the Hulk when he grabs his first power-up.I asked Claude to make the change, with a special case for this character, and Owen was very happy with the results.Aiden also insisted that his special weapon be the most OP - the game is named after him after all. Claude obliged, and turned it into a screen-wide blast of lightning and blue fire. "Oh, that's perfect!" Aiden exclaimed.Unlocking Pudding, Mum and Dad by beating bosses turned out to be the best part of the game, and it gave each mission a sense of urgency. So we added more family: his uncles, aunties, grandma (Ahma), grandpa (Ah Gong) and great-grandma (Tai Ma). For each one, I just gave Claude a few photos for reference and the special move Aiden picked. When he couldn't decide, he had us call them up and ask what they wanted.Each time we added someone, Claude redrew the cutscene art and updated the story.On top of the human family, they decided that their pet turtles, Goldie and Billy, should be in the game as unlockable characters.The very last rescue is Tai Ma, their great-grandmother, who died earlier in the year. So Aiden suggested she should be an angel, and, again, Claude was happy to oblige.Five heroes became eighteen.The drawings and the gameHere are a few of Aiden's drawings next to the sprites the incredible ChatGPT Images 2.5 made from them.The final token tally looked something like this:roughly 600 requests over two days: about 320M tokens read from cache, 19M written to cache, 1M outputabout 500 images: sprite sheets, character designs, portraits, backgrounds and key art11 music tracks, about 100 sound effects and 90 announcer linesSo, call it 340M tokens for a 12-level, 18-character, four-player beat 'em up with original art, music and an announcer who shouts everyone's name.I must admit I never tested this with Opus 5.5, so I'm not sure whether this was possible before Fable 5.2 rolled around. Still, whether it's thanks to this generation or the last, this is a pretty wild milestone. Claude Code with Fable 5.2 is capable of making entire 12-level games - in one shot.

item.title: TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max
item.author: _benx_
item.content:encoded: While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads.The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements, our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry.Building the computer around the chipToday, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system.Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases.When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer, so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.2 scores 65 on Artificial Analysis, highest so far
item.author: theanonymousone
item.content:encoded: Claude Fable 5.2 (Max, Default Fallback) is amongst the leading models in intelligence, but particularly expensive when comparing to other models of similar price. It's also notably slow per task and very verbose. The model supports text and image input, outputs text, and has a 1M tokens context window.Claude Fable 5.2 (Max, Default Fallback) scores 65 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it well above average among comparable models (median: 40). When evaluating the Intelligence Index, it generated 275M tokens, which is very verbose in comparison to the median of 72.8M.Pricing for Claude Fable 5.2 (Max, Default Fallback) is $8.00 per 1M input tokens (expensive, median: $2.00) and $40.00 per 1M output tokens (expensive, median: $10.00). On average, it costs $26.54 per task to evaluate Claude Fable 5.2 (Max, Default Fallback) on the Intelligence Index.At 48.0 minutes per Intelligence Index task, Claude Fable 5.2 (Max, Default Fallback) is notably slow compared with the median of 12.7 minutes for comparable models (lower is better).

item.title: USPS now offers official ZIP Code boundary polygons
item.author: munro
item.content:encoded: USPS® ZIP Code BoundariesUSPS® ZIP Code Boundaries is a national ZIP Code™ map utilizing USPS delivery address and location information to ensure accurate boundaries. Temporal fluctuation is based on changing delivery distribution for new or changed delivery locations. Many industries, such as mapping, mailing, marketing, insurance, real estate, logistics, navigation, and transportation can benefit from access to the ZIP Code boundary data.As the ground truth for ZIP Code boundaries, users can incorporate these polygons as joint features or correct existing ZIP Code data as changes are made.As a tool for organizing and displaying demographic data, ZIP Codes serve as a support structure for real estate and insurance industries.ZIP Codes can serve as a proxy for the delivery location groupings for optimized routing.

item.title: Parking-app convenience fees in 312 U.S. cities (median $0.35 per session)
item.author: parkgraph
item.content:encoded: Park Graph collected the per-session fee a driver pays to start a parking session by app in each U.S. place where an app company or the city publishes it: ParkMobile, PayByPhone, Passport, Flowbird, Park Smarter and city-branded apps run by those companies. Sources are the app companies' own help pages and official city pages. Where a company page and a city page disagree, the CSV's fee_notes column says so.A place with no published fee keeps its row, shown here as Not published. Membership plans the app companies offer, and their prices, are in the CSV's membership columns. Every row was checked onNov 5, 2026.
