item.title: I saw your HN comment
item.author: joshstrange
item.content:encoded: I used to love getting emails from people in response to things I’ve written online, blog posts or Hacker News comments, but in the last 2 years it’s changed from mostly signal to mostly noise. I’ve met people in real life as a result of these emails, I’ve hired people based on these emails, and I’ve learned cool things through these emails but today it’s almost all pitches. I (had Claude) look through all the emails I’ve gotten about my posts and comments since 2013 to check my gut feeling:LLMs have made this much easier, they can write convincing emails personalized to a real comment I wrote on HN. What’s worse is that they are often very deceptive. They don’t come out and say they are pitching you something, they ask a question, posing as if they care about the answer. Something like:Hi Josh, saw your HN comment about [thing you said]. [Compliment.] I’m curious, [open-ended question]?If someone took the time to email me asking a question I almost always respond to it but I’m having to rethink that policy. It’s like having an amplification attack pointed at you, someone sends 2-3 sentences (sometimes more) with an open-ended question then I turn around and write 2-3+ paragraphs to answer the question, only to get a response that is pitching a product/service. Here are a few real pivots I’ve received:“That’s close to what I’m building…”“The tool I mentioned, [product], works from the other end…”“Worth saying this is what we build at [company], so I’m not a neutral party.”“Would you have 15 min next week?”It saddens me that what was once a rare joy and way to meet interesting people is now being abused to send cold emails. Look, I get it, cold emails are a fact of life, I’ve sent them before as well, but the deceptive ones are where I draw the line. I would never waste someone’s time without being upfront about why I’m contacting them. Personally I find this “growth hacking” to be disgusting and I will never use a product advertised to me in this way.Because these people are obscuring the real reason, it’s impossible to tell what is a real question and what is just a setup to pitch. I resent having to read every one of these emails as a potential pitch, but I also try not to assume the worst about everyone that reaches out. I wouldn’t want to snub someone because I thought they were going to pitch to me when they had a legitimate question or just wanted to talk. I’ve started sending short emails back and only if I don’t get a pitch back do I actually engage but I dislike feeling distrustful, treating people as guilty until proven innocent. I love talking about tech, I love talking to other people about cool things they are doing, I hate being advertised to and I hate it even more when it’s wrapped up in fake interest.I know there is nothing HN can do about this, it’s not their fault, I publicly post my email address on my profile, that’s on me. In the past it’s led to serendipity, now it more often leads to frustration.My comments used to introduce me to interesting people, now they’re mostly LLM context for a sales pitch, grist for the mill. The internet I pine for might not be coming back, but I can’t bring myself to take my email address down. I’ll keep separating the wheat from the chaff. But I’ll be grumpy about it.

item.title: Taking another shot at the cheap IP camera, part 2
item.author: ericswpark
item.content:encoded: About a year ago, I ranted about this particular cheap IP camera that was based on some proprietary Chinese IoT platform named Tuya. After trying and failing to get a local video stream from it without going through their servers, I concluded that my time would be better served by using cameras that actually exposed their streaming capabilities, and set it aside.Well, I recently dug the camera out while moving to my new job in New Jersey, and thought it might be worthwhile to give it another shot. I had plenty of spare time, and if I couldn’t figure it out, LLMs are recently all the rage for being really great at reverse-engineering things. But my initial goal was, I’d attempt it myself first, and then hand it off to an LLM if I failed and try and learn something from what it had figured out.So what’s our goal, exactly? We know from last time that the camera has some sort of ONVIF server built in. That’s basically a standardized interface for IP cameras, defined by the Open Network Vision Interface Forum (or ONVIF!) And most ONVIF cameras expose their video streams using RTSP, or the Real-Time Streaming Protocol. You may have come across this protocol if you’ve ever streamed to a live-streaming platform like YouTube or Twitch.The problem is that these servers are disabled on the firmware side, and their ports are closed off. Last time, we tried to enable them using the configuration options, but that didn’t work. Now, it’s time to figure out why that failed, and if there’s truly a way to enable those streams.So with that in mind, let’s first extract the firmware image with :CRC32 polynomial table, little endianuImage firmware image, header size: 64 bytes, data size: 2803328 bytes, compression: none, CPU: ARM, OS: Linux, image type: OS, Kernel Image, load address: 0x81C08000, entry point: 0x81C08040, creation time: 2021-06-21 03:03:42, image name: “Linux-3.4.35”CramFS filesystem, little endian, 3 files, total size: 3248128 bytesJFFS2 filesystem, little endian, nodes: 256, total size: 648000 bytesOK, so it runs Linux 3.4.35. When was that released again? March 2013. A 13-year old kernel! (I guess it was only 8-years old when they compiled it.)Last time, we found the Tuya configuration file with the ONVIF config at ./extractions/cctv.bin.extracted/760CCC/jffs2-root/tuya_config.json. I think the reason it might not have worked is because we edited the firmware image itself with a hex editor, and doing so probably corrupted some checksum.But, we have the image extraction, so why not trace where the config option is being used? Perhaps the binary doesn’t even use that option at all.So what binary is launched? We should look at the initialization script of the camera at .\extractions\cctv.bin.extracted\370000\initrun.sh. That script extracts some app tarball, then runs the script at , which in turn runs the other init scripts inside .Most of the scripts are like, setting up the kernel parameters regarding memory and networking and DHCP and what not, so we’ll skip past all that. The important bit is the last script, which is , which runs in .One command and we find extractions\cctv.bin.extracted\370000\app.tar.gz.extracted\0\decompressed.bin.extracted\0\home\app\ppsapp. And tells us it has ONVIF stuff in it:OK, but is there some reference to the ONVIF streaming within the binary itself?OK, that’s good! We now know the ONVIF streaming URL format, though we still need to know what port it runs on.So let’s throw the binary itself into Ghidra and run the analyzer. Looking through the strings, a lot of the hardcoded paths reference /var/lib/jenkins/workspace/, so whoever built this image probably did so with a Jenkins pipeline. Does it really matter for what we’re doing? No, but I thought it was interesting. They probably have a Jenkins workflow for each camera SKU they push out the door, although I’m sure they use it only once, considering that support is an afterthought.The binary itself is 2.4 MB, and I’m not that familiar with reading ARM assembly, but we don’t have to, just yet! We just need to look around for the onvif part since we know the config string there.On Ghidra, strings can be found by going to “Search -> For Strings…”. After you select the options the string search window shows up. Luckily for me, filtering for shows only two places where they are used:…yeah, that’s not very fun to read. But we can figure out several things just from reasoning it out.For starters, when we open the configuration file , notice the first function’s call is with , and the second parameter being . Whereas with the second function, the same call is at the end of the function with . This tells us that the first function is a config reader and the second function is a config writer!OK, and there’s a bunch of calls to a function named . What is that?OK, what is then?Hm, a bit of renaming later, and:Oh, this is just ! I’m going to call it because it does null checks unlike the one. Back up a layer, a bit of renaming, and we get:OK, so this function is just looking for the specific configuration key-value pair from the given configuration data, and it does this by iterating through some array/linked-list structure. Since we have the overall idea on how this function works we just rename it to and go up a layer.What is , then?Yeesh. I have no idea what those constants and magic numbers are. But maybe an LLM will. And it does!This function converts an IEEE 754 double-precision floating-point number into a signed 32-bit integer.Oh, okay, so it’s literally to but in decompiled C. That was helpful.So now we look at the calls again:That is much better to look at! So all that was just reading the ONVIF key-value pairs from the configuration file. Now we need to check where is used, but I’m going to rename that as .Searching for references to brings up 10 locations:But, we can focus on the context only since that is probably where the binary checks the config before enabling ONVIF functionality. Filter out the reference in the function earlier, and we’re left with two callsites:Right off the bat, because of the call to in function , we know that this is the function that is called when the ONVIF functionality is changed while the camera is running. The first function, , is a bit more interesting. Let’s look at what it’s calling:Strangely, there are two data locations where the ONVIF flag is set, so we’ll map it to: -> -> Unfortunately, I hit a wall here, because both of those variables got passed around a bunch of functions that kept updating different variables.I also want to check out the string “Starting onvif server on port %s” since my (rather uneducated) guess is that’s where the ONVIF server is started. (God my brain actually works sometimes)Oh great, so it runs on port ! And by referencing the variables from earlier, we can guesstimate that there aren’t any additional checks to enable ONVIF. Here’s the final disassembly I got to:OK, cool. So how do we actually edit the configuration file, then repack it in a way that the camera will actually accept it?Well, we know that the configuration file is at ./extractions/cctv.bin.extracted/760CCC/jffs2-root/tuya_config.json, so instead of doing the dumb thing from last time where we tried to hex-edit the raw firmware image, maybe we can edit the file and re-pack a JFFS2 partition image.But why didn’t the hex-edit work? Well, JFFS2 is a special filesystem that is log-structured, and it’s designed for flash memory devices. I guess it’s sorta like F2FS, which is another filesystem designed for flash memory devices, but unlike its usage on Android devices JFFS2 is designed for flash memory that doesn’t have a wear-leveling mechanism on the hardware side. TL;DR: Flash chips and SSDs have flash cells. Flash cells have a limited lifespan and don’t like it when you write to them repeatedly. Wear-leveling mechanisms thus try and make sure writes are evenly distributed across flash cells to prolong their lifespan.Because flash memory can only be addressed in terms of blocks, and because JFFS2 has to handle the wear-leveling mechanism in software, you can’t just overwrite the old block when you change one byte in it (in this case the config option), because you’re then writing to that same spot in memory. JFFS2 thus writes another block to the flash memory with a higher version number.Now, I don’t remember if I changed all of the occurrences of last time or not, but it doesn’t really matter. If a given block is bad, JFFS2 will go back to the older block with a lower version number. And if I did change all the blocks and corrupted them, I’m assuming the binary then fell back to sane system defaults, which was probably why I got the chime during boot.We can actually grep for the block occurrences in the image:OK, OK, all that failure analysis is fun and good, but I need a working camera by the end of this blog post. Back to making our own JFFS2 image.Then we edit to in jffs2-root_modified/tuya_config.json.Finally, repack the JFFS2 image. When we issue the call, we need to keep in mind that the file should be in little-endian (because of the Anyka AK3918), and the erase block size is 4 KB (0x1000), and the image size is 640 KB (0xA0000), since the entire firmware image is 0x800000 and the JFFS2 image starts at 0x760000. Since the original image was -able, we also do not want any compression.Unfortunately, this causes the following warning to be printed:That’s a problem for us, because the original image used an erase block size of 4 KB. Looking through the Linux mailing lists, I came across this thread where someone already tried to patch to get rid of the size check, and it worked fine.But that’s really strange, because I got curious as to when the check was added, and found that it was there since the utility was first created. Going through the Git history and blame for , it seems like the check was there ever since the initial commit, which was made in April of 2006.It seemed strange that Tuya would go out of their way to change this value down to by themselves, but after researching it a bit more I came across a patch in the official OpenWrt repository. They also patch the size check down to , so I guess it is common for embedded systems!At any rate, we can do the same thing ourselves:Then download this patch and apply it:Now we can build :Now we can go back out and use the new binary to create the image:And inject it back into the original firmware image:Yay, so we just need to flash this new image. Grab the CH341A, flash it with , connect it to the Wi-Fi, and…OK, that’s annoying. Turns out, the function that enables the ONVIF server isn’t referenced anywhere, according to Ghidra anyway. Nor is the function that sets up the RTSP streams.Perhaps I was reversing code that never gets called.But hey, we can flash whatever we want to this device, right? Let’s try running by editing the initialization step../extractions/cctv.bin.extracted/370000/initrun.sh:And inject it back into the firmware image:Turns out, the binary built into the camera doesn’t have .At this point, I decided to search online if had ever come across this camera. Surely, Tuya was a massive ecosystem of products and there must’ve been who did this before I did.So if you are reading this, thanks @guino.Going back to the binary, I decided to do exactly what he did and just patch all the calls that have to do with to . But I also decided, just for fun, to just patch out all the checks for the variable and make sure it would always unconditionally launch the ONVIF server. It really is satisfying when all the instructions get turned away into s.Now, packaging this back into the original firmware is even more annoying than it already is, because is within , which is again within the CramFS partition, which is then within the original firmware. So I guess I have to package it three times now.(We’ll assume I’ve already copied the modified binary to the directory listed below…)Unfortunately, after flashing this image, the camera became unhappy and wouldn’t connect to the Wi-Fi anymore, and the blue LED would continuously blink, a change from the usual solid indicator.I spent several weeks (yes, weeks!) banging my head against the wall, doing all kinds of detours. I found a bunch of UART pads on the board itself and decided it might be worthwhile to hook up a serial monitor to it. I grabbed an Arduino I had lying around and hooked it up, but nothing got printed to the console.On a hunch, I pulled out my multimeter and my heart dropped when I read 3.3V on the pads. The Arduino Uno ran at 5V. Thankfully, I hadn’t fried the board, because I got a USB logic analyzer to determine whether the pads were UART pads at all. And yes, they were UART pads, as evidenced by PulseView:So I bought a proper USB-to-TTL adapter that could do multiple voltage levels. My hope was that something in the boot output would tell me why the initialization was failing.…yeah, that’s me using the screw and pad as a ground because the last pad that is ground refused to wick up solder. Thank god it was that pad and not the TX/RX ones.However, when I booted up the camera, my hopes were dashed. After the following printout, it just… stopped.I tried power-cycling the camera and pressing Enter, to be greeted with a password prompt:Hm. What can I do here, really?I tried a couple of password guesses, but they were all wrong, and each time, the board would reset and start over.I thought about going through the U-Boot region on the firmware extraction and trying to piece together how the password was compared and where it was stored on memory. But I realized that part wasn’t that interesting to me, so I decided to try giving it to an LLM.Claude immediately refused:It’d be really funny if the AI bubble popped because the companies are being responsible, puritan, and hoity-toity about how you use their models.Fine. If the US won’t help me, China will. I filed a refund request for the Claude subscription which had lasted all but 40 seconds, then went on OpenRouter, created an account, loaded up some credits, then made an API key. I then connected it to OpenCode, selected Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017, and then told it where I had the firmware binary file, and the specific password string that U-Boot spat out.After about 3 minutes of searching, it didn’t disappoint:Yes — it’s in the firmware dump.U-Boot password: I tried it, and it worked. I was in the U-Boot environment!OK, but this feels like cheating. I’ll admit, it kinda is. I was curious as to what learning opportunity I missed out by giving this task to the LLM, so I expanded the “thinking” portion to see what it had done to get to that output:The auth routine is at ; it prints and compares your input with a string at (file offset ).That string isn’t stored as plaintext — it’s obfuscated with a bitwise NOT. Raw bytes: 8f 8f 8c a0 8f 9e 8c 8c 88 90 8d 9b ffInverted gives: OK, maybe I could’ve gotten this, but maybe not? I don’t know if I would’ve gotten the obfuscation part without a lot more head-meet-table sessions. But personally, that part is not that interesting to me. What is interesting is getting this damn camera to talk to me.After another LLM prompt, Deepseek told me to append ignore_loglevel printk.time=1 ppsdebug=onshow to the kernel boot arguments, so that the binary would give me more log output. OK, sure!(Keep in mind that appends a bunch more parameters after the line, like the partition layout of the flash memory. You need to copy those and append them to after . I actually had to remove the parameter entirely, because U-Boot complained about the command being too long.)And now we got a lot more log output. I looked at the lines where it was doing the Wi-Fi authentication:Remember when I issued the following command to repack the last image?Guess what folders there are when I do an ?Yeah… oops. Let’s pretend that never happened and try again.After flashing the new firmware image, we finally got somewhere! The camera showed back up on the WiFi network, and a network scan showed port was open, for the ONVIF server. I tried the credentials as @guino documented, but I got no response back from the server.Searching online, I found that Tuya cameras basically stop working if you block access to their SDK servers. And indeed, I’d blocked them from ever contacting the outside world.I decided to ask Deepseek once more to see if it could figure out where in the binary it was doing the online connectivity check. It found the following offsets:I tried to make sense of why these patches were important by looking at the disassembly on Ghidra. The first one was for the ONVIF server, and the decompile in Ghidra showed that it was the function body of function . With the patch, it removed the block in the decompiled code, which I guess was the part that ran whenever it couldn’t reach the Tuya servers.The other two patches were interesting. It basically turned the entire body of function into:I guess if I learned anything from this, it’s that ARM’s equivalent to x86_64’s is .If you’re interested in what the LLM had to say about how the connectivity check worked, you could click below to open up the transcript:After repackaging and building the modified firmware image again, I flashed it, and got promising results from :And when I checked the RTSP stream…I learned a attempting this. But at the same time, the ending might not be quite so satisfying.On one hand, it feels like I used LLMs as a crutch, because I’m not yet skilled at reading ARM assembly and actually going through the motions of reverse engineering binaries by hand through Ghidra.On the other hand, I still learned a lot by actually going through the motions of decompressing, searching, soldering, packaging, compressing, flashing, and the large amount of research and time that went into this. I actually started this blog post in the second week of September! Even though I was quite busy with work at the same time, the roughly two months of work didn’t seem wasteful.I also think that it’s cool that LLMs are making this more accessible, and even though it brings the temptation where you just offload everything to it and have it do all the patching and re-compressing for you to have a perfect working binary firmware image at the end (because yes, I’m sure it could definitely do that now), making sure that you do that and go through the intermediary steps that you know how to do yourself really helps.Also, for those that are curious: the total cost of running the Deepseek model on OpenRouter was 22 cents. Yes, . You don’t need an expensive subscription or sell your soul to Altman or Amodei.Would I try this again? Not for this particular class of camera. As I said in the previous post, this was basically an e-waste camera that a relative of mine gave me for free, and we all know by now to not buy any crap from Tuya. And again, good cameras that don’t pull this bullshit are cheap! I did this just because I wanted to see if I could.

item.title: Semi-transparent, colored cadmium telluride photovoltaic panels in agrivoltaics
item.author: speckx
item.content:encoded: Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them.A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels—without sacrificing the harvest.But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses.A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land.In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity.Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants.The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower.This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. It suggests that for now, the future of agrivoltaics might be best seen through rose-colored glasses.Image: Broccoli growing beneath semi-transparent, colored solar panels at the experimental site at Kärrbo Prästgård farm in Sweden. ©Silvia Ma Lu

item.title: Try Gleam
item.author: nchagnet
item.content:encoded: If you have read my recent rant about programming languages, you'll know I've been quite interested in Gleam. Gleam is a functional language that targets BEAM, the Erlang VM, with a simple syntax and interoperability with the wider BEAM ecosystem (Erlang and Elixir). Interestingly, Gleam can target JavaScript i.e., Gleam can be compiled into JavaScript and run through Node.js.I've been mostly using Rust for hobby projects, which at the moment is the only language that really makes coding enjoyable for me, and Gleam has managed to scratch that itch too. If you're a Rust , then Gleam will feel familiar to you, bar a few key differences. I feel like 80% of the code I write could be copy pasted to Rust (with a tinge of search-and-replace for syntax) and it'd compile.This post won't give an exhaustive overview of the language, if you want to learn more, I recommend the excellent interactive tour. You'll get a good feel for Gleam in under half an hour.On its homepage, Gleam is described as "a language for building systems that !" (emphasis theirs) which does a good job of conveying what Gleam is all about.The syntax is extremely simple, most of the complex stuff is hidden by the Erlang runtime which you don't really have to interact with unless you want to! Of course, Gleam is a functional language, so if you have lived in a C-shaped imperative world your whole life, it might be a bit daunting at first. But if you compare it to other functional languages (OCaml, Haskell, Erlang), you'll quickly notice Gleam is much simpler. After using it a bit, it feels like all the functional parts of Rust, with a few missing ones, and none of the imperative parts.Let's start from an example piece of code:Dissecting this a bit, you can see a few specificities of Gleam:variables in Gleam are (so no keyword or anything like that), chained functions here all return a new element. You can still a binding with a new , which is how you "update" a value. (typed ) is the pipe operator used to chain functions on data. The main constraint is that the piped variable should be the first argument of the function in the pipe.just like Rust, errors in Gleam are just values as part of the monad.Comparing with the Rust code snippet, you can see that, up to a few naming choices, they look pretty similar. The main difference in this example is really the piping vs. chaining syntax. Gleam types have no methods so piping is used instead.The piping operator is the first of the three mascot features of Gleam you will meet in this post, the other two being the pattern and tail-call optimization.If you've written a lot of JavaScript, you might be used to the indentation creep that arises when nesting many callbacks into one anotherIn Gleam, many functions expect a callback, for example because as a way to control access to a resource and clean up when the process is done (closing a database connection, releasing a file handle, etc.). To avoid this kind of tower of callbacks, Gleam provides some syntactic sugar: use param <- some_func(arg) is equivalent to some_func(arg, fn(param) { ... }). The callback must always be the argument of the function. That is the opposite of , which fills the first one.This one might genuinely trip you up if you're not familiar with it. The first thing you need to know is there are no loops in Gleam! Again, if you've written OCaml or Haskell before, you won't be surprised by this. In 98% of cases, loops are simple operations over bounded iterations. Think loops on a list or a set. Exactly the kind of thing which in Rust you always have two ways of doing: one imperative with the exact loop, one more functional with a combination of operations on iterators. Well, if you look at the code example in the previous section, you'll see Gleam uses the second kind and has a plethora of functions to iterate over lists, sets, tuples, strings, anything.But what if you need something more complicated? What about the 2%? This is where you would instead use ! A simple algorithm which illustrates this is Euclid's algorithm to compute the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD). Below you can find a Rust iterative example, and a Gleam recursive example.Of course, you can also write the recursive version in Rust, but this usually isn't such a great idea. Recursion in imperative languages can quickly get out of hand: every call adds a new stack frame, and a deeply recursive function can blow the stack (the infamous ).On the BEAM there is no fixed-size stack, so runaway recursion eats heap memory until the process is killed instead, but the point remains: deep recursions equals trouble. To avoid that problem, compilers for functional languages implement a technique called Tail Call Optimization (TCO), which applies when the recursive call is the last thing the function does. The existing stack frame is then reused instead of stacking a new one, giving performance close to an imperative loop.This piece of the slogan is mostly there to answer the obvious question "why Gleam and not Elixir?" (another Erlang-based language). While Elixir is a dynamically-typed language (with gradual typing now!), Gleam was as a statically-typed language with a strong type system: strong types are its .A in Gleam encompasses both the and the concepts in Rust:Because Gleam types are algebraic data types, they are very useful to ensure undesired states are impossible. A great aspect of Gleam, which will be relevant a little bit later, is that it compiles to the BEAM virtual machine to JavaScript. So you can share these strong type definitions across different applications in both targets. This is particularly handy if you need a web application to communicate with a BEAM app.Gleam is made for systems that scaleThat, of course, refers to BEAM, the Erlang VM. Unlike languages which target the native system (Rust, Go, C++), a VM provides an extra abstraction layer between the system and the program. In the case of BEAM, that layer is exceptionally good at handling concurrent processes and failures while remaining fast.Gleam makes good use of that, and this is what a concurrent program would look like:What you should take away from this code is that it's the BEAM that handles processes.The call to triggers a new process with no link to its creator, so when order 102 crashes, neither the parent nor siblings are affected. With a plain the child would be linked to the caller, and that would have taken the whole program down. If you look closely, I also added so the parent wouldn't close the children could finish: this is a hack, since the delay is only a guess and a slower child would still be cut off.Thankfully, a great advantage of the BEAM is how easy inter-process communication is, which the following code piece illustrates well:OTP: the gift that keeps on givingIn the paragraph above, I briefly showed how the BEAM virtual machine is great for concurrent programs communicating by message passing. If you're familiar with Go, this is similar to how it handles the same problem with . But the OTP (Open Telecom Platform), the set of libraries that ships with Erlang, is more powerful than that. It provides you with a built-in supervisor-actor paradigm which enables you to create scalable, concurrent services which can crash without taking down the whole application.In a nutshell, the OTP exposes : lightweight processes that hold state and communicate with each other via messages (like in the example above). When paired with a , the whole application becomes more resilient to any individual actor crashing: the supervisor will monitor processes and restart them as needed. It can also help start/stop groups of actors dynamically.If you're reading this and thinking "uh that sounds a lot like how I used Kubernetes", you're not alone. The OTP model is extremely similar to the controller-pod architecture of Kubernetes and solves a lot of the same problems. However, in my experience, of workflows using Kubernetes don't really need a cluster but still use one (and that's expensive!) because of the added bonus of the distributive experience. For those cases, the OTP provides a really interesting alternative.Let me give you a concrete example. Without going in too much detail, we have a common setup in my team which involves a handwritten Go job scheduler handling some other processes.The scheduler, each worker, and the user interface are all pods inside the cluster, managed by Kubernetes. To be honest, this works well, but it does introduce a lot of complexity. First of all, most of these services do not need to be so isolated from each other. The consequence here is that we need duplicate REST APIs in various places to enable communication between different services.What if we wanted to reorganize this within a Gleam application? There are two parts where Gleam would shine here:the OTP would essentially unify all scheduling services as actors within a single application,the user interface (currently a Node.js app) can be written in Gleam and compiled to JavaScript.Here is the revised architecture:Within the BEAM application, all actors would communicate via messages:the HTTP server receives requests and saves them to the DB,the workers would pick up jobs and write the status back to the DB.So instead of handling the deployment of multiple applications in separate pods, you can just let the OTP handle all process management within one VM (for the scheduling part).What does it mean to reuse code between the frontend and the backend?As mentioned before, one of the big advantages of Gleam is that it compiles to JavaScript. So you can bundle shared type definitions between the user interface and the job scheduler instead of keeping duplicate APIs in sync.Every language has its flaws, and it's time for some honest feedback on Gleam. I don't pretend I have much experience with the language yet, so if any of these complaints feel unfair to you, feel free to correct me. So far, these are the things I noticed:the ecosystem is small. This is not Gleam's fault per se, just a consequence of being a young language, and there are mitigating factors such as the possibility to use functions quite easily (Erlang, Elixir on BEAM, JavaScript on its own runtime) directly from Gleam. Yet, the community itself favours Gleam-first packages and as of today, there are some gaps in package variety.The language is . Well, to be honest I don't per se with this, I like it like this. But I totally understand that the lack of macros or other complex features can put a few people off (for example, I read that currying is dearly missed).The BEAM virtual machine is an target, but it's also a peculiarity. I couldn't really name any big company/system using it. Yet, a quick search shows that WhatsApp, Discord and Pinterest, as well as Cisco, Nintendo, and even the NHS rely on it. Erlang and BEAM are quietly powering huge platforms due to their reliability, but it's not as flashy as "Made in Rust" marketing. Where Rust had Mozilla, Go had Google and Java had Oracle, there isn't a big tech player pushing for Gleam/Erlang right now.Of course this is a very biased account. I think I'm missing a lot of flaws in the language itself, flaws that will show themselves once the honeymoon period is over. But for now, I'm having a blast with Gleam, and I can only encourage you to give it a try too! I'm sure just like me, you'll have a lot of fun!

item.title: What is malloc doing, anyway?
item.author: benmandrew
item.content:encoded: has a very nice and simple interface: you ask for a certain amount of memory, and you’re given a pointer to your block of contiguous bytes that’s been magicked into existence. Once you’re done with it, you call with the same pointer and the memory disappears into the ether.But what’s actually happening here? Obviously, as we’re running as a userspace program, must be asking the kernel for the memory through . However, we may be allocating many small blocks, and syscalls are expensive (575 ns for an empty one, as measured below), so some bookkeeping is done in the background. We’ll demonstrate this on GNU () with the program snippet below, which calls a thousand times.ptrs i i i ptrsiUsing , we can see that the whole loop makes only two syscalls: the first asks where the is (the address where the process’s heap ends), and the second grows the heap by 132 KiB. These are both done in the first call — the other 999 just take from that already allocated memory.You may see both and mentioned in discussions. is a syscall that sets the program break to the address it is provided, and is a convenience wrapper that takes a , increasing the program break by that amount.A running process gets its own , split into a number of regions. These include for executable code, for initialised global variables, and for uninitialised global variables, among others. The following program prints one address from each region of the process. maininitialiseduninitialised printflocalThe addresses rise from the binary’s code up to its stack.Some of these regions can change as the program runs. For example, grows the heap and moves the break up. Note that in this run, the break and in are 23.4 TiB apart, about 1,530 times the machine’s 15.6 GiB of RAM. Nearly all of that range is unmapped, so it costs no physical memory.Because we can move the program break directly, we can write a little allocator of our own. This is called a allocator, because each call simply bumps up the amount of memory that we are allowed to use. sizep size p pptrptrThis allocator is not very good! It moves the break on every single request, and each move is a syscall. We can time a syscall against to see why requests large blocks from the kernel and cuts them up itself. Each of the following three functions is timed over a million calls. sinkSYS_getppid sink sink costs only 35 ns more than the empty syscall, whereas runs 22.7 times faster than .The bump allocator also has no way to reuse freed memory. Each request lands straight after the one before, so in the following example, goes after even though has been freed.The rest of the post improves the allocator one stage at a time. actually allocates more memory than you request. This is because each allocation, or , has a size header just before the returned pointer; this is how works without passing an explicit size. Chunk sizes are always multiples of 16, so the low bits of the size are always zero, and keeps three flags in them. requests count requests requests i i count ip requestsi chunk p requestsi chunkEach chunk is the request plus 8 bytes for the header, rounded up to a multiple of 16, with a minimum of 32. The rounding keeps every pointer that returns 16-byte aligned, which is the alignment x86-64 gives , so the memory suits any C type. The 32-byte minimum leaves room for the list pointers that a chunk stores once it is freed.When we free a chunk, it is put into what’s called a to allow reuse. When more data is requested, looks through this free list and splits large chunks to fit small requests, and merges free neighbours back together. Each chunk in the free list needs two pieces of information: its size (which we already have), and a pointer to the next chunk in the free list. stores the pointer after the size, reusing the memory that the user stored their data in before it was freed!The toy allocator stores the same two fields in each chunk. sizenextWe can improve our by rounding the request plus its header up to a multiple of 16 bytes, and taking the first chunk in the free list that is big enough. To keep things simple, the toy’s header is the whole , so a chunk keeps room for even while it is in use. That makes the header 16 bytes where ’s is 8, and takes a 128-byte chunk where takes 112. size need size HEADER_SIZE ALIGNlink free_listlink link linknextlinksize needlink needneedsizeWe define to split that chunk, leaving whatever the request does not need in the free list.link needc linkcsize needrest c need restsize csize need restnext cnext csize needlink restlink cnextc HEADER_SIZEWhen no free chunk fits, moves the program break up in 64 KiB steps using and puts the new space on the free list as one chunk.With headers, we can now actually implement a proper function! It steps back from the pointer to the header and hands the chunk to . That function walks the list to find the free chunks either side of by address, and , and links in between them. Then, if ends where starts, or starts where ends, the two become one chunk.next c csize next csize nextsize cnext nextnextprev prev prevsize c prevsize csize prevnext cnextA test program allocates , and , frees and , allocates , then frees the rest.Each line shows the chunk that the call allocated, if any, and then the free list. Every chunk is an pair counted from the start of the heap, and the offset is where its header starts, 16 bytes before the pointer that returns. gets the chunk at offset 0, split from the 352-byte chunk that and merged into. The bump allocator put its fourth request after everything else. Freeing merges three chunks into one, and freeing leaves the single 64 KiB chunk that added. reuses memory, but it never returns any to the kernel. Whether a free chunk still costs RAM depends on when the kernel puts physical memory behind an address. Each process sees , which the kernel maps onto physical RAM in 4 KiB . That separation allows the kernel to hand out address ranges with no physical RAM behind them — a virtual page only needs to be backed by physical memory on its .The following program moves the break up by 1 GiB, then writes one byte to every page and prints a row after each 256 MiB.p SIZE offset offset SIZE offset PAGE_SIZE poffsetoffset PAGE_SIZESIZE offset PAGE_SIZEVirtual size counts the addresses the process has mapped, and (RSS) counts the pages that are in RAM. Straight after , virtual size is already just over 1 GiB, while RSS is 1308 KiB. Each 256 MiB written then costs 65,536 page faults, one per 4 KiB page, increasing the RSS.Once a chunk’s pages have been written, they stay resident after , until the allocator gives them back to the kernel.We give memory back to the kernel by the break. We introduce a new function, , that lowers the break once the free chunk at the top of the heap reaches 128 KiB, keeping 64 KiB so that the next few requests don’t move the break straight back up.top free_listtop topnext top topnextend top topsizeend topsize TRIM_THRESHOLD release topsize TOP_PAD PAGE_SIZE PAGE_SIZE topsize releasereleaseA test program allocates 1 MiB and then a 16-byte chunk above it, then writes to every page of the 1 MiB block. ( counts resident memory with no backing file, which keeps ’s code out of the numbers.)Freeing the 1 MiB block leaves the break at 1088 KiB and anonymous RSS at 1124 KiB, because the 16-byte chunk above it is still live. Once that chunk goes too, lowers the break to 64 KiB, dropping the anonymous RSS to 160 KiB.Only the top of the heap can be given back. A live chunk holds the break above it, so every free chunk below it stays resident, as the 1 MiB block did here. Over a long run, many allocations and deallocations leave free gaps between live chunks that later requests rarely fill, which is called . These gaps stay resident, so in a long-running program, fragmentation can grow RSS until a memory limit kills the process.The syscall usually maps a file into the address space. With the flag there is no backing file, and the kernel creates a zero-filled, page-aligned mapping anywhere in the address space. Like the heap, its resident pages count towards the anonymous RSS. The syscall returns a block with its own mapping to the kernel as soon as it is freed, whatever lies next to it.To integrate this into our own allocator, chooses between and by the size of the request. Any request of 128 KiB or more, header included, gets a mapping of its own from , rounded up to whole pages; smaller requests take the existing free list path. need len need PAGE_SIZEc len PROT_READ PROT_WRITE MAP_PRIVATE MAP_ANONYMOUSc MAP_FAILED csize len MMAPPEDc HEADER_SIZEFor ped chunks, we use one of the three flags in the size header (M) to record that this chunk has its own mapping. checks this bit to know how to free it. It unmaps a mapped chunk with , and puts any other chunk back on the free list, where can release it.ptrptr c ptr HEADER_SIZEcsize MMAPPEDc csize MMAPPEDcRunning the previous demo again, we see that freeing the 1 MiB block drops the anonymous RSS while the 16-byte chunk is still live.The following diagram shows how this might look in the address space.Why not everything? Some allocators do! Even creates extra heaps, called , with , and spreads threads across them so that they don’t all contend for the lock on the main heap. However, separate mappings have separate regions with no guarantee of contiguity, and chunks can’t be coalesced across these gaps. On the other hand, allocating with just bumps up the one contiguous region that you already have. A freed chunk that stays on the heap keeps its pages resident, so reusing it causes no page faults. Each new mapping starts with no physical memory behind it, and faults on every page it writes.We compare the performance of our allocators against ’s with a workload that repeatedly allocates and deallocates blocks of varying sizes. To measure the speed, we find the average time of a : free a random live block, allocate a replacement of random size, and write to each of its pages. At the end of the run, the live blocks hold 10.3 MiB. The last two columns give the anonymous RSS at that point, and again after every block is freed, which is the memory the allocator keeps. never frees or reuses memory, so its RSS is the 1425 MiB that the run allocates in total. Its 1.72 µs per step comes from an call for every request and page faults on new pages. reuses memory, so its RSS of 17.8 MiB is much closer to the 10.3 MiB of live data. However, each step walks the list twice: walks it to find a fit, and walks it to find the chunk’s neighbours. adds a third walk, because looks for the last free chunk on every . and run 65 and 142 times slower than respectively. In return, keeps only 0.188 MiB once every block is freed. calls for large requests, which raises its time per step to 11.8 µs but gives it the lowest RSS with blocks live, at 11.2 MiB.Why is so fast? The slowdowns in our allocators are due to having to walk a long free list of chunks multiple times. instead keeps free chunks in , separate lists by size, so a request can walk a list of appropriately sized chunks directly. It also keeps up to seven freed chunks of each small size in a thread-local cache (tcache) and hands them straight back to the next request of that size.The tcache also explains the last column, where keeps 19.0 MiB after every block is freed. The heap counts a cached chunk as in use, so one near the top stops from lowering the break. The environment variable can turn the tcache off with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_count=0, or fix the threshold at 128 KiB with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.mmap_threshold=131072.With the tcache off, freeing everything leaves 0.250 MiB, and each step takes 1.5 times as long as before. makes 51 calls in the whole run, against the 5040 that makes. Freeing a mapped chunk raises ’s threshold to that chunk’s size, so later large requests come from the heap. With the threshold fixed at 128 KiB, every large request pays for its syscalls and page faults again, and runs 10.7 times slower. spends memory to stay away from the kernel, parcelling out large blocks in userspace so that most calls never make a syscall.Reproducible snippets for each program (link).’s own description of its allocator’s internals, covering chunks, bins, arenas and the tcache (link).The man pages for and (link), (link), (link) and (link).

item.title: RIP, Harvest
item.author: zdw
item.content:encoded: I’ve been a self-employed contractor for about a decade now, and I’m bummed about Harvest.Harvest was a time-tracking and invoicing service. You’d track how many hours or weeks you spent on a project, put together an invoice, email it to the client, and close it out when they paid. There was a little Stripe integration for accepting credit and ACH payments on the invoice web view. A historical chart of total billed/paid amounts over time, and a table of invoices. Harvest was exactly what you want from small-business software: it solved a well-defined problem with a reliable, simple interface, and did so at a reasonable monthly price. They managed to avoid scope creep and never tried to become an accounting platform, or a blockchain for washing machines. I loved Harvest and raved about it to every self-employed person I met.Back in 2025 Harvest got bought out by Bending Spoons, the company that gutted Vimeo. I was worried they might ruin it, but was busy with other things and didn’t have time to look for new invoicing software.Long story short, they raised my price from $13.32 to $133.98 per month by moving everyone to a new “enterprise” plan and “unlimited” usage billing model, which is, as far as I can tell, exactly what I had before. There’s also a “flex” plan which costs $12.65 per month… but that plan now skims an additional 2% on top of the usual ~3% card transaction fees. To be clear, that 3% pays for the whole credit card network, plus all the people working at Stripe and Mastercard, plus the financial risk of chargebacks and fraud, etc. Harvest isn’t doing any of that work. I don’t know about you, but I don’t think I need to spend 2% of my gross revenue to send a couple PDFs a month and wrap a Stripe web form.I wrote to Harvest about this, and discovered that they don’t read customer emails any more. Instead they have a Large Language Model repeatedly vomit thousands of words at you. I’m no stranger to enshittification, but man, I did not anticipate the speed at which Bending Spoons would drive a perfectly good company into the ground.Time to find a new invoicing service, I guess. Maybe bookkeeping too—Intuit’s Quickbooks Online seems to have completely jumped the shark. Any of y’all freelancers have a system you like?
